The meaning is: when the believers heard the saying of the people of slander, they should have measured it against themselves. If such a thing is unlikely among them, it is even more unlikely concerning the Mother of the Believers.

al-Ḥasan said: The meaning of "among themselves" is "among the people of their religion," because the believers are like one soul. Do you not see His words: ﴿nor kill yourselves﴾? al-Zajjāj said: For this reason, people who kill one another are said to be killing themselves. al-Mubarrad said: Similar to this is His saying: ﴿so kill yourselves﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:54]. al-Naḥḥās said: "Among themselves" means "among their brothers." So God made it obligatory upon the Muslims, when they hear a man accuse someone and mention about him something ugly that they do not know of him, to deny it to him and declare him a liar.

The scholars said: The verse is evidence that the rank of faith and chastity is not removed by a report that is merely possible, even if it spreads. ﴿And they say, "This is a clear lie."﴾ That is, the believers said upon hearing the slander: "This is a manifest, evident lie."

The sentence ﴿Why did they not bring four witnesses for it?﴾ is part of what the believers say. That is: "Would that the slanderers had brought four witnesses to testify to what they said." (p-١٠٠٢) ﴿Since they did not bring the witnesses, those, in God's sight, are the liars﴾, that is, the slanderers, ﴿in the judgment of God, they are the liars, the complete liars.﴾

﴿And were it not for the bounty of God upon you and His mercy in this world and the Hereafter﴾. This is an address to the listeners, and it contains a great warning. "Were it not" (*lawlā*) here is the one indicating the non-occurrence of one thing because of the occurrence of another. ﴿Would have touched you for what you plunged into﴾, that is, because of what you engaged in of the account of the slander. One says: he poured forth (*afāḍa*) in speech, and rushed on, and plunged in (*khāḍa*).

The meaning: Were it not that I decreed for you bounty in this world through blessings, among which is respite, and mercy in the Hereafter through pardon, I would have hastened punishment upon you for what you plunged into of the account of the slander.

It has also been said that the meaning is: Were it not for God's bounty upon you, punishment would have touched you in this world and in the Hereafter together, but by His mercy He concealed it from you in this world, and He will show mercy in the Hereafter to whoever comes to Him repentant.

﴿When you were receiving it with your tongues﴾. The clause of time (*ẓarf*) is in the accusative, governed either by "touched you" or by "plunged." The majority read *idh talaqqawnahu* from *talaqqī* (receiving), the original being *tatalaqqawnahu*, and one of the two *tāʾ*s was dropped.

Mujāhid and Muqātil said: The meaning is that some of you narrate it from others.

al-Kalbī said: That is because a man among them meets another and says: "It has reached me that such-and-such," and they receive it from one another in a receiving manner.

al-Zajjāj said: Its meaning is that some of you cast it to others.

Muḥammad ibn al-Sumayfiʿ read *tulqawnahu* with a *ḍammah* on the *tāʾ*, a *sukūn* on the *lām*, and a *ḍammah* on the *qāf*, from *ilqāʾ* (casting). The meaning of this reading is clear.

Ubayy and Ibn Masʿūd read *tatalaqqawnahu* from *talaqqī*, and it is like the reading of the majority.

Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿĀʾishah, ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar, Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmur, and Zayd ibn ʿAlī read *talaqqawnahu* with a *fatḥah* on the *tāʾ*, a *kasrah* on the *lām*, and a *ḍammah* on the *qāf*. This reading is derived from the Arab saying *waliqa yalīqu waluqan*, meaning he lied.

Ibn Sīdah said: They used the transitive verb as evidence for the intransitive one.

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: In my view, he meant "they cast into it," so the preposition was dropped and the pronoun became attached.

al-Khalīl and Abū ʿAmr said: The origin of *walq* is haste. One says: "The camels came *talaqu*," that is, they hastened. From this is the saying of the poet:

*When they saw an army upon them that had come by night, they came with troops from Syria, hastening.*

Another said:

*Ṣ‘ Īs brought him from Syria, hastening.*

Abū al-Baqāʾ said: That is, they hasten in it. Ibn Jarīr said: This word, that is "*talqūnahu*" according to the last reading, is derived from *walq*, which is the hastening of a thing after another thing, like a number following a number, and speech following speech.

Zayd ibn Aslam and Abū Jaʿfar read *tālqūnahu* with a *fatḥah* on the *tāʾ*, a *hamzah* with *sukūn*, a *kasrah* on the *lām*, and a *ḍammah* on the *qāf*, from *alq*, which is lying. Yaʿqūb read *tīlqūnahu* with a *kasrah* on the *tāʾ* from above, followed by a *yāʾ* with *sukūn* below, a *fatḥah* on the *lām*, and a *ḍammah* on the *qāf*. It is the present tense of *waliqa* with a *kasrah* on the *lām*.

The meaning of ﴿and you say with your mouths what you have no knowledge of﴾ is that their saying is confined to the mouths without being actual in the external world or held in the hearts. It has also been said that the mention of the mouths is for emphasis, as in His saying: ﴿flying with its two wings﴾ [al-Anʿām 6:38] and similar.

The pronoun in ﴿you think it﴾ refers to the account into which they plunged and which they spread. ﴿And you think it trivial﴾, that is, a small matter on which no sin will fall upon you. The sentence ﴿and it is, in God's sight, grave﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning its sin and its punishment are great.

﴿And were it not, when you heard it, that you said, "It is not for us to speak of this"﴾. This is a rebuke to all the believers, meaning: "Why did you not, when you heard the account of the slander, say, denying it to those who plunged into it and fabricated it: 'It is not proper for us, nor is it possible for us, to speak of this account, and such a thing does not come from us in any way.'" The meaning of His words ﴿Glory be to You, this is a great calumny﴾ is an expression of wonder at those who brought the slander. Its origin is the declaration of God's transcendence, glorified is He, and then it became frequent until it was used for anything that is wondered at. *Buhtān* is saying of a person what is not in him. That is: "This is a great lie, because it was said about the Mother of the Believers, may Allah be pleased with her, and its occurrence is impossible under the Sharīʿah from one like her."

Then God, glorified is He, admonished those who plunged into the slander.

﴿God admonishes you never to return to the like of it﴾, that is, God advises you, or forbids you, or prohibits you out of dislike that you return, or from returning, or in returning to the like of this slander for the duration of your lives. ﴿If you are believers﴾, for faith requires that you do not fall into its like as long as you live. In this there is great incitement and profound reproach.

﴿And God makes clear to you the signs﴾ regarding commands and prohibitions, so that you may act upon them, adopt God's manners, and refrain from falling into His prohibitions. ﴿And God is Knowing﴾ of what you reveal and what you conceal, ﴿Wise﴾ in His arrangements for His creation.

Then God, glorified is He, threatened the slanderers and whoever wished to spread among people the faults and sins of the believers.

He said: ﴿Indeed, those who love that indecency should spread among those who believe﴾, that is, they love that indecency should spread and become widespread. It comes from the expression *shāʿa al-shayʾu yashīʿu shuyūʿan, shayʿan, and shayaʿānan*, meaning when a thing appears and spreads. The ones meant by "those who believe" are the chaste and the modest, or everyone who is characterized by the attribute of faith. *Al-fāḥishah* is the indecency of fornication and also evil speech. ﴿For them is a painful punishment in this world﴾, by the enforcement of the prescribed punishment upon them, ﴿and in the Hereafter﴾, by the punishment of the Fire. ﴿And God knows﴾ all that is knowable, ﴿and you do not know﴾ except what He has taught you and revealed to you. Among what God knows is the enormity of the sin of slander and the punishment of the one who commits it.

Then, were it not for Allah's bounty upon you and His mercy, [and that Allah is Most Kind, Most Merciful]. This repeats what came before, as a reminder of the favour from Him, glory be to Him, to His servants in delaying punishment for them. And from His kindness to His servants is that He does not hasten to punish them for their sins, and from His mercy to them is that He sends forth warnings and admonitions like this one. The clause "and that Allah is Most Kind, Most Merciful" is coordinated with "Allah's bounty." The answer to "were it not" (law la) is omitted, because what precedes it indicates it, meaning: "He would have hastened the punishment upon you."

﴿O you who have believed, do not follow the steps of Satan.﴾ The word khutuwat is the plural of khutwah, which is the distance between the two feet. Khatwah with a fatha is the verbal noun. The meaning is: do not follow Satan's paths and ways, and do not take the roads he calls you to.

The majority of reciters read khutuwat with a damma on the kha and the ta. ʿĀṣim and al-Akhfash read it with a damma on the kha and a sukun on the ta.

﴿And whoever follows the steps of Satan—indeed, he enjoins immorality and wrongdoing.﴾ It has been said that the response of the conditional clause is omitted and replaced by what serves as its cause, as if it were said: "Then he has committed immorality and wrongdoing, because his habit is to continue commanding others with them." Fahsha' is that whose ugliness is extreme, and munkar is that which the Sharia denounces. The pronoun in innahu refers to Satan. It has been said that it refers to the matter at hand, but the better view is that it refers back to "whoever follows the steps of Satan," because whoever follows Satan becomes his imitator in commanding immorality and wrongdoing.

﴿And were it not for Allah's bounty upon you and His mercy...﴾ Its explanation has already passed. Its answer is His saying: ﴿No one among you would ever have been purified, ever.﴾ That is, were it not for Allah's grace and mercy, no one among you would have purified himself from its defilement for as long as he lived.

The majority read zakā with light (takhfif) pronunciation. Al-A'mash, Ibn Muhaysin and Abu Ja'far read it with emphasis (tashdid), meaning: "Allah would not have purified him."

Muqatil said: that is, "would not have become righteous."

The better interpretation of zakā is "purification and cleansing," which is what Ibn Qutaybah mentioned.

Al-Kisa'i said: His saying "O you who have believed, do not follow the steps of Satan" is an interjection (mu'taridah), and His saying "No one among you would ever have been purified" is the answer to His earlier saying and to "And were it not for Allah's bounty."

The reading with light pronunciation is more preferred, because of His saying: ﴿But Allah purifies whom He wills.﴾ That is, of His servants, through His grace upon them and His mercy toward them. ﴿And Allah is All-Hearing﴾ of what they say, ﴿All-Knowing﴾ of all that is known. In this there is strong encouragement toward sincerity, a great incitement for His repentant servants, and a severe warning for whoever follows Satan and loves that immorality spread among the believing servants of Allah and does not restrain himself with Allah's prohibitions, glory be to Him.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, the authors of the Sunan and others have related the long hadith of ʿĀʾishah concerning the occasion of revelation of these verses, in multiple wordings and various chains.

Its summary is that the occasion of revelation was what occurred from the people of the slander (ahl al-ifk), whose mention has already passed, concerning ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her. That was because she went out from her howdah (litter) searching for a necklace of hers that had broken off out of anxiety. They set off while thinking she was in her howdah. She returned, and the army had already departed with the howdah among them. She remained in that place, and Safwan ibn al-Mu'attal passed by her; he had been lagging behind the army. He made his mount kneel, and he carried her onto it. When the people of the slander saw that, they said what they said, and Allah cleared her of what they had said.

This is the summary of the story, despite its length and the diversity of its branches, so we will not lengthen it by mentioning all of that.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ahmad, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, the authors of the four Sunan, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il have related from ʿĀʾishah, she said: "When my innocence was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood on the pulpit, mentioned that, and recited the Qur'an. When he descended, he ordered two men and a woman, and they were given their prescribed punishment (hadd)."

At-Tirmidhi said: this is a ḥasan (sound-good) hadith.

Abu Dawud's narration names them as Hassan ibn Thabit, Mistah ibn Uthathah, and Hamnah bint Jahsh.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir have related from Ibn ʿAbbas, he said: "Those who slandered ʿĀʾishah were ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, Mistah, Hassan, and Hamnah bint Jahsh."

Al-Bukhari, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il have related from al-Zuhri, he said: "I was with al-Walid ibn ʿAbd al-Malik, and he said: 'The one who took upon himself its greatest part among them was ʿAli.' I said: 'No. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr, ʿAlqamah ibn Waqqas, and ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUtbah ibn Mas'ud all told me, all of them having heard ʿĀʾishah say: "The one who took upon himself its greatest part among them was ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy."'" He said: "He said to me: 'Then what was his crime?' I said: 'Two shaykhs from your people told me, Abu Salamah ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAwf and Abu Bakr ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn al-Harith ibn Hisham, that they both heard ʿĀʾishah say: "He was wrongdoing in my matter."'"

Ya'qub ibn Shaybah said in his Musnad: al-Hasan ibn ʿAli al-Hulwani related to us, al-Shafi'i related to us, my paternal uncle related to us, he said: Sulayman ibn Yasar entered upon Hisham ibn ʿAbd al-Malik, and he said to him: "O Sulayman, the one who took upon himself its greatest part, who is he?" He said: "ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy." He said: "You lie; it is ʿAli." He said: "The Commander of the Faithful knows best what he says." Then al-Zuhri entered and he said: "O Ibn Shihab, who is the one who took upon himself its greatest part?" He said: "Ibn Ubayy." He said: "You lie; it is ʿAli." He said: "Am I lying? No father for you! By Allah, if a caller from heaven were to call out that Allah has made lying lawful, I would not lie. ʿUrwah, Sa'id, ʿAbd Allah and ʿAlqamah related to me from ʿĀʾishah that the one who took upon himself its greatest part was ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy."

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others have related from Masruq, he said: "Hassan ibn Thabit entered upon ʿĀʾishah and praised her (in verse) and said:

*Chaste, dignified, you are never suspected of doubt,*
*and you wake up empty-bellied of the flesh of the heedless.*

She said: 'But you are not like that.' I said: 'You claim that such a man enters upon you, when Allah has revealed: "And the one who took upon himself its greatest part among them has a great punishment"?' She said: 'And what punishment is more severe than blindness?'"

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn ʿAsakir have related from some of the Ansar that the wife of Abu Ayyub said to him when the people of the slander said what they said: "Do you not hear what people are saying about ʿĀʾishah?" He said: "Yes, and that is a lie. Would you have done such a thing, O Umm Ayyub?" She said: "No, by Allah." He said: "Then ʿĀʾishah, by Allah, is better and purer than you. This is only a lie and a baseless fabrication." Then, when the Qur'an was revealed, Allah mentioned those who spoke the immorality that the people of the slander had spoken.

Then He said: ﴿Why, when you heard it, did the believing men and believing women not think good of one another and say, "This is an obvious falsehood"?﴾ That is, as Abu Ayyub and his wife said.

Al-Waqidi, al-Hakim and Ibn ʿAsakir have related from Aflah, the freedman of Abu Ayyub, that Umm Ayyub... and he mentioned something similar.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh have related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ﴿Allah admonishes you never to return to the like of it, ever.﴾ He said: "Allah forbids you (yuharrij) from it."

Al-Bukhari in al-Adab and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman have related from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, he said: "The one who speaks the immorality and the one who spreads it are equal in sin."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim have related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: ﴿Not one among you would ever have been purified, ever.﴾ He said: "No creature would have been guided to any good at all."

(p-١٠٠١).
The predicate (khabar) of *inna* is, in His words ﴿Indeed, those who came with the slander﴾, "a band (ʿusbah) among you." "Among you" is a qualifier (ṣifah) of "a band." It has also been said that the predicate is ﴿do not consider it bad for you﴾, and that "a band" is a substitute (badal) for the subject of "came."

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: This is more coherent in meaning and more beneficial than taking the predicate to be "a band." The sentence ﴿do not consider it﴾, although it is in the imperative form (ṭalabiyyah), can be made a predicate by supposition (taqdir), as in similar cases. The *ifk* (slander) is the worst and most abominable of lies. It is derived from *afaka al-shayʾ*, meaning he turned the thing away from its true direction. Thus *ifk* is a reversed account. It has also been said that *ifk* is calumny (buhtān). The Muslims agreed that what is meant in the verse is the slander that was directed at ʿĀʾishah, the Mother of the Believers. God described it as *ifk* because what was well known of her condition, may Allah be pleased with her, was the opposite of it.

al-Wāḥidī said: The sense of "reversal" in this account, which those people brought, is that ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, deserved praise for her chastity, her noble lineage and her standing, not slander. Those who accused her with evil reversed the matter from its true direction. So it is a vile slander and a manifest lie.

The *ʿuṣbah* are a group from ten to forty. Here it refers to ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy, the leader of the hypocrites; Zayd ibn Rifāʿah; Ḥassān ibn Thābit; Misṭaḥ ibn Uthāthah; Ḥamnah bint Jaḥsh; and those who supported them. It has also been said that the *ʿuṣbah* are from three to ten, and it has been said from ten to fifteen. Its original linguistic sense is a group whose members support one another with partisan zeal (yataʿaṣṣabu baʿḍuhum li-baʿḍ).

As for the sentence ﴿do not consider it bad for you﴾: if it is the predicate of *inna*, the matter is clear. If the predicate is "a band," as was mentioned earlier, then it is a new (mustaʾnafah) sentence. It is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ), to ʿĀʾishah, and to Ṣafwān ibn al-Muʿaṭṭal, who was slandered along with the Mother of the Believers, as a consolation to them.

Evil (sharr) is that whose harm exceeds its benefit, and good (khayr) is that whose benefit exceeds its harm. As for the good in which there is no evil, it is Paradise, and the evil in which there is no good is the Fire. The reason it is good for them is that through it they obtain great reward, together with the clearing of the Mother of the Believers' name, and this story becomes a general law. ﴿For every man among them is what he earned of sin﴾, meaning because of his speaking the slander. ﴿And the one among them who took upon himself the greater part of it, for him is a great punishment﴾. Al-Ḥasan, al-Zuhrī, Abū Rajāʾ, Ḥumayd al-Aʿraj, Yaʿqūb, Ibn Abī ʿUlayyah, Mujāhid, and ʿAmrah bint ʿAbd al-Raḥmān read *kibrahu* with a *ḍammah* on the *kāf* (*kubrahu*). Al-Farrāʾ said: This is a good reading, because the Arabs say: "So-and-so took upon himself the great part (*ʿaẓīm*) of such-and-such," meaning the greatest part of it. The rest read it with a *kasrah* (*kibrahu*).

It has been said that the two are dialectal variants. It has also been said that with *ḍammah* it means the principal part of the slander, and with *kasrah* it means initiating it. It has also been said that with *kasrah* it means sin.

The meaning is: the one among the band who took upon himself the principal part of the slander has a great punishment, in this world, or in the Hereafter, or in both.

There is disagreement about who, among the band of slanderers, is meant by "the one who took upon himself the greater part." It has been said he is ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy; it has been said he is Ḥassān. The first is the sound view.

Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq and others narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) flogged two men and a woman for the slander: Misṭaḥ ibn Uthāthah, Ḥassān ibn Thābit, and Ḥamnah bint Jaḥsh.

It has been said that he flogged ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy, Ḥassān ibn Thābit, and Ḥamnah bint Jaḥsh, and did not flog Misṭaḥ, because he did not openly make the accusation but heard and spread it without explicit declaration. It has also been said that he flogged none of them.

al-Qurṭubī said: The well-known report, and what is known among the scholars, is that those who received the *ḥadd* (prescribed punishment) were Ḥassān, Misṭaḥ, and Ḥamnah. Nothing has been heard about a *ḥadd* for ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy. This is confirmed by what is in the Sunan of Abū Dāwūd from ʿĀʾishah, who said: When my innocence was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) stood up, mentioned that, and recited the Qur'an. When he came down from the pulpit, he ordered the two men and the woman, and they were punished with their *ḥadd*. He named them: Ḥassān, Misṭaḥ ibn Uthāthah, and Ḥamnah bint Jaḥsh.

They differed about the reason the Prophet (ﷺ) left ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy unpunished. It has been said that it was to保留 (leave for) the great punishment for him in the Hereafter, while the others were punished so that it would be an expiation (*takfīr*) for their sin, as was established from him (ﷺ) concerning *ḥudūd*, that he said: "It is an expiation for the one upon whom it is carried out." It has also been said that he left his punishment to win over his people and out of respect for his son, for he was among the righteous believers, and to extinguish the spark of strife, for its beginnings had already appeared from Saʿd ibn ʿUbādah and those with him, as in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim.

Then God, glorified is He, turned the address away from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and those with him toward the believers by way of *iltifāt* (shift of address). He said: ﴿Why, when you heard it, did the believing men and believing women not think good of one another and say, "This is a clear lie"?﴾ The word "why" (*lawlā*) here is the one of reproach (*taḥḍīḍiyyah*), a strong rebuke and an intensified reprimand. The meaning is: when the believers heard the saying of the people of slander, they should have measured it against themselves. If such a thing is unlikely among them, it is even more unlikely concerning the Mother of the Believers.

al-Ḥasan said: The meaning of "among themselves" is "among the people of their religion," because the believers are like one soul. Do you not see His words: ﴿nor kill yourselves﴾? al-Zajjāj said: For this reason, people who kill one another are said to be killing themselves. al-Mubarrad said: Similar to this is His saying: ﴿so kill yourselves﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:54]. al-Naḥḥās said: "Among themselves" means "among their brothers." So God made it obligatory upon the Muslims, when they hear a man accuse someone and mention about him something ugly that they do not know of him, to deny it to him and declare him a liar.

The scholars said: The verse is evidence that the rank of faith and chastity is not removed by a report that is merely possible, even if it spreads. ﴿And they say, "This is a clear lie."﴾ That is, the believers said upon hearing the slander: "This is a manifest, evident lie."

The sentence ﴿Why did they not bring four witnesses for it?﴾ is part of what the believers say. That is: "Would that the slanderers had brought four witnesses to testify to what they said." (p-١٠٠٢) ﴿Since they did not bring the witnesses, those, in God's sight, are the liars﴾, that is, the slanderers, ﴿in the judgment of God, they are the liars, the complete liars.﴾

﴿And were it not for the bounty of God upon you and His mercy in this world and the Hereafter﴾. This is an address to the listeners, and it contains a great warning. "Were it not" (*lawlā*) here is the one indicating the non-occurrence of one thing because of the occurrence of another. ﴿Would have touched you for what you plunged into﴾, that is, because of what you engaged in of the account of the slander. One says: he poured forth (*afāḍa*) in speech, and rushed on, and plunged in (*khāḍa*).

The meaning: Were it not that I decreed for you bounty in this world through blessings, among which is respite, and mercy in the Hereafter through pardon, I would have hastened punishment upon you for what you plunged into of the account of the slander.

It has also been said that the meaning is: Were it not for God's bounty upon you, punishment would have touched you in this world and in the Hereafter together, but by His mercy He concealed it from you in this world, and He will show mercy in the Hereafter to whoever comes to Him repentant.

﴿When you were receiving it with your tongues﴾. The clause of time (*ẓarf*) is in the accusative, governed either by "touched you" or by "plunged." The majority read *idh talaqqawnahu* from *talaqqī* (receiving), the original being *tatalaqqawnahu*, and one of the two *tāʾ*s was dropped.

Mujāhid and Muqātil said: The meaning is that some of you narrate it from others.

al-Kalbī said: That is because a man among them meets another and says: "It has reached me that such-and-such," and they receive it from one another in a receiving manner.

al-Zajjāj said: Its meaning is that some of you cast it to others.

Muḥammad ibn al-Sumayfiʿ read *tulqawnahu* with a *ḍammah* on the *tāʾ*, a *sukūn* on the *lām*, and a *ḍammah* on the *qāf*, from *ilqāʾ* (casting). The meaning of this reading is clear.

Ubayy and Ibn Masʿūd read *tatalaqqawnahu* from *talaqqī*, and it is like the reading of the majority.

Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿĀʾishah, ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar, Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmur, and Zayd ibn ʿAlī read *talaqqawnahu* with a *fatḥah* on the *tāʾ*, a *kasrah* on the *lām*, and a *ḍammah* on the *qāf*. This reading is derived from the Arab saying *waliqa yalīqu waluqan*, meaning he lied.

Ibn Sīdah said: They used the transitive verb as evidence for the intransitive one.

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: In my view, he meant "they cast into it," so the preposition was dropped and the pronoun became attached.

al-Khalīl and Abū ʿAmr said: The origin of *walq* is haste. One says: "The camels came *talaqu*," that is, they hastened. From this is the saying of the poet:

*When they saw an army upon them that had come by night, they came with troops from Syria, hastening.*

Another said:

*Ṣ‘ Īs brought him from Syria, hastening.*

Abū al-Baqāʾ said: That is, they hasten in it. Ibn Jarīr said: This word, that is "*talqūnahu*" according to the last reading, is derived from *walq*, which is the hastening of a thing after another thing, like a number following a number, and speech following speech.

Zayd ibn Aslam and Abū Jaʿfar read *tālqūnahu* with a *fatḥah* on the *tāʾ*, a *hamzah* with *sukūn*, a *kasrah* on the *lām*, and a *ḍammah* on the *qāf*, from *alq*, which is lying. Yaʿqūb read *tīlqūnahu* with a *kasrah* on the *tāʾ* from above, followed by a *yāʾ* with *sukūn* below, a *fatḥah* on the *lām*, and a *ḍammah* on the *qāf*. It is the present tense of *waliqa* with a *kasrah* on the *lām*.

The meaning of ﴿and you say with your mouths what you have no knowledge of﴾ is that their saying is confined to the mouths without being actual in the external world or held in the hearts. It has also been said that the mention of the mouths is for emphasis, as in His saying: ﴿flying with its two wings﴾ [al-Anʿām 6:38] and similar.

The pronoun in ﴿you think it﴾ refers to the account into which they plunged and which they spread. ﴿And you think it trivial﴾, that is, a small matter on which no sin will fall upon you. The sentence ﴿and it is, in God's sight, grave﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning its sin and its punishment are great.

﴿And were it not, when you heard it, that you said, "It is not for us to speak of this"﴾. This is a rebuke to all the believers, meaning: "Why did you not, when you heard the account of the slander, say, denying it to those who plunged into it and fabricated it: 'It is not proper for us, nor is it possible for us, to speak of this account, and such a thing does not come from us in any way.'" The meaning of His words ﴿Glory be to You, this is a great calumny﴾ is an expression of wonder at those who brought the slander. Its origin is the declaration of God's transcendence, glorified is He, and then it became frequent until it was used for anything that is wondered at. *Buhtān* is saying of a person what is not in him. That is: "This is a great lie, because it was said about the Mother of the Believers, may Allah be pleased with her, and its occurrence is impossible under the Sharīʿah from one like her."

Then God, glorified is He, admonished those who plunged into the slander.

﴿God admonishes you never to return to the like of it﴾, that is, God advises you, or forbids you, or prohibits you out of dislike that you return, or from returning, or in returning to the like of this slander for the duration of your lives. ﴿If you are believers﴾, for faith requires that you do not fall into its like as long as you live. In this there is great incitement and profound reproach.

﴿And God makes clear to you the signs﴾ regarding commands and prohibitions, so that you may act upon them, adopt God's manners, and refrain from falling into His prohibitions. ﴿And God is Knowing﴾ of what you reveal and what you conceal, ﴿Wise﴾ in His arrangements for His creation.

Then God, glorified is He, threatened the slanderers and whoever wished to spread among people the faults and sins of the believers.

He said: ﴿Indeed, those who love that indecency should spread among those who believe﴾, that is, they love that indecency should spread and become widespread. It comes from the expression *shāʿa al-shayʾu yashīʿu shuyūʿan, shayʿan, and shayaʿānan*, meaning when a thing appears and spreads. The ones meant by "those who believe" are the chaste and the modest, or everyone who is characterized by the attribute of faith. *Al-fāḥishah* is the indecency of fornication and also evil speech. ﴿For them is a painful punishment in this world﴾, by the enforcement of the prescribed punishment upon them, ﴿and in the Hereafter﴾, by the punishment of the Fire. ﴿And God knows﴾ all that is knowable, ﴿and you do not know﴾ except what He has taught you and revealed to you. Among what God knows is the enormity of the sin of slander and the punishment of the one who commits it.

Then, were it not for Allah's bounty upon you and His mercy, [and that Allah is Most Kind, Most Merciful]. This repeats what came before, as a reminder of the favour from Him, glory be to Him, to His servants in delaying punishment for them. And from His kindness to His servants is that He does not hasten to punish them for their sins, and from His mercy to them is that He sends forth warnings and admonitions like this one. The clause "and that Allah is Most Kind, Most Merciful" is coordinated with "Allah's bounty." The answer to "were it not" (law la) is omitted, because what precedes it indicates it, meaning: "He would have hastened the punishment upon you."

﴿O you who have believed, do not follow the steps of Satan.﴾ The word khutuwat is the plural of khutwah, which is the distance between the two feet. Khatwah with a fatha is the verbal noun. The meaning is: do not follow Satan's paths and ways, and do not take the roads he calls you to.

The majority of reciters read khutuwat with a damma on the kha and the ta. ʿĀṣim and al-Akhfash read it with a damma on the kha and a sukun on the ta.

﴿And whoever follows the steps of Satan—indeed, he enjoins immorality and wrongdoing.﴾ It has been said that the response of the conditional clause is omitted and replaced by what serves as its cause, as if it were said: "Then he has committed immorality and wrongdoing, because his habit is to continue commanding others with them." Fahsha' is that whose ugliness is extreme, and munkar is that which the Sharia denounces. The pronoun in innahu refers to Satan. It has been said that it refers to the matter at hand, but the better view is that it refers back to "whoever follows the steps of Satan," because whoever follows Satan becomes his imitator in commanding immorality and wrongdoing.

﴿And were it not for Allah's bounty upon you and His mercy...﴾ Its explanation has already passed. Its answer is His saying: ﴿No one among you would ever have been purified, ever.﴾ That is, were it not for Allah's grace and mercy, no one among you would have purified himself from its defilement for as long as he lived.

The majority read zakā with light (takhfif) pronunciation. Al-A'mash, Ibn Muhaysin and Abu Ja'far read it with emphasis (tashdid), meaning: "Allah would not have purified him."

Muqatil said: that is, "would not have become righteous."

The better interpretation of zakā is "purification and cleansing," which is what Ibn Qutaybah mentioned.

Al-Kisa'i said: His saying "O you who have believed, do not follow the steps of Satan" is an interjection (mu'taridah), and His saying "No one among you would ever have been purified" is the answer to His earlier saying and to "And were it not for Allah's bounty."

The reading with light pronunciation is more preferred, because of His saying: ﴿But Allah purifies whom He wills.﴾ That is, of His servants, through His grace upon them and His mercy toward them. ﴿And Allah is All-Hearing﴾ of what they say, ﴿All-Knowing﴾ of all that is known. In this there is strong encouragement toward sincerity, a great incitement for His repentant servants, and a severe warning for whoever follows Satan and loves that immorality spread among the believing servants of Allah and does not restrain himself with Allah's prohibitions, glory be to Him.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, the authors of the Sunan and others have related the long hadith of ʿĀʾishah concerning the occasion of revelation of these verses, in multiple wordings and various chains.

Its summary is that the occasion of revelation was what occurred from the people of the slander (ahl al-ifk), whose mention has already passed, concerning ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her. That was because she went out from her howdah (litter) searching for a necklace of hers that had broken off out of anxiety. They set off while thinking she was in her howdah. She returned, and the army had already departed with the howdah among them. She remained in that place, and Safwan ibn al-Mu'attal passed by her; he had been lagging behind the army. He made his mount kneel, and he carried her onto it. When the people of the slander saw that, they said what they said, and Allah cleared her of what they had said.

This is the summary of the story, despite its length and the diversity of its branches, so we will not lengthen it by mentioning all of that.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ahmad, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, the authors of the four Sunan, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il have related from ʿĀʾishah, she said: "When my innocence was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood on the pulpit, mentioned that, and recited the Qur'an. When he descended, he ordered two men and a woman, and they were given their prescribed punishment (hadd)."

At-Tirmidhi said: this is a ḥasan (sound-good) hadith.

Abu Dawud's narration names them as Hassan ibn Thabit, Mistah ibn Uthathah, and Hamnah bint Jahsh.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir have related from Ibn ʿAbbas, he said: "Those who slandered ʿĀʾishah were ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, Mistah, Hassan, and Hamnah bint Jahsh."

Al-Bukhari, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il have related from al-Zuhri, he said: "I was with al-Walid ibn ʿAbd al-Malik, and he said: 'The one who took upon himself its greatest part among them was ʿAli.' I said: 'No. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr, ʿAlqamah ibn Waqqas, and ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUtbah ibn Mas'ud all told me, all of them having heard ʿĀʾishah say: "The one who took upon himself its greatest part among them was ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy."'" He said: "He said to me: 'Then what was his crime?' I said: 'Two shaykhs from your people told me, Abu Salamah ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAwf and Abu Bakr ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn al-Harith ibn Hisham, that they both heard ʿĀʾishah say: "He was wrongdoing in my matter."'"

Ya'qub ibn Shaybah said in his Musnad: al-Hasan ibn ʿAli al-Hulwani related to us, al-Shafi'i related to us, my paternal uncle related to us, he said: Sulayman ibn Yasar entered upon Hisham ibn ʿAbd al-Malik, and he said to him: "O Sulayman, the one who took upon himself its greatest part, who is he?" He said: "ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy." He said: "You lie; it is ʿAli." He said: "The Commander of the Faithful knows best what he says." Then al-Zuhri entered and he said: "O Ibn Shihab, who is the one who took upon himself its greatest part?" He said: "Ibn Ubayy." He said: "You lie; it is ʿAli." He said: "Am I lying? No father for you! By Allah, if a caller from heaven were to call out that Allah has made lying lawful, I would not lie. ʿUrwah, Sa'id, ʿAbd Allah and ʿAlqamah related to me from ʿĀʾishah that the one who took upon himself its greatest part was ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy."

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others have related from Masruq, he said: "Hassan ibn Thabit entered upon ʿĀʾishah and praised her (in verse) and said:

*Chaste, dignified, you are never suspected of doubt,*
*and you wake up empty-bellied of the flesh of the heedless.*

She said: 'But you are not like that.' I said: 'You claim that such a man enters upon you, when Allah has revealed: "And the one who took upon himself its greatest part among them has a great punishment"?' She said: 'And what punishment is more severe than blindness?'"

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn ʿAsakir have related from some of the Ansar that the wife of Abu Ayyub said to him when the people of the slander said what they said: "Do you not hear what people are saying about ʿĀʾishah?" He said: "Yes, and that is a lie. Would you have done such a thing, O Umm Ayyub?" She said: "No, by Allah." He said: "Then ʿĀʾishah, by Allah, is better and purer than you. This is only a lie and a baseless fabrication." Then, when the Qur'an was revealed, Allah mentioned those who spoke the immorality that the people of the slander had spoken.

Then He said: ﴿Why, when you heard it, did the believing men and believing women not think good of one another and say, "This is an obvious falsehood"?﴾ That is, as Abu Ayyub and his wife said.

Al-Waqidi, al-Hakim and Ibn ʿAsakir have related from Aflah, the freedman of Abu Ayyub, that Umm Ayyub... and he mentioned something similar.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh have related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ﴿Allah admonishes you never to return to the like of it, ever.﴾ He said: "Allah forbids you (yuharrij) from it."

Al-Bukhari in al-Adab and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman have related from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, he said: "The one who speaks the immorality and the one who spreads it are equal in sin."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim have related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: ﴿Not one among you would ever have been purified, ever.﴾ He said: "No creature would have been guided to any good at all."

(p-١٠٠١).
The predicate (khabar) of *inna* is, in His words ﴿Indeed, those who came with the slander﴾, "a band (ʿusbah) among you." "Among you" is a qualifier (ṣifah) of "a band." It has also been said that the predicate is ﴿do not consider it bad for you﴾, and that "a band" is a substitute (badal) for the subject of "came."

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: This is more coherent in meaning and more beneficial than taking the predicate to be "a band." The sentence ﴿do not consider it﴾, although it is in the imperative form (ṭalabiyyah), can be made a predicate by supposition (taqdir), as in similar cases. The *ifk* (slander) is the worst and most abominable of lies. It is derived from *afaka al-shayʾ*, meaning he turned the thing away from its true direction. Thus *ifk* is a reversed account. It has also been said that *ifk* is calumny (buhtān). The Muslims agreed that what is meant in the verse is the slander that was directed at ʿĀʾishah, the Mother of the Believers. God described it as *ifk* because what was well known of her condition, may Allah be pleased with her, was the opposite of it.

al-Wāḥidī said: The sense of "reversal" in this account, which those people brought, is that ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, deserved praise for her chastity, her noble lineage and her standing, not slander. Those who accused her with evil reversed the matter from its true direction. So it is a vile slander and a manifest lie.

The *ʿuṣbah* are a group from ten to forty. Here it refers to ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy, the leader of the hypocrites; Zayd ibn Rifāʿah; Ḥassān ibn Thābit; Misṭaḥ ibn Uthāthah; Ḥamnah bint Jaḥsh; and those who supported them. It has also been said that the *ʿuṣbah* are from three to ten, and it has been said from ten to fifteen. Its original linguistic sense is a group whose members support one another with partisan zeal (yataʿaṣṣabu baʿḍuhum li-baʿḍ).

As for the sentence ﴿do not consider it bad for you﴾: if it is the predicate of *inna*, the matter is clear. If the predicate is "a band," as was mentioned earlier, then it is a new (mustaʾnafah) sentence. It is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ), to ʿĀʾishah, and to Ṣafwān ibn al-Muʿaṭṭal, who was slandered along with the Mother of the Believers, as a consolation to them.

Evil (sharr) is that whose harm exceeds its benefit, and good (khayr) is that whose benefit exceeds its harm. As for the good in which there is no evil, it is Paradise, and the evil in which there is no good is the Fire. The reason it is good for them is that through it they obtain great reward, together with the clearing of the Mother of the Believers' name, and this story becomes a general law. ﴿For every man among them is what he earned of sin﴾, meaning because of his speaking the slander. ﴿And the one among them who took upon himself the greater part of it, for him is a great punishment﴾. Al-Ḥasan, al-Zuhrī, Abū Rajāʾ, Ḥumayd al-Aʿraj, Yaʿqūb, Ibn Abī ʿUlayyah, Mujāhid, and ʿAmrah bint ʿAbd al-Raḥmān read *kibrahu* with a *ḍammah* on the *kāf* (*kubrahu*). Al-Farrāʾ said: This is a good reading, because the Arabs say: "So-and-so took upon himself the great part (*ʿaẓīm*) of such-and-such," meaning the greatest part of it. The rest read it with a *kasrah* (*kibrahu*).

It has been said that the two are dialectal variants. It has also been said that with *ḍammah* it means the principal part of the slander, and with *kasrah* it means initiating it. It has also been said that with *kasrah* it means sin.

The meaning is: the one among the band who took upon himself the principal part of the slander has a great punishment, in this world, or in the Hereafter, or in both.

There is disagreement about who, among the band of slanderers, is meant by "the one who took upon himself the greater part." It has been said he is ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy; it has been said he is Ḥassān. The first is the sound view.

Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq and others narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) flogged two men and a woman for the slander: Misṭaḥ ibn Uthāthah, Ḥassān ibn Thābit, and Ḥamnah bint Jaḥsh.

It has been said that he flogged ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy, Ḥassān ibn Thābit, and Ḥamnah bint Jaḥsh, and did not flog Misṭaḥ, because he did not openly make the accusation but heard and spread it without explicit declaration. It has also been said that he flogged none of them.

al-Qurṭubī said: The well-known report, and what is known among the scholars, is that those who received the *ḥadd* (prescribed punishment) were Ḥassān, Misṭaḥ, and Ḥamnah. Nothing has been heard about a *ḥadd* for ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy. This is confirmed by what is in the Sunan of Abū Dāwūd from ʿĀʾishah, who said: When my innocence was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) stood up, mentioned that, and recited the Qur'an. When he came down from the pulpit, he ordered the two men and the woman, and they were punished with their *ḥadd*. He named them: Ḥassān, Misṭaḥ ibn Uthāthah, and Ḥamnah bint Jaḥsh.

They differed about the reason the Prophet (ﷺ) left ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy unpunished. It has been said that it was to保留 (leave for) the great punishment for him in the Hereafter, while the others were punished so that it would be an expiation (*takfīr*) for their sin, as was established from him (ﷺ) concerning *ḥudūd*, that he said: "It is an expiation for the one upon whom it is carried out." It has also been said that he left his punishment to win over his people and out of respect for his son, for he was among the righteous believers, and to extinguish the spark of strife, for its beginnings had already appeared from Saʿd ibn ʿUbādah and those with him, as in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim.

Then God, glorified is He, turned the address away from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and those with him toward the believers by way of *iltifāt* (shift of address). He said: ﴿Why, when you heard it, did the believing men and believing women not think good of one another and say, "This is a clear lie"?﴾ The word "why" (*lawlā*) here is the one of reproach (*taḥḍīḍiyyah*), a strong rebuke and an intensified reprimand. The meaning is: when the believers heard the saying of the people of slander, they should have measured it against themselves. If such a thing is unlikely among them, it is even more unlikely concerning the Mother of the Believers.

al-Ḥasan said: The meaning of "among themselves" is "among the people of their religion," because the believers are like one soul. Do you not see His words: ﴿nor kill yourselves﴾? al-Zajjāj said: For this reason, people who kill one another are said to be killing themselves. al-Mubarrad said: Similar to this is His saying: ﴿so kill yourselves﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:54]. al-Naḥḥās said: "Among themselves" means "among their brothers." So God made it obligatory upon the Muslims, when they hear a man accuse someone and mention about him something ugly that they do not know of him, to deny it to him and declare him a liar.

The scholars said: The verse is evidence that the rank of faith and chastity is not removed by a report that is merely possible, even if it spreads. ﴿And they say, "This is a clear lie."﴾ That is, the believers said upon hearing the slander: "This is a manifest, evident lie."

The sentence ﴿Why did they not bring four witnesses for it?﴾ is part of what the believers say. That is: "Would that the slanderers had brought four witnesses to testify to what they said." (p-١٠٠٢) ﴿Since they did not bring the witnesses, those, in God's sight, are the liars﴾, that is, the slanderers, ﴿in the judgment of God, they are the liars, the complete liars.﴾

﴿And were it not for the bounty of God upon you and His mercy in this world and the Hereafter﴾. This is an address to the listeners, and it contains a great warning. "Were it not" (*lawlā*) here is the one indicating the non-occurrence of one thing because of the occurrence of another. ﴿Would have touched you for what you plunged into﴾, that is, because of what you engaged in of the account of the slander. One says: he poured forth (*afāḍa*) in speech, and rushed on, and plunged in (*khāḍa*).

The meaning: Were it not that I decreed for you bounty in this world through blessings, among which is respite, and mercy in the Hereafter through pardon, I would have hastened punishment upon you for what you plunged into of the account of the slander.

It has also been said that the meaning is: Were it not for God's bounty upon you, punishment would have touched you in this world and in the Hereafter together, but by His mercy He concealed it from you in this world, and He will show mercy in the Hereafter to whoever comes to Him repentant.

﴿When you were receiving it with your tongues﴾. The clause of time (*ẓarf*) is in the accusative, governed either by "touched you" or by "plunged." The majority read *idh talaqqawnahu* from *talaqqī* (receiving), the original being *tatalaqqawnahu*, and one of the two *tāʾ*s was dropped.

Mujāhid and Muqātil said: The meaning is that some of you narrate it from others.

al-Kalbī said: That is because a man among them meets another and says: "It has reached me that such-and-such," and they receive it from one another in a receiving manner.

al-Zajjāj said: Its meaning is that some of you cast it to others.

Muḥammad ibn al-Sumayfiʿ read *tulqawnahu* with a *ḍammah* on the *tāʾ*, a *sukūn* on the *lām*, and a *ḍammah* on the *qāf*, from *ilqāʾ* (casting). The meaning of this reading is clear.

Ubayy and Ibn Masʿūd read *tatalaqqawnahu* from *talaqqī*, and it is like the reading of the majority.

Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿĀʾishah, ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar, Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmur, and Zayd ibn ʿAlī read *talaqqawnahu* with a *fatḥah* on the *tāʾ*, a *kasrah* on the *lām*, and a *ḍammah* on the *qāf*. This reading is derived from the Arab saying *waliqa yalīqu waluqan*, meaning he lied.

Ibn Sīdah said: They used the transitive verb as evidence for the intransitive one.

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: In my view, he meant "they cast into it," so the preposition was dropped and the pronoun became attached.

al-Khalīl and Abū ʿAmr said: The origin of *walq* is haste. One says: "The camels came *talaqu*," that is, they hastened. From this is the saying of the poet:

*When they saw an army upon them that had come by night, they came with troops from Syria, hastening.*

Another said:

*Ṣ‘ Īs brought him from Syria, hastening.*

Abū al-Baqāʾ said: That is, they hasten in it. Ibn Jarīr said: This word, that is "*talqūnahu*" according to the last reading, is derived from *walq*, which is the hastening of a thing after another thing, like a number following a number, and speech following speech.

Zayd ibn Aslam and Abū Jaʿfar read *tālqūnahu* with a *fatḥah* on the *tāʾ*, a *hamzah* with *sukūn*, a *kasrah* on the *lām*, and a *ḍammah* on the *qāf*, from *alq*, which is lying. Yaʿqūb read *tīlqūnahu* with a *kasrah* on the *tāʾ* from above, followed by a *yāʾ* with *sukūn* below, a *fatḥah* on the *lām*, and a *ḍammah* on the *qāf*. It is the present tense of *waliqa* with a *kasrah* on the *lām*.

The meaning of ﴿and you say with your mouths what you have no knowledge of﴾ is that their saying is confined to the mouths without being actual in the external world or held in the hearts. It has also been said that the mention of the mouths is for emphasis, as in His saying: ﴿flying with its two wings﴾ [al-Anʿām 6:38] and similar.

The pronoun in ﴿you think it﴾ refers to the account into which they plunged and which they spread. ﴿And you think it trivial﴾, that is, a small matter on which no sin will fall upon you. The sentence ﴿and it is, in God's sight, grave﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning its sin and its punishment are great.

﴿And were it not, when you heard it, that you said, "It is not for us to speak of this"﴾. This is a rebuke to all the believers, meaning: "Why did you not, when you heard the account of the slander, say, denying it to those who plunged into it and fabricated it: 'It is not proper for us, nor is it possible for us, to speak of this account, and such a thing does not come from us in any way.'" The meaning of His words ﴿Glory be to You, this is a great calumny﴾ is an expression of wonder at those who brought the slander. Its origin is the declaration of God's transcendence, glorified is He, and then it became frequent until it was used for anything that is wondered at. *Buhtān* is saying of a person what is not in him. That is: "This is a great lie, because it was said about the Mother of the Believers, may Allah be pleased with her, and its occurrence is impossible under the Sharīʿah from one like her."

Then God, glorified is He, admonished those who plunged into the slander.

﴿God admonishes you never to return to the like of it﴾, that is, God advises you, or forbids you, or prohibits you out of dislike that you return, or from returning, or in returning to the like of this slander for the duration of your lives. ﴿If you are believers﴾, for faith requires that you do not fall into its like as long as you live. In this there is great incitement and profound reproach.

﴿And God makes clear to you the signs﴾ regarding commands and prohibitions, so that you may act upon them, adopt God's manners, and refrain from falling into His prohibitions. ﴿And God is Knowing﴾ of what you reveal and what you conceal, ﴿Wise﴾ in His arrangements for His creation.

Then God, glorified is He, threatened the slanderers and whoever wished to spread among people the faults and sins of the believers.

He said: ﴿Indeed, those who love that indecency should spread among those who believe﴾, that is, they love that indecency should spread and become widespread. It comes from the expression *shāʿa al-shayʾu yashīʿu shuyūʿan, shayʿan, and shayaʿānan*, meaning when a thing appears and spreads. The ones meant by "those who believe" are the chaste and the modest, or everyone who is characterized by the attribute of faith. *Al-fāḥishah* is the indecency of fornication and also evil speech. ﴿For them is a painful punishment in this world﴾, by the enforcement of the prescribed punishment upon them, ﴿and in the Hereafter﴾, by the punishment of the Fire. ﴿And God knows﴾ all that is knowable, ﴿and you do not know﴾ except what He has taught you and revealed to you. Among what God knows is the enormity of the sin of slander and the punishment of the one who commits it.

Then, were it not for Allah's bounty upon you and His mercy, [and that Allah is Most Kind, Most Merciful]. This repeats what came before, as a reminder of the favour from Him, glory be to Him, to His servants in delaying punishment for them. And from His kindness to His servants is that He does not hasten to punish them for their sins, and from His mercy to them is that He sends forth warnings and admonitions like this one. The clause "and that Allah is Most Kind, Most Merciful" is coordinated with "Allah's bounty." The answer to "were it not" (law la) is omitted, because what precedes it indicates it, meaning: "He would have hastened the punishment upon you."

﴿O you who have believed, do not follow the steps of Satan.﴾ The word khutuwat is the plural of khutwah, which is the distance between the two feet. Khatwah with a fatha is the verbal noun. The meaning is: do not follow Satan's paths and ways, and do not take the roads he calls you to.

The majority of reciters read khutuwat with a damma on the kha and the ta. ʿĀṣim and al-Akhfash read it with a damma on the kha and a sukun on the ta.

﴿And whoever follows the steps of Satan—indeed, he enjoins immorality and wrongdoing.﴾ It has been said that the response of the conditional clause is omitted and replaced by what serves as its cause, as if it were said: "Then he has committed immorality and wrongdoing, because his habit is to continue commanding others with them." Fahsha' is that whose ugliness is extreme, and munkar is that which the Sharia denounces. The pronoun in innahu refers to Satan. It has been said that it refers to the matter at hand, but the better view is that it refers back to "whoever follows the steps of Satan," because whoever follows Satan becomes his imitator in commanding immorality and wrongdoing.

﴿And were it not for Allah's bounty upon you and His mercy...﴾ Its explanation has already passed. Its answer is His saying: ﴿No one among you would ever have been purified, ever.﴾ That is, were it not for Allah's grace and mercy, no one among you would have purified himself from its defilement for as long as he lived.

The majority read zakā with light (takhfif) pronunciation. Al-A'mash, Ibn Muhaysin and Abu Ja'far read it with emphasis (tashdid), meaning: "Allah would not have purified him."

Muqatil said: that is, "would not have become righteous."

The better interpretation of zakā is "purification and cleansing," which is what Ibn Qutaybah mentioned.

Al-Kisa'i said: His saying "O you who have believed, do not follow the steps of Satan" is an interjection (mu'taridah), and His saying "No one among you would ever have been purified" is the answer to His earlier saying and to "And were it not for Allah's bounty."

The reading with light pronunciation is more preferred, because of His saying: ﴿But Allah purifies whom He wills.﴾ That is, of His servants, through His grace upon them and His mercy toward them. ﴿And Allah is All-Hearing﴾ of what they say, ﴿All-Knowing﴾ of all that is known. In this there is strong encouragement toward sincerity, a great incitement for His repentant servants, and a severe warning for whoever follows Satan and loves that immorality spread among the believing servants of Allah and does not restrain himself with Allah's prohibitions, glory be to Him.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, the authors of the Sunan and others have related the long hadith of ʿĀʾishah concerning the occasion of revelation of these verses, in multiple wordings and various chains.

Its summary is that the occasion of revelation was what occurred from the people of the slander (ahl al-ifk), whose mention has already passed, concerning ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her. That was because she went out from her howdah (litter) searching for a necklace of hers that had broken off out of anxiety. They set off while thinking she was in her howdah. She returned, and the army had already departed with the howdah among them. She remained in that place, and Safwan ibn al-Mu'attal passed by her; he had been lagging behind the army. He made his mount kneel, and he carried her onto it. When the people of the slander saw that, they said what they said, and Allah cleared her of what they had said.

This is the summary of the story, despite its length and the diversity of its branches, so we will not lengthen it by mentioning all of that.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ahmad, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, the authors of the four Sunan, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il have related from ʿĀʾishah, she said: "When my innocence was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood on the pulpit, mentioned that, and recited the Qur'an. When he descended, he ordered two men and a woman, and they were given their prescribed punishment (hadd)."

At-Tirmidhi said: this is a ḥasan (sound-good) hadith.

Abu Dawud's narration names them as Hassan ibn Thabit, Mistah ibn Uthathah, and Hamnah bint Jahsh.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir have related from Ibn ʿAbbas, he said: "Those who slandered ʿĀʾishah were ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, Mistah, Hassan, and Hamnah bint Jahsh."

Al-Bukhari, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il have related from al-Zuhri, he said: "I was with al-Walid ibn ʿAbd al-Malik, and he said: 'The one who took upon himself its greatest part among them was ʿAli.' I said: 'No. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr, ʿAlqamah ibn Waqqas, and ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUtbah ibn Mas'ud all told me, all of them having heard ʿĀʾishah say: "The one who took upon himself its greatest part among them was ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy."'" He said: "He said to me: 'Then what was his crime?' I said: 'Two shaykhs from your people told me, Abu Salamah ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAwf and Abu Bakr ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn al-Harith ibn Hisham, that they both heard ʿĀʾishah say: "He was wrongdoing in my matter."'"

Ya'qub ibn Shaybah said in his Musnad: al-Hasan ibn ʿAli al-Hulwani related to us, al-Shafi'i related to us, my paternal uncle related to us, he said: Sulayman ibn Yasar entered upon Hisham ibn ʿAbd al-Malik, and he said to him: "O Sulayman, the one who took upon himself its greatest part, who is he?" He said: "ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy." He said: "You lie; it is ʿAli." He said: "The Commander of the Faithful knows best what he says." Then al-Zuhri entered and he said: "O Ibn Shihab, who is the one who took upon himself its greatest part?" He said: "Ibn Ubayy." He said: "You lie; it is ʿAli." He said: "Am I lying? No father for you! By Allah, if a caller from heaven were to call out that Allah has made lying lawful, I would not lie. ʿUrwah, Sa'id, ʿAbd Allah and ʿAlqamah related to me from ʿĀʾishah that the one who took upon himself its greatest part was ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy."

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others have related from Masruq, he said: "Hassan ibn Thabit entered upon ʿĀʾishah and praised her (in verse) and said:

*Chaste, dignified, you are never suspected of doubt,*
*and you wake up empty-bellied of the flesh of the heedless.*

She said: 'But you are not like that.' I said: 'You claim that such a man enters upon you, when Allah has revealed: "And the one who took upon himself its greatest part among them has a great punishment"?' She said: 'And what punishment is more severe than blindness?'"

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn ʿAsakir have related from some of the Ansar that the wife of Abu Ayyub said to him when the people of the slander said what they said: "Do you not hear what people are saying about ʿĀʾishah?" He said: "Yes, and that is a lie. Would you have done such a thing, O Umm Ayyub?" She said: "No, by Allah." He said: "Then ʿĀʾishah, by Allah, is better and purer than you. This is only a lie and a baseless fabrication." Then, when the Qur'an was revealed, Allah mentioned those who spoke the immorality that the people of the slander had spoken.

Then He said: ﴿Why, when you heard it, did the believing men and believing women not think good of one another and say, "This is an obvious falsehood"?﴾ That is, as Abu Ayyub and his wife said.

Al-Waqidi, al-Hakim and Ibn ʿAsakir have related from Aflah, the freedman of Abu Ayyub, that Umm Ayyub... and he mentioned something similar.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh have related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ﴿Allah admonishes you never to return to the like of it, ever.﴾ He said: "Allah forbids you (yuharrij) from it."

Al-Bukhari in al-Adab and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman have related from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, he said: "The one who speaks the immorality and the one who spreads it are equal in sin."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim have related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: ﴿Not one among you would ever have been purified, ever.﴾ He said: "No creature would have been guided to any good at all."

(p-١٠٠١).
The predicate (khabar) of *inna* is, in His words ﴿Indeed, those who came with the slander﴾, "a band (ʿusbah) among you." "Among you" is a qualifier (ṣifah) of "a band." It has also been said that the predicate is ﴿do not consider it bad for you﴾, and that "a band" is a substitute (badal) for the subject of "came."

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: This is more coherent in meaning and more beneficial than taking the predicate to be "a band." The sentence ﴿do not consider it﴾, although it is in the imperative form (ṭalabiyyah), can be made a predicate by supposition (taqdir), as in similar cases. The *ifk* (slander) is the worst and most abominable of lies. It is derived from *afaka al-shayʾ*, meaning he turned the thing away from its true direction. Thus *ifk* is a reversed account. It has also been said that *ifk* is calumny (buhtān). The Muslims agreed that what is meant in the verse is the slander that was directed at ʿĀʾishah, the Mother of the Believers. God described it as *ifk* because what was well known of her condition, may Allah be pleased with her, was the opposite of it.

al-Wāḥidī said: The sense of "reversal" in this account, which those people brought, is that ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, deserved praise for her chastity, her noble lineage and her standing, not slander. Those who accused her with evil reversed the matter from its true direction. So it is a vile slander and a manifest lie.

The *ʿuṣbah* are a group from ten to forty. Here it refers to ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy, the leader of the hypocrites; Zayd ibn Rifāʿah; Ḥassān ibn Thābit; Misṭaḥ ibn Uthāthah; Ḥamnah bint Jaḥsh; and those who supported them. It has also been said that the *ʿuṣbah* are from three to ten, and it has been said from ten to fifteen. Its original linguistic sense is a group whose members support one another with partisan zeal (yataʿaṣṣabu baʿḍuhum li-baʿḍ).

As for the sentence ﴿do not consider it bad for you﴾: if it is the predicate of *inna*, the matter is clear. If the predicate is "a band," as was mentioned earlier, then it is a new (mustaʾnafah) sentence. It is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ), to ʿĀʾishah, and to Ṣafwān ibn al-Muʿaṭṭal, who was slandered along with the Mother of the Believers, as a consolation to them.

Evil (sharr) is that whose harm exceeds its benefit, and good (khayr) is that whose benefit exceeds its harm. As for the good in which there is no evil, it is Paradise, and the evil in which there is no good is the Fire. The reason it is good for them is that through it they obtain great reward, together with the clearing of the Mother of the Believers' name, and this story becomes a general law. ﴿For every man among them is what he earned of sin﴾, meaning because of his speaking the slander. ﴿And the one among them who took upon himself the greater part of it, for him is a great punishment﴾. Al-Ḥasan, al-Zuhrī, Abū Rajāʾ, Ḥumayd al-Aʿraj, Yaʿqūb, Ibn Abī ʿUlayyah, Mujāhid, and ʿAmrah bint ʿAbd al-Raḥmān read *kibrahu* with a *ḍammah* on the *kāf* (*kubrahu*). Al-Farrāʾ said: This is a good reading, because the Arabs say: "So-and-so took upon himself the great part (*ʿaẓīm*) of such-and-such," meaning the greatest part of it. The rest read it with a *kasrah* (*kibrahu*).

It has been said that the two are dialectal variants. It has also been said that with *ḍammah* it means the principal part of the slander, and with *kasrah* it means initiating it. It has also been said that with *kasrah* it means sin.

The meaning is: the one among the band who took upon himself the principal part of the slander has a great punishment, in this world, or in the Hereafter, or in both.

There is disagreement about who, among the band of slanderers, is meant by "the one who took upon himself the greater part." It has been said he is ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy; it has been said he is Ḥassān. The first is the sound view.

Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq and others narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) flogged two men and a woman for the slander: Misṭaḥ ibn Uthāthah, Ḥassān ibn Thābit, and Ḥamnah bint Jaḥsh.

It has been said that he flogged ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy, Ḥassān ibn Thābit, and Ḥamnah bint Jaḥsh, and did not flog Misṭaḥ, because he did not openly make the accusation but heard and spread it without explicit declaration. It has also been said that he flogged none of them.

al-Qurṭubī said: The well-known report, and what is known among the scholars, is that those who received the *ḥadd* (prescribed punishment) were Ḥassān, Misṭaḥ, and Ḥamnah. Nothing has been heard about a *ḥadd* for ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy. This is confirmed by what is in the Sunan of Abū Dāwūd from ʿĀʾishah, who said: When my innocence was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) stood up, mentioned that, and recited the Qur'an. When he came down from the pulpit, he ordered the two men and the woman, and they were punished with their *ḥadd*. He named them: Ḥassān, Misṭaḥ ibn Uthāthah, and Ḥamnah bint Jaḥsh.

They differed about the reason the Prophet (ﷺ) left ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy unpunished. It has been said that it was to保留 (leave for) the great punishment for him in the Hereafter, while the others were punished so that it would be an expiation (*takfīr*) for their sin, as was established from him (ﷺ) concerning *ḥudūd*, that he said: "It is an expiation for the one upon whom it is carried out." It has also been said that he left his punishment to win over his people and out of respect for his son, for he was among the righteous believers, and to extinguish the spark of strife, for its beginnings had already appeared from Saʿd ibn ʿUbādah and those with him, as in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim.

Then God, glorified is He, turned the address away from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and those with him toward the believers by way of *iltifāt* (shift of address). He said: ﴿Why, when you heard it, did the believing men and believing women not think good of one another and say, "This is a clear lie"?﴾ The word "why" (*lawlā*) here is the one of reproach (*taḥḍīḍiyyah*), a strong rebuke and an intensified reprimand. The meaning is: when the believers heard the saying of the people of slander, they should have measured it against themselves. If such a thing is unlikely among them, it is even more unlikely concerning the Mother of the Believers.

al-Ḥasan said: The meaning of "among themselves" is "among the people of their religion," because the believers are like one soul. Do you not see His words: ﴿nor kill yourselves﴾? al-Zajjāj said: For this reason, people who kill one another are said to be killing themselves. al-Mubarrad said: Similar to this is His saying: ﴿so kill yourselves﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:54]. al-Naḥḥās said: "Among themselves" means "among their brothers." So God made it obligatory upon the Muslims, when they hear a man accuse someone and mention about him something ugly that they do not know of him, to deny it to him and declare him a liar.

The scholars said: The verse is evidence that the rank of faith and chastity is not removed by a report that is merely possible, even if it spreads. ﴿And they say, "This is a clear lie."﴾ That is, the believers said upon hearing the slander: "This is a manifest, evident lie."

The sentence ﴿Why did they not bring four witnesses for it?﴾ is part of what the believers say. That is: "Would that the slanderers had brought four witnesses to testify to what they said." (p-١٠٠٢) ﴿Since they did not bring the witnesses, those, in God's sight, are the liars﴾, that is, the slanderers, ﴿in the judgment of God, they are the liars, the complete liars.﴾

﴿And were it not for the bounty of God upon you and His mercy in this world and the Hereafter﴾. This is an address to the listeners, and it contains a great warning. "Were it not" (*lawlā*) here is the one indicating the non-occurrence of one thing because of the occurrence of another. ﴿Would have touched you for what you plunged into﴾, that is, because of what you engaged in of the account of the slander. One says: he poured forth (*afāḍa*) in speech, and rushed on, and plunged in (*khāḍa*).

The meaning: Were it not that I decreed for you bounty in this world through blessings, among which is respite, and mercy in the Hereafter through pardon, I would have hastened punishment upon you for what you plunged into of the account of the slander.

It has also been said that the meaning is: Were it not for God's bounty upon you, punishment would have touched you in this world and in the Hereafter together, but by His mercy He concealed it from you in this world, and He will show mercy in the Hereafter to whoever comes to Him repentant.

﴿When you were receiving it with your tongues﴾. The clause of time (*ẓarf*) is in the accusative, governed either by "touched you" or by "plunged." The majority read *idh talaqqawnahu* from *talaqqī* (receiving), the original being *tatalaqqawnahu*, and one of the two *tāʾ*s was dropped.

Mujāhid and Muqātil said: The meaning is that some of you narrate it from others.

al-Kalbī said: That is because a man among them meets another and says: "It has reached me that such-and-such," and they receive it from one another in a receiving manner.

al-Zajjāj said: Its meaning is that some of you cast it to others.

Muḥammad ibn al-Sumayfiʿ read *tulqawnahu* with a *ḍammah* on the *tāʾ*, a *sukūn* on the *lām*, and a *ḍammah* on the *qāf*, from *ilqāʾ* (casting). The meaning of this reading is clear.

Ubayy and Ibn Masʿūd read *tatalaqqawnahu* from *talaqqī*, and it is like the reading of the majority.

Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿĀʾishah, ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar, Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmur, and Zayd ibn ʿAlī read *talaqqawnahu* with a *fatḥah* on the *tāʾ*, a *kasrah* on the *lām*, and a *ḍammah* on the *qāf*. This reading is derived from the Arab saying *waliqa yalīqu waluqan*, meaning he lied.

Ibn Sīdah said: They used the transitive verb as evidence for the intransitive one.

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: In my view, he meant "they cast into it," so the preposition was dropped and the pronoun became attached.

al-Khalīl and Abū ʿAmr said: The origin of *walq* is haste. One says: "The camels came *talaqu*," that is, they hastened. From this is the saying of the poet:

*When they saw an army upon them that had come by night, they came with troops from Syria, hastening.*

Another said:

*Ṣ‘ Īs brought him from Syria, hastening.*

Abū al-Baqāʾ said: That is, they hasten in it. Ibn Jarīr said: This word, that is "*talqūnahu*" according to the last reading, is derived from *walq*, which is the hastening of a thing after another thing, like a number following a number, and speech following speech.

Zayd ibn Aslam and Abū Jaʿfar read *tālqūnahu* with a *fatḥah* on the *tāʾ*, a *hamzah* with *sukūn*, a *kasrah* on the *lām*, and a *ḍammah* on the *qāf*, from *alq*, which is lying. Yaʿqūb read *tīlqūnahu* with a *kasrah* on the *tāʾ* from above, followed by a *yāʾ* with *sukūn* below, a *fatḥah* on the *lām*, and a *ḍammah* on the *qāf*. It is the present tense of *waliqa* with a *kasrah* on the *lām*.

The meaning of ﴿and you say with your mouths what you have no knowledge of﴾ is that their saying is confined to the mouths without being actual in the external world or held in the hearts. It has also been said that the mention of the mouths is for emphasis, as in His saying: ﴿flying with its two wings﴾ [al-Anʿām 6:38] and similar.

The pronoun in ﴿you think it﴾ refers to the account into which they plunged and which they spread. ﴿And you think it trivial﴾, that is, a small matter on which no sin will fall upon you. The sentence ﴿and it is, in God's sight, grave﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning its sin and its punishment are great.

﴿And were it not, when you heard it, that you said, "It is not for us to speak of this"﴾. This is a rebuke to all the believers, meaning: "Why did you not, when you heard the account of the slander, say, denying it to those who plunged into it and fabricated it: 'It is not proper for us, nor is it possible for us, to speak of this account, and such a thing does not come from us in any way.'" The meaning of His words ﴿Glory be to You, this is a great calumny﴾ is an expression of wonder at those who brought the slander. Its origin is the declaration of God's transcendence, glorified is He, and then it became frequent until it was used for anything that is wondered at. *Buhtān* is saying of a person what is not in him. That is: "This is a great lie, because it was said about the Mother of the Believers, may Allah be pleased with her, and its occurrence is impossible under the Sharīʿah from one like her."

Then God, glorified is He, admonished those who plunged into the slander.

﴿God admonishes you never to return to the like of it﴾, that is, God advises you, or forbids you, or prohibits you out of dislike that you return, or from returning, or in returning to the like of this slander for the duration of your lives. ﴿If you are believers﴾, for faith requires that you do not fall into its like as long as you live. In this there is great incitement and profound reproach.

﴿And God makes clear to you the signs﴾ regarding commands and prohibitions, so that you may act upon them, adopt God's manners, and refrain from falling into His prohibitions. ﴿And God is Knowing﴾ of what you reveal and what you conceal, ﴿Wise﴾ in His arrangements for His creation.

Then God, glorified is He, threatened the slanderers and whoever wished to spread among people the faults and sins of the believers.

He said: ﴿Indeed, those who love that indecency should spread among those who believe﴾, that is, they love that indecency should spread and become widespread. It comes from the expression *shāʿa al-shayʾu yashīʿu shuyūʿan, shayʿan, and shayaʿānan*, meaning when a thing appears and spreads. The ones meant by "those who believe" are the chaste and the modest, or everyone who is characterized by the attribute of faith. *Al-fāḥishah* is the indecency of fornication and also evil speech. ﴿For them is a painful punishment in this world﴾, by the enforcement of the prescribed punishment upon them, ﴿and in the Hereafter﴾, by the punishment of the Fire. ﴿And God knows﴾ all that is knowable, ﴿and you do not know﴾ except what He has taught you and revealed to you. Among what God knows is the enormity of the sin of slander and the punishment of the one who commits it.

Then, were it not for Allah's bounty upon you and His mercy, [and that Allah is Most Kind, Most Merciful]. This repeats what came before, as a reminder of the favour from Him, glory be to Him, to His servants in delaying punishment for them. And from His kindness to His servants is that He does not hasten to punish them for their sins, and from His mercy to them is that He sends forth warnings and admonitions like this one. The clause "and that Allah is Most Kind, Most Merciful" is coordinated with "Allah's bounty." The answer to "were it not" (law la) is omitted, because what precedes it indicates it, meaning: "He would have hastened the punishment upon you."

﴿O you who have believed, do not follow the steps of Satan.﴾ The word khutuwat is the plural of khutwah, which is the distance between the two feet. Khatwah with a fatha is the verbal noun. The meaning is: do not follow Satan's paths and ways, and do not take the roads he calls you to.

The majority of reciters read khutuwat with a damma on the kha and the ta. ʿĀṣim and al-Akhfash read it with a damma on the kha and a sukun on the ta.

﴿And whoever follows the steps of Satan—indeed, he enjoins immorality and wrongdoing.﴾ It has been said that the response of the conditional clause is omitted and replaced by what serves as its cause, as if it were said: "Then he has committed immorality and wrongdoing, because his habit is to continue commanding others with them." Fahsha' is that whose ugliness is extreme, and munkar is that which the Sharia denounces. The pronoun in innahu refers to Satan. It has been said that it refers to the matter at hand, but the better view is that it refers back to "whoever follows the steps of Satan," because whoever follows Satan becomes his imitator in commanding immorality and wrongdoing.

﴿And were it not for Allah's bounty upon you and His mercy...﴾ Its explanation has already passed.
