He said: ﴿Indeed, those who love that indecency should spread among those who believe﴾, that is, they love that indecency should spread and become widespread. It comes from the expression *shāʿa al-shayʾu yashīʿu shuyūʿan, shayʿan, and shayaʿānan*, meaning when a thing appears and spreads. The ones meant by "those who believe" are the chaste and the modest, or everyone who is characterized by the attribute of faith. *Al-fāḥishah* is the indecency of fornication and also evil speech. ﴿For them is a painful punishment in this world﴾, by the enforcement of the prescribed punishment upon them, ﴿and in the Hereafter﴾, by the punishment of the Fire. ﴿And God knows﴾ all that is knowable, ﴿and you do not know﴾ except what He has taught you and revealed to you. Among what God knows is the enormity of the sin of slander and the punishment of the one who commits it.

Then, were it not for Allah's bounty upon you and His mercy, [and that Allah is Most Kind, Most Merciful]. This repeats what came before, as a reminder of the favour from Him, glory be to Him, to His servants in delaying punishment for them. And from His kindness to His servants is that He does not hasten to punish them for their sins, and from His mercy to them is that He sends forth warnings and admonitions like this one. The clause "and that Allah is Most Kind, Most Merciful" is coordinated with "Allah's bounty." The answer to "were it not" (law la) is omitted, because what precedes it indicates it, meaning: "He would have hastened the punishment upon you."

﴿O you who have believed, do not follow the steps of Satan.﴾ The word khutuwat is the plural of khutwah, which is the distance between the two feet. Khatwah with a fatha is the verbal noun. The meaning is: do not follow Satan's paths and ways, and do not take the roads he calls you to.

The majority of reciters read khutuwat with a damma on the kha and the ta. ʿĀṣim and al-Akhfash read it with a damma on the kha and a sukun on the ta.

﴿And whoever follows the steps of Satan—indeed, he enjoins immorality and wrongdoing.﴾ It has been said that the response of the conditional clause is omitted and replaced by what serves as its cause, as if it were said: "Then he has committed immorality and wrongdoing, because his habit is to continue commanding others with them." Fahsha' is that whose ugliness is extreme, and munkar is that which the Sharia denounces. The pronoun in innahu refers to Satan. It has been said that it refers to the matter at hand, but the better view is that it refers back to "whoever follows the steps of Satan," because whoever follows Satan becomes his imitator in commanding immorality and wrongdoing.

﴿And were it not for Allah's bounty upon you and His mercy...﴾ Its explanation has already passed. Its answer is His saying: ﴿No one among you would ever have been purified, ever.﴾ That is, were it not for Allah's grace and mercy, no one among you would have purified himself from its defilement for as long as he lived.

The majority read zakā with light (takhfif) pronunciation. Al-A'mash, Ibn Muhaysin and Abu Ja'far read it with emphasis (tashdid), meaning: "Allah would not have purified him."

Muqatil said: that is, "would not have become righteous."

The better interpretation of zakā is "purification and cleansing," which is what Ibn Qutaybah mentioned.

Al-Kisa'i said: His saying "O you who have believed, do not follow the steps of Satan" is an interjection (mu'taridah), and His saying "No one among you would ever have been purified" is the answer to His earlier saying and to "And were it not for Allah's bounty."

The reading with light pronunciation is more preferred, because of His saying: ﴿But Allah purifies whom He wills.﴾ That is, of His servants, through His grace upon them and His mercy toward them. ﴿And Allah is All-Hearing﴾ of what they say, ﴿All-Knowing﴾ of all that is known. In this there is strong encouragement toward sincerity, a great incitement for His repentant servants, and a severe warning for whoever follows Satan and loves that immorality spread among the believing servants of Allah and does not restrain himself with Allah's prohibitions, glory be to Him.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, the authors of the Sunan and others have related the long hadith of ʿĀʾishah concerning the occasion of revelation of these verses, in multiple wordings and various chains.

Its summary is that the occasion of revelation was what occurred from the people of the slander (ahl al-ifk), whose mention has already passed, concerning ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her. That was because she went out from her howdah (litter) searching for a necklace of hers that had broken off out of anxiety. They set off while thinking she was in her howdah. She returned, and the army had already departed with the howdah among them. She remained in that place, and Safwan ibn al-Mu'attal passed by her; he had been lagging behind the army. He made his mount kneel, and he carried her onto it. When the people of the slander saw that, they said what they said, and Allah cleared her of what they had said.

This is the summary of the story, despite its length and the diversity of its branches, so we will not lengthen it by mentioning all of that.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ahmad, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, the authors of the four Sunan, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il have related from ʿĀʾishah, she said: "When my innocence was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood on the pulpit, mentioned that, and recited the Qur'an. When he descended, he ordered two men and a woman, and they were given their prescribed punishment (hadd)."

At-Tirmidhi said: this is a ḥasan (sound-good) hadith.

Abu Dawud's narration names them as Hassan ibn Thabit, Mistah ibn Uthathah, and Hamnah bint Jahsh.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir have related from Ibn ʿAbbas, he said: "Those who slandered ʿĀʾishah were ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, Mistah, Hassan, and Hamnah bint Jahsh."

Al-Bukhari, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il have related from al-Zuhri, he said: "I was with al-Walid ibn ʿAbd al-Malik, and he said: 'The one who took upon himself its greatest part among them was ʿAli.' I said: 'No. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr, ʿAlqamah ibn Waqqas, and ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUtbah ibn Mas'ud all told me, all of them having heard ʿĀʾishah say: "The one who took upon himself its greatest part among them was ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy."'" He said: "He said to me: 'Then what was his crime?' I said: 'Two shaykhs from your people told me, Abu Salamah ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAwf and Abu Bakr ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn al-Harith ibn Hisham, that they both heard ʿĀʾishah say: "He was wrongdoing in my matter."'"

Ya'qub ibn Shaybah said in his Musnad: al-Hasan ibn ʿAli al-Hulwani related to us, al-Shafi'i related to us, my paternal uncle related to us, he said: Sulayman ibn Yasar entered upon Hisham ibn ʿAbd al-Malik, and he said to him: "O Sulayman, the one who took upon himself its greatest part, who is he?" He said: "ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy." He said: "You lie; it is ʿAli." He said: "The Commander of the Faithful knows best what he says." Then al-Zuhri entered and he said: "O Ibn Shihab, who is the one who took upon himself its greatest part?" He said: "Ibn Ubayy." He said: "You lie; it is ʿAli." He said: "Am I lying? No father for you! By Allah, if a caller from heaven were to call out that Allah has made lying lawful, I would not lie. ʿUrwah, Sa'id, ʿAbd Allah and ʿAlqamah related to me from ʿĀʾishah that the one who took upon himself its greatest part was ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy."

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others have related from Masruq, he said: "Hassan ibn Thabit entered upon ʿĀʾishah and praised her (in verse) and said:

*Chaste, dignified, you are never suspected of doubt,*
*and you wake up empty-bellied of the flesh of the heedless.*

She said: 'But you are not like that.' I said: 'You claim that such a man enters upon you, when Allah has revealed: "And the one who took upon himself its greatest part among them has a great punishment"?' She said: 'And what punishment is more severe than blindness?'"

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn ʿAsakir have related from some of the Ansar that the wife of Abu Ayyub said to him when the people of the slander said what they said: "Do you not hear what people are saying about ʿĀʾishah?" He said: "Yes, and that is a lie. Would you have done such a thing, O Umm Ayyub?" She said: "No, by Allah." He said: "Then ʿĀʾishah, by Allah, is better and purer than you. This is only a lie and a baseless fabrication." Then, when the Qur'an was revealed, Allah mentioned those who spoke the immorality that the people of the slander had spoken.

Then He said: ﴿Why, when you heard it, did the believing men and believing women not think good of one another and say, "This is an obvious falsehood"?﴾ That is, as Abu Ayyub and his wife said.

Al-Waqidi, al-Hakim and Ibn ʿAsakir have related from Aflah, the freedman of Abu Ayyub, that Umm Ayyub... and he mentioned something similar.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh have related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ﴿Allah admonishes you never to return to the like of it, ever.﴾ He said: "Allah forbids you (yuharrij) from it."

Al-Bukhari in al-Adab and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman have related from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, he said: "The one who speaks the immorality and the one who spreads it are equal in sin."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim have related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: ﴿Not one among you would ever have been purified, ever.﴾ He said: "No creature would have been guided to any good at all."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 24, verse 22–26 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: "lā yata'al" means "yahlif" (swears). Its form is yaf'Ali, from al-ālīyah, which is the oath. From it is the poet's saying:

"Ibn Aws swore an oath that he would return me to women who are like gazelles."

And another's saying:

"Few are his oaths; he guards his oath, and if an oath escapes from him, he is righteous."

It is said: ta'ālā yata'lī, when he swore.

From it is His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Those who swear off their wives﴾ [al-Baqarah: 226]. A group said it is from alawtu fī kadhā, "if I fell short," and from it "lam ālu juhdan," i.e., "I did not fall short." Likewise from it is His saying: ﴿They do not spare you corruption﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 118]. From it is the poet's saying:

"A man, as long as the breath of his soul remains, does not reach the extremities of calamities nor falls short."

The first meaning is preferable, by the evidence of the occasion of revelation, which will come. By "bounty" is meant wealth and abundance of property. ﴿That they should give to the near of kin, and the needy, and the emigrants in the way of Allah﴾, i.e., "that they should not give."

Al-Zajjaj said: "an lā yu'tū", with lā deleted. From it is the poet's saying:

"I said, by Allah's oath, I will not leave off sitting, even if they cut off my head before you and my limbs."

Abū ʿUbayda said: there is no need to suppose a hidden lā. The meaning is: "Let them not swear that they will not do good to those deserving of goodness who possess those qualities." And according to the other reading, the meaning is: "Let them not fall short in doing good to them, even if there is enmity between them due to a sin they committed." Abū Ḥaywa read ("an tu'tū") with the second-person address, by way of iltifāt (shift of person).

Then He, glorified is He, taught them another etiquette, saying: ﴿And let them pardon﴾ their sin that they committed against them and the offense they perpetrated. It is from ʿafā al-rabʿ, i.e., it was effaced. The meaning is the erasure of the sin until it is effaced just as the trace of the encampment is effaced. ﴿And let them overlook﴾, by turning away from the offender and closing the eye to his offense. It was also read with the second-person form in both verbs.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned a great encouragement for whoever pardons and overlooks, saying: ﴿Do you not love that Allah should forgive you?﴾ because of your pardoning and overlooking those who do evil to you. ﴿And Allah is Forgiving, Merciful﴾, i.e., abundant in forgiveness and mercy toward His servants despite the abundance of their sins. So how could the servants not follow their Lord in pardoning and overlooking those who wrong them?

﴿Indeed, those who accuse chaste women﴾. The explanation of "muhṣanāt" has already passed, and we mentioned the consensus that the ruling for chaste men is the ruling for chaste women regarding the punishment for slander (ḥadd al-qadhf).

There has been disagreement about this verse: is it specific or general? Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: it is specific to whoever accused ʿĀ'isha, may Allah be pleased with her.

Muqātil said: it is specific to ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy, the chief of the hypocrites.

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and al-Kalbī said: this verse is about ʿĀ'isha and the rest of the wives of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, to the exclusion of the rest of the believing men and women. So whoever slanders one of the wives of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, is among the people of this verse.

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: among the rulings of this verse is that there is no repentance for one who accuses one of the wives of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, whereas for whoever slanders other than them, Allah has made repentance possible, as was mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿except those who repent﴾ [al-Nūr: 5]. It was said: this verse is specific to those who persist in slander and do not repent. It was said: it encompasses every slanderer and slandered person among the chaste women and chaste men, and al-Naḥḥās chose this, and it is what agrees with what the scholars of legal theory (uṣūl) established, that the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the occasion.

It was said: it is specific to the polytheists of Makkah, because they used to say of a woman when she emigrated: "She only left to commit fornication."

The people of knowledge said: if the intended meaning of this verse is the believing slanderers, then "curse" means distancing, inflicting the prescribed punishment, the shunning of the rest of the believers toward them, their loss of the rank of uprightness, and their distance from good praise on the tongues of believers. If the intended meaning is whoever slanders ʿĀ'isha specifically, then these matters apply to ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy, the chief of the hypocrites. If it refers to the polytheists of Makkah, then they are cursed ﴿in this world and the Hereafter, and for them is a great punishment﴾. By "the heedless" is meant those who were unaware of indecency, such that it does not occur to their minds and they do not perceive it. In this there is an indication of complete purity and cleanliness of the heart, which is not present in the chaste women. It was said: they are those whose breasts are sound and whose hearts are pure.

﴿On the day when their tongues, their hands, and their feet will bear witness against them﴾. This clause confirms what precedes it, explaining the time when that punishment befalls them, and specifying the day serves to increase the terror through the punishment in it, which no description can encompass.

The majority read ﴿yawma tashhadu﴾ with the feminine (taʾ), and Abū Ḥātim chose this reading. Al-Aʿmash, Yaḥyā ibn Wathhāb, al-Kisāʾī, and Khalaf read it with the masculine (yāʾ), and Abū ʿUbayd chose this reading because the prepositional phrase has come between the noun and the verb.

The meaning: the tongues of some of them bear witness against others on that day. It was also said: their tongues bear witness against them on that day for what they uttered, ﴿and their hands and their feet﴾ for what they did with them in the world. Allah, glorified is He, makes them speak in testimony against them. The object of witness is omitted, and it is their sins which they committed, i.e., these members bear witness against them concerning their sins which they perpetrated and their disobediences which they did.

﴿On that day Allah will pay them their due reward in full﴾, i.e., on the day their limbs bear witness against them for their ugly deeds, Allah gives them their recompense for them in full. Thus "dīn" here means recompense, and "al-ḥaqq" means the established truth about which there is no doubt of its establishment.

Zayd ibn ʿAlī read yuwfīhim, lightened, from awfā, and the rest read it doubled, from waffā.

Abū Ḥaywa and Mujāhid read (al-ḥaqqu) with the nominative, as an epithet of Allah, and this is narrated from Ibn Masʿūd. The rest read it with the accusative, as an epithet of their dīn.

Abū ʿUbayda said: were it not for disliking to oppose the people, the correct reading would be the nominative, so that it is an epithet of Allah, and so that it agrees with the reading of Ubayy. For Jarīr ibn Ḥāzim said: "I saw in the muṣḥaf of Ubayy: (yuwaffīhimu Allāhu al-ḥaqqa dīnahum)." Al-Naḥḥās said: this statement of Abū ʿUbayda is not acceptable, because he argued with something that opposes the great majority, and there is no proof in it either, for even if it is true that it is in the muṣḥaf of Ubayy, it would be possible for dīnahum to be an apposition (badal) of al-ḥaqq.

﴿And they will know that Allah is the Manifest Truth﴾, i.e., and they will know, upon witnessing that and its occurrence, in accordance with what the Mighty Book has declared, that Allah is the Truth, established in His essence, attributes, and actions, the Manifest, who makes things clear as they are in themselves. Glorified is He is named "the Truth" because His worship is the truth, to the exclusion of the worship of others.

It was also said: He is named "the Truth," i.e., the Existent, because its opposite is falsehood, which is non-existence.

Then, glorified is He, concluded the verses concerning the people of the slander with a comprehensive statement, saying: ﴿Wicked women are for wicked men, and wicked men for wicked women﴾, i.e., wicked women among women are for wicked men among men, meaning they are specific to them and do not go beyond them; likewise wicked men are specific to wicked women and do not go beyond them. Similarly is His saying: ﴿And good women are for good men, and good men for good women﴾. Mujāhid, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, ʿAṭāʾ, and most of the exegetes said: the meaning is: wicked words are for wicked men, and wicked men are for wicked words; and good words are for good men, and good men are for good words. Al-Naḥḥās said: this is the best of what has been said.

Al-Zajjāj said: its meaning is that none speaks wicked words except wicked men and women. This is a censure of those who slandered ʿĀ'isha with wickedness and a praise of those who cleared her.

It was said: this verse is built upon His saying: ﴿The fornicator marries none but a fornicatress﴾ [al-Nūr: 3]. So the wicked women are the adulteresses, and the good women are the chaste; likewise the wicked men and the good men. The indication here by His saying: ﴿Those are cleared of what they say﴾ refers to the good men and good women, i.e., they are cleared of what the wicked men and wicked women say. It was said: the indication is to the wives of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace. It was said: to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, ʿĀ'isha, and Ṣafwān ibn al-Muʿaṭṭal. It was said: ʿĀ'isha and Ṣafwān only.

Al-Farrāʾ said: it is in the plural as in His saying: ﴿But if he has brothers﴾, where the intended meaning is two brothers. ﴿For them is forgiveness﴾, i.e., these cleared ones have great forgiveness for what humans are not free from of sins. ﴿And a noble provision﴾, which is the provision of Paradise.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās concerning His saying: ﴿And let not those of virtue among you and abundance swear﴾, the verse: he said, it means: let them not swear that they will not benefit anyone.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from ʿĀ'isha, she said: Mistaḥ ibn Uthāthah was among those who took upon himself the greater part of the slander from the people of the slander, and he was a relative of Abū Bakr and was under his maintenance. So Abū Bakr swore that he would never give him any good. Then Allah revealed: ﴿And let not those of virtue among you and abundance swear...﴾ the verse. She said: so Abū Bakr returned him to his maintenance and said: "I will not swear an oath and then see something other than it as better, except that I will break it and do what is better." This has been narrated through various chains from a group of the Successors.

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās concerning the verse, he said: some men among the companions of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, had accused ʿĀ'isha of something ugly, spread it, and spoke about her. So some of the companions of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, including Abū Bakr, swore that they would not give charity to a man who spoke any of this and would not join ties with him. So Allah said: "Let not those of virtue among you and abundance swear that they will not join their kin and give them of their wealth as they used to do before that." Then Allah commanded that they be forgiven and pardoned.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ḥākim (who authenticated it), and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him concerning His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who accuse chaste women﴾, the verse, he said: it was revealed concerning ʿĀ'isha specifically.

Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr, Ibn Jarīr, al-Ṭabarānī, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him also concerning the verse, he said: this is about ʿĀ'isha and the wives of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, and no repentance was granted to whoever did that, while repentance was granted to whoever slandered a believing woman other than the wives of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace. Then he recited: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women﴾ up to His saying: ﴿except those who repent﴾.

Abū Yaʿlā, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ṭabarānī, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abū Saʿīd that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, said: "When the Day of Resurrection comes, the disbeliever will be made to recognize his deeds, but he will deny and dispute. It will be said: 'These are your neighbours, who bear witness against you,' and he will say: 'They lie.' It will be said: 'Your family and your kin,' and he will say: 'They lie.' It will be said: 'Swear,' and they will swear. Then Allah will seal their mouths, and their tongues and their hands will bear witness against them. Then He will cause them to enter the Fire."

It has been narrated from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, through a number of the Companions, what includes the testimony of the limbs against the disobedient.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās concerning His saying, glorified is He: ﴿On that day Allah will pay them their due reward in full﴾, he said: their reckoning. And everything in the Qur'an that is "dīn" means the reckoning.

al-Ṭabarānī and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Bahz ibn Ḥakīm, from his father, from his grandfather, that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, recited: ﴿On that day Allah will pay them their due reward in full﴾.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 24, verses 22–26 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Jarir, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: ﴿The evil women [are] for evil men﴾, he said: "From speech (al-kalam)." ﴿And evil men [are] for evil women﴾: "From men." ﴿And the good women [are] for good men﴾: "From speech." ﴿And the good men [are] for good women﴾: "From people." ﴿And the good men [are] for good women﴾: "From people." ﴿And the good women [are] for good men﴾: "From speech." It was revealed concerning those who said about the wife of the Prophet (ﷺ) what they said of slander (buhtan).

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani narrated from Mujahid something similar to it.

Ibn Jarir and al-Tabarani narrated from Qatadah something similar to it as well, and likewise it was related from a group of the Successors (tabiʿun).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani narrated from Ibn Zayd regarding the verse, he said: "It was revealed concerning ʿAʾishah when the hypocrites accused her with slander (buhtan) and false charge (fiyra), and Allah cleared her of that. ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy was the evil one, so he was most fitting to have the evil woman, and she to have him. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was good, so he was most fitting to have the good woman, and ʿAʾishah was the good one, and she was most fitting to have the good man." And regarding His saying: ﴿Those are cleared of what they say﴾, he said: "Here ʿAʾishah was cleared."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from ʿAʾishah that she said: "My excuse was revealed from the heaven. I was created good, and with a good man. I was promised forgiveness and a great reward."

﴿And they will know that Allah is the Manifest Truth﴾, i.e., and they will know, upon witnessing that and its occurrence, in accordance with what the Mighty Book has declared, that Allah is the Truth, established in His essence, attributes, and actions, the Manifest, who makes things clear as they are in themselves. ﴿And they will know that Allah is the Manifest Truth﴾, i.e., and they will know, upon witnessing that and its occurrence, in accordance with what the Mighty Book has declared, that Allah is the Truth, established in His essence, attributes, and actions, the Manifest, who makes things clear as they are in themselves. Ibn Jarir and al-Tabarani narrated from Qatadah something similar to it as well, and likewise it was related from a group of the Successors (tabiʿun).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani narrated from Ibn Zayd regarding the verse, he said: "It was revealed concerning ʿAʾishah when the hypocrites accused her with slander (buhtan) and false charge (fiyra), and Allah cleared her of that. ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy was the evil one, so he was most fitting to have the evil woman, and she to have him. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was good, so he was most fitting to have the good woman, and ʿAʾishah was the good one, and she was most fitting to have the good man." And regarding His saying: ﴿Those are cleared of what they say﴾, he said: "Here ʿAʾishah was cleared."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from ʿAʾishah that she said: "My excuse was revealed from the heaven. I was created good, and with a good man. I was promised forgiveness and a great reward."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 24, verses 27–29:

When God, glory be to Him, finished mentioning the prohibition of fornication and false accusation, He began to mention the prohibition of entering houses without seeking permission, because mixing of men with women in such houses could lead to one of the two matters mentioned. Also, a person is in his house and place of privacy in a state that he may not like anyone else to see him in. So God, glory be to Him, forbade entering the houses of others until a specified limit, which is His saying: ﴿until you seek familiarity [tasta'nisu]﴾. Al-istinas (seeking familiarity) means al-istila' (seeking knowledge) and al-istikhbar (seeking information), that is: until you seek to know who is in the house. The meaning is: until you know that the owner of the house has become aware of you, and you know that he has permitted your entry. When you know that, you enter. From the same root is His saying: ﴿But if you perceive in them maturity of judgment [rushdan]﴾ [al-Nisa': 6], meaning, if you know.

Al-Khalil said: al-istinas is al-istikshaf (uncovering, discovering), from anisa al-shay' when one sees it, like His saying: ﴿Indeed, I have perceived a fire [anastu naran]﴾ [Ta-Ha: 10; al-Naml: 7], meaning, I saw.

Ibn Jarir said: it means "and that you may make yourselves familiar [tu'nisu anfusakum]."

Ibn Atiyyah said: the morphology of the verb rules out that it is from anisa.

The meaning of Ibn Jarir's words is that it is from al-istinas, which is the opposite of al-istiwhash (feeling of strangeness), because one who knocks on the door of another does not know whether he will be permitted or not. He is thus like one who feels estranged until he is permitted; when he is permitted, he becomes familiar. So God, glory be to Him, forbade entering those houses until the one entering is given permission.

It was also said: it is from al-ins (humankind), meaning to ascertain whether there is a person there or not. It was also said: the meaning of al-istinas is al-isti'dhan (seeking permission), that is: do not enter them until you seek permission.

Al-Wahidi said: a group of exegetes said: until you seek permission. This is supported by what al-Qurtubi related from Ibn Abbas, Ubayy and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, that they recited: ﴿until you seek permission [tasta'dhinu]﴾. Malik said, as Ibn Wahb related from him: al-istinas, as it seems to me, and God knows best, is al-isti'dhan. His saying: ﴿and greet its occupants﴾ has been explained by the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, as will come, namely by saying: "Peace be upon you, may I enter?" once or three times, as will come.

They differed as to whether one should give precedence to seeking permission or to greeting. It was said one gives precedence to seeking permission, so he says: "May I enter? Peace be upon you," because the verse mentions familiarity before greeting.

Most scholars said: he gives precedence to greeting before seeking permission, so he says: "Peace be upon you, may I enter?" and this is the truth, because the Prophet's explanation of the verse was like this.

It was also said: if his gaze falls upon a person, he gives precedence to greeting; otherwise he gives precedence to seeking permission.

﴿That is better for you﴾: the reference is to seeking familiarity and greeting, that is: your entering with seeking permission and greeting is better for you than entering suddenly. ﴿that you may remember﴾ that seeking permission is better for you. This clause is connected to an implied element, that is: you were commanded to seek permission. By "remembrance" is meant taking admonition and acting upon what they were commanded.

﴿But if you find no one therein, then do not enter them until permission is given to you﴾: that is, if you do not find in the houses that belong to others anyone from whom permission is to be sought, then do not enter them until permission is given to you to enter from the one who has the authority to grant permission.

Ibn Jarir related from Mujahid that he said: the meaning of the verse, "if you find no one therein," is: if there is no property of yours therein. He deemed this weak, and it is indeed deserving of weakness, because the intended "no one" mentioned refers to the occupants of the houses who grant permission to others to enter, not to the belongings of those entering them.

﴿And if you are told, "Go back," then go back﴾: that is, if the people of the house say to you, "Go back," then go back, and do not repeat seeking permission a second time, and do not wait after that for them to grant you permission after their command to you to return.

Then God, glory be to Him, made clear that returning is better than insistence, repeated seeking of permission, and sitting at the door. So He said: ﴿That is purer for you﴾, that is, more excellent and purer than being defiled by contention over entering, because in that there is the soundness of the heart, distance from suspicion, and flight from baseness. ﴿And God is Knowing of what you do﴾: no deed of yours is hidden from Him.

﴿There is no blame upon you for entering houses not inhabited in which there is [some] benefit for you﴾: that is, there is no blame upon you for entering, without seeking permission, houses that are not inhabited.

The people differed concerning what is meant by these houses. Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah, Qatadah and Mujahid said: they are the inns on the travelled roads, established for the wayfarer to take shelter in.

Ibn Zayd and al-Sha'bi said: they are the shops of the qaysariyyat (covered markets). Al-Sha'bi said: because they brought their goods and placed them in them, and said to the people, "Come [halumma]."

Ata' said: what is meant by them is the ruined houses which people enter for urination and defecation, so in this too there is benefit.

It was also said: they are the houses of Makkah. This was related from Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah as well, and it agrees with the view of the one who said that people share in them. However, God, glory be to Him, has restricted the houses mentioned here by describing them as uninhabited.

Al-mata' (benefit): according to the lexicographers, it is al-manfa'ah (benefit), so the meaning of the verse is: there is benefit for you in them. From the same root is His saying: ﴿and provide for them [wa matti'uhunna]﴾ [al-Baqarah: 236], and the saying: "May God give you enjoyment [amta'a Allahu bika]." Al-Sha'bi explained al-mata' in his earlier statement as the goods that are sold.

Jabir ibn Zayd said: what is meant by al-mata' is not the household furnishings, but whatever else is needed.

Al-Nahhas said: this is good and agrees with the language.

﴿And God knows what you reveal and what you conceal﴾: that is, what you show and what you hide. In this there is a warning to whoever does not observe God's etiquette concerning entering the houses of others.

Al-Firyabi and Ibn Jarir related, by way of Adi ibn Thabit, from a man of the Ansar who said: "A woman said: O Messenger of God, I am in my house in a state in which I do not like anyone to see me, neither a child nor a parent, and my father comes in upon me and enters upon me, so what should I do?" The wording of Ibn Jarir is: "And a man from my family keeps entering upon me while I am in that state, so God revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, do not enter houses other than your own﴾," the verse.

Al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Anbari in al-Masahif, Ibn Mandah in Gharib Shu'bah, al-Hakim who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab, and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtarah related from several routes from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying: ﴿until you seek familiarity﴾, that he said: "The scribe made an error: 'until you seek permission' ﴿and greet its occupants﴾."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi related from Ibrahim al-Nakha'i that he said, in the codex of Abdullah: ("until you greet its occupants and seek permission"). Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir related the same from Ikrimah.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Abbas that he said: "Al-istinas is al-isti'dhan."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Hakim, al-Tirmidhi, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn Abi Hatim related, "from Abu Ayyub who said: I said, O Messenger of God, what do you think of God's saying, ﴿until you seek familiarity and greet its occupants﴾ (p-1007) — we know this greeting, so what is the familiarity?" He said: "A man speaks with a glorification (tasbihah), a magnification (takbirah) and a praise (tahmidah), and clears his throat, and thereby informs the occupants of the house."

Ibn Kathir said: this is a gharib (unusual) hadith.

Al-Tabarani related from Abu Ayyub that the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, said: "Familiarity is that he calls the servant until the occupants of the house with whom he greets become familiar."

Ibn Sa'd, Ahmad, al-Bukhari in al-Adab, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab related by way of Kaladah: "that Safwan ibn Umayyah sent him during the conquest (of Makkah) with milk and young cucumbers, while the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, was at the upper part of the valley. He said: I entered upon him without greeting and without seeking permission, so the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, said: 'Go back, and say: Peace be upon you, may I enter?'" al-Tirmidhi said: "Hasan gharib; we do not know it except from his hadith."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, al-Bukhari in al-Adab, Abu Dawud and al-Bayhaqi in al-Sunan related by way of Rib'i, who said: "A man from Banu Amir narrated to us that he sought permission from the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, while he was in a house, so he said: 'May I come in?' The Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, said to his servant: 'Go out to this man and teach him the seeking of permission. Tell him: Say, Peace be upon you, may I enter?'"

Ibn Jarir related from Umar ibn Sa'id al-Thaqafi something similar, raised (to the Prophet), but he said: "The Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, said to a female slave of his called Rawdah: 'Stand up to this man and teach him.'"

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri who said: "I was sitting in a gathering of the Ansar when Abu Musa came, frightened. We said to him: What has frightened you? He said: Umar commanded me to come to him, so I came to him and sought permission three times, but was not given permission. He said: What prevented you from coming to me? I said: I came and sought permission three times, but was not given permission, and the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, said: 'If one of you seeks permission three times and is not given permission, let him go back.'"

He said: "You must bring evidence for this." They said: "Only the youngest of the people will stand (to testify)." So Abu Sa'id stood up with him to testify for him. Umar said to Abu Musa: "I did not accuse you, but the hadith from the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, is weighty."

In the Two Sahihs and elsewhere, from the hadith of Sahl ibn Sa'd, who said: "A man looked through a hole in the room of the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, while he had a comb with which he was scratching his head. He said: 'If I knew you were looking, I would have stabbed you in your eye with it. Permission was only prescribed because of the gaze.'"

In another wording: "Permission was only prescribed because of the gaze."

Abu Ya'la, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh related from Anas who said: "A man from the Muhajirun said: I sought this verse my whole life, but I did not attain it, that I should seek permission to enter upon some of my brothers, and he says to me: Go back, and I go back, rejoicing at His saying: ﴿And if you are told, 'Go back,' then go back; it is purer for you.'"

Al-Bukhari in al-Adab, Abu Dawud in al-Nasikh wa al-Mansukh (on naskh, abrogation), and Ibn Jarir related from Ibn Abbas who said: "﴿O you who have believed, do not enter houses other than your own until you seek familiarity and greet its occupants﴾ was abrogated by this: ﴿There is no blame upon you for entering houses not inhabited in which there is [some] benefit for you﴾."

This is supported by what al-Qurtubi related from Ibn Abbas, Ubayy and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, that they recited: ﴿until you seek permission [tasta'dhinu]﴾. His saying: ﴿and greet its occupants﴾ has been explained by the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, as will come, namely by saying: "Peace be upon you, may I enter?" once or three times, as will come.

They differed as to whether one should give precedence to seeking permission or to greeting. It was said one gives precedence to seeking permission, so he says: "May I enter? Peace be upon you," because the verse mentions familiarity before greeting.

Most scholars said: he gives precedence to greeting before seeking permission, so he says: "Peace be upon you, may I enter?" and this is the truth, because the Prophet's explanation of the verse was like this.

It was also said: if his gaze falls upon a person, he gives precedence to greeting; otherwise he gives precedence to seeking permission.

﴿That is better for you﴾: the reference is to seeking familiarity and greeting, that is: your entering with seeking permission and greeting is better for you than entering suddenly. ﴿that you may remember﴾ that seeking permission is better for you. This clause is connected to an implied element, that is: you were commanded to seek permission. By "remembrance" is meant taking admonition and acting upon what they were commanded.

﴿But if you find no one therein, then do not enter them until permission is given to you﴾: that is, if you do not find in the houses that belong to others anyone from whom permission is to be sought, then do not enter them until permission is given to you to enter from the one who has the authority to grant permission.

Ibn Jarir related from Mujahid that he said: the meaning of the verse, "if you find no one therein," is: if there is no property of yours therein. He deemed this weak, and it is indeed deserving of weakness, because the intended "no one" mentioned refers to the occupants of the houses who grant permission to others to enter, not to the belongings of those entering them.

﴿And if you are told, "Go back," then go back﴾: that is, if the people of the house say to you, "Go back," then go back, and do not repeat seeking permission a second time, and do not wait after that for them to grant you permission after their command to you to return.

Then God, glory be to Him, made clear that returning is better than insistence, repeated seeking of permission, and sitting at the door. So He said: ﴿That is purer for you﴾, that is, more excellent and purer than being defiled by contention over entering, because in that there is the soundness of the heart, distance from suspicion, and flight from baseness. ﴿And God is Knowing of what you do﴾: no deed of yours is hidden from Him.

﴿There is no blame upon you for entering houses not inhabited in which there is [some] benefit for you﴾: that is, there is no blame upon you for entering, without seeking permission, houses that are not inhabited.

The people differed concerning what is meant by these houses. Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah, Qatadah and Mujahid said: they are the inns on the travelled roads, established for the wayfarer to take shelter in.

Ibn Zayd and al-Sha'bi said: they are the shops of the qaysariyyat (covered markets). Al-Sha'bi said: because they brought their goods and placed them in them, and said to the people, "Come [halumma]."

Ata' said: what is meant by them is the ruined houses which people enter for urination and defecation, so in this too there is benefit.

It was also said: they are the houses of Makkah. This was related from Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah as well, and it agrees with the view of the one who said that people share in them. However, God, glory be to Him, has restricted the houses mentioned here by describing them as uninhabited.

Al-mata' (benefit): according to the lexicographers, it is al-manfa'ah (benefit), so the meaning of the verse is: there is benefit for you in them. From the same root is His saying: ﴿and provide for them [wa matti'uhunna]﴾ [al-Baqarah: 236], and the saying: "May God give you enjoyment [amta'a Allahu bika]." Al-Sha'bi explained al-mata' in his earlier statement as the goods that are sold.

Jabir ibn Zayd said: what is meant by al-mata' is not the household furnishings, but whatever else is needed.

Al-Nahhas said: this is good and agrees with the language.

﴿And God knows what you reveal and what you conceal﴾: that is, what you show and what you hide. In this there is a warning to whoever does not observe God's etiquette concerning entering the houses of others.

Al-Firyabi and Ibn Jarir related, by way of Adi ibn Thabit, from a man of the Ansar who said: "A woman said: O Messenger of God, I am in my house in a state in which I do not like anyone to see me, neither a child nor a parent, and my father comes in upon me and enters upon me, so what should I do?" The wording of Ibn Jarir is: "And a man from my family keeps entering upon me while I am in that state, so God revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, do not enter houses other than your own﴾," the verse.

Al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Anbari in al-Masahif, Ibn Mandah in Gharib Shu'bah, al-Hakim who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab, and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtarah related from several routes from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying: ﴿until you seek familiarity﴾, that he said: "The scribe made an error: 'until you seek permission' ﴿and greet its occupants﴾."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi related from Ibrahim al-Nakha'i that he said, in the codex of Abdullah: ("until you greet its occupants and seek permission"). Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir related the same from Ikrimah.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Abbas that he said: "Al-istinas is al-isti'dhan."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Hakim, al-Tirmidhi, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn Abi Hatim related, "from Abu Ayyub who said: I said, O Messenger of God, what do you think of God's saying, ﴿until you seek familiarity and greet its occupants﴾ (p-1007) — we know this greeting, so what is the familiarity?" He said: "A man speaks with a glorification (tasbihah), a magnification (takbirah) and a praise (tahmidah), and clears his throat, and thereby informs the occupants of the house."

Ibn Kathir said: this is a gharib (unusual) hadith.

Al-Tabarani related from Abu Ayyub that the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, said: "Familiarity is that he calls the servant until the occupants of the house with whom he greets become familiar."

Ibn Sa'd, Ahmad, al-Bukhari in al-Adab, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab related by way of Kaladah: "that Safwan ibn Umayyah sent him during the conquest (of Makkah) with milk and young cucumbers, while the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, was at the upper part of the valley. He said: I entered upon him without greeting and without seeking permission, so the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, said: 'Go back, and say: Peace be upon you, may I enter?'" al-Tirmidhi said: "Hasan gharib; we do not know it except from his hadith."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, al-Bukhari in al-Adab, Abu Dawud and al-Bayhaqi in al-Sunan related by way of Rib'i, who said: "A man from Banu Amir narrated to us that he sought permission from the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, while he was in a house, so he said: 'May I come in?' The Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, said to his servant: 'Go out to this man and teach him the seeking of permission. Tell him: Say, Peace be upon you, may I enter?'"

Ibn Jarir related from Umar ibn Sa'id al-Thaqafi something similar, raised (to the Prophet), but he said: "The Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, said to a female slave of his called Rawdah: 'Stand up to this man and teach him.'"

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri who said: "I was sitting in a gathering of the Ansar when Abu Musa came, frightened. We said to him: What has frightened you? He said: Umar commanded me to come to him, so I came to him and sought permission three times, but was not given permission. He said: What prevented you from coming to me? I said: I came and sought permission three times, but was not given permission, and the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, said: 'If one of you seeks permission three times and is not given permission, let him go back.'"

He said: "You must bring evidence for this." They said: "Only the youngest of the people will stand (to testify)." So Abu Sa'id stood up with him to testify for him. Umar said to Abu Musa: "I did not accuse you, but the hadith from the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, is weighty."

In the Two Sahihs and elsewhere, from the hadith of Sahl ibn Sa'd, who said: "A man looked through a hole in the room of the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, while he had a comb with which he was scratching his head. He said: 'If I knew you were looking, I would have stabbed you in your eye with it. Permission was only prescribed because of the gaze.'"

In another wording: "Permission was only prescribed because of the gaze."

Abu Ya'la, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh related from Anas who said: "A man from the Muhajirun said: I sought this verse my whole life, but I did not attain it, that I should seek permission to enter upon some of my brothers, and he says to me: Go back, and I go back, rejoicing at His saying: ﴿And if you are told, 'Go back,' then go back; it is purer for you.'"

Al-Bukhari in al-Adab, Abu Dawud in al-Nasikh wa al-Mansukh (on naskh, abrogation), and Ibn Jarir related from Ibn Abbas who said: "﴿O you who have believed, do not enter houses other than your own until you seek familiarity and greet its occupants﴾ was abrogated by this: ﴿There is no blame upon you for entering houses not inhabited in which there is [some] benefit for you﴾."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 24, verses 30–31 (part 1 of 2):

.
When He, glory be to Him, mentioned the ruling on seeking permission (istidhan), He followed it with mention of the ruling on looking in general, so that lowering the gaze on the part of the one seeking permission falls within it, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Permission was only enjoined for the sake of the gaze." He specified the believers, although it is forbidden for others too, because cutting off the means to fornication, of which looking is one, is most incumbent upon them than upon others, and they are more deserving of it than anyone else.

It has been said: in the verse there is evidence that the disbelievers are not addressed by the legal rulings (shar'iyyat), as some scholars maintain. In the speech there is an ellipsis, and the implied meaning is ﴿Say to the believing men﴾ — "lower" (ghuddu), "they should lower" (yaghuddu). The meaning of lowering the gaze is closing the eyelid over the eye so that sight is prevented. From it is the saying of Jarir:

"So lower your glance, for you are from Numayr; you have not reached Ka'b, nor Kilab."

And the saying of 'Antarah:

"I lower my glance whenever my neighbour appears to me, until my neighbour conceals her dwelling."

The "min" in His saying ﴿of their gaze﴾ is partitive (tab'id), and this is the view of most scholars, who explained it as meaning: lowering the gaze from what is forbidden and confining it to what is permitted. It has been said: the partitive sense is that the one who looks is excused for the first glance that falls upon him without intention. Al-Akhfash said it is extra (za'ida), but Sibawayh rejected this. It has been said it is for explaining the category (li-bayan al-jins), as stated by Abu al-Baqa', and this was objected to on the grounds that no vague noun had preceded it that would be explained by "min." It has been said it is for the beginning of the goal (ibtida' al-ghayah), as stated by Ibn 'Atiyyah. It has been said: al-ghadd means reduction; one says "ghadda fulan min fulan," meaning he belittled him. So when the eye is not allowed to perform its function, it is lowered and diminished, and thus "min" is connected to the verb "ghadd" and is not one of the four meanings mentioned.

In this verse there is evidence for the prohibition of looking at anyone whom it is not permitted to look at. The meaning of ﴿and guard their private parts﴾ is that it is obligatory for them to guard them from what is forbidden to them.

It has been said: the intended meaning is covering their private parts from being seen by one for whom seeing them is not lawful, and there is no barrier to intending both meanings, for all of it falls under guarding the private parts.

It has been said that the reason for using "min" with the eyes but not with the private parts is that the matter of gaze is broader, for nothing is forbidden of it except what is excluded, whereas guarding the private parts is restricted, for nothing of them is lawful except what is excluded.

It has been said: the reason is that lowering the gaze entirely is almost impossible, unlike guarding the private parts, which is possible in every respect. The reference of "that" (dhalika) in His saying is to what was mentioned of lowering the gaze and guarding, and it is a subject (mubtada'), whose predicate is ﴿is purer for them﴾, meaning cleaner for them from the filth of doubt and more pure than being involved in this base act. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Aware of what they do﴾ — nothing of their doing is hidden from Him.

In this there is a warning for whoever does not lower his gaze and guard his private parts.

﴿And say to the believing women that they should lower their gaze from their eyes⦆ — He, glory be to Him, specified the females with this address for emphasis, since they enter under the address to the believers by way of predominance (taghlib), as in the rest of the Qur'anic addresses. The doubling appears in "yaghdudna" but does not appear in "yaghuddu," because the final consonant of the verb in the first is vowelled, while in the second it is quiescent; both are in the position of jussive as an answer to the imperative. He, glory be to Him, began with lowering the gaze in both places before guarding the private parts, because looking is a means to failing to guard the private parts, and the means precedes that to which it leads. The meaning of "yaghdudna min absarihinna" is the same as the meaning of "yaghuddu min absarihim," so it is used as evidence for the prohibition of women looking at what is forbidden to them. Likewise, it is obligatory for them to guard their private parts in the manner already mentioned for the men's guarding of theirs. ﴿And not to display their adornment﴾ — that is, what they adorn themselves with, of jewellery and other things. In the prohibition against displaying the places of adornment on their bodies there is a fortiori.

Then He, glory be to Him, made an exception to this prohibition, saying: ﴿except what appears thereof﴾. People differed concerning the apparent adornment and what it is. Ibn Mas'ud and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the apparent adornment is the clothing, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr added the face. 'Ata' and al-Awza'i said: the face and the palms. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah and al-Miswar ibn Makhramah said: the apparent adornment is kohl, siwak, dye up to the middle of the shin, and the like, for it is permissible for the woman to display it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said that the woman displays nothing of her adornment and conceals all of her adornment, and the exception applies to what appears of it by necessity. You are not unaware that the apparent wording of the Qur'anic text is a prohibition against displaying adornment except what appears of it, such as the outer garment, the veil and the like, and of the jewellery on the hands and feet and the like; and if by adornment is meant its places, then the exception refers to what it is hard for the woman to cover, such as the two palms and the two feet and the like.

Likewise, when the prohibition against displaying adornment entails the prohibition against displaying its places by implication of the address, the exception is taken as we have stated for both cases. As for when adornment includes both the places of adornment and what women adorn themselves with, the matter is clear, and the exception applies to all of it.

Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir: adornment is of two kinds: natural (khilqiyyah) and acquired (muktasabah). The natural is the face, for it is the root of adornment; the acquired adornment is what the woman strives for in beautifying her creation, such as clothing, jewellery, kohl and dye. From this is His saying ﴿Take your adornment﴾ [al-A'raf: 31], and the saying of the poet:

"They take their adornment, the finest you see; and when they are left bare, they are the best of the bare ones."

﴿And let them draw their veils over their bosoms﴾ — the majority read the lam of command with sukun. Abu 'Amr read it with kasra according to the original, since the original of the lam of command is kasra; this reading is reported from Ibn 'Abbas. "Khumur" is the plural of "khimar," which is what a woman covers her head with, and from it come "ikhtamarat al-mar'ah" and "takhammarat."

"Juyub" is the plural of "jayb," which is the opening of the shift and the shirt, derived from "jawb," meaning cutting.

The exegetes said: the women of the Jahiliyyah used to let their veils hang behind them, while their collars in front were wide, so their necks and necklaces would be exposed; so they were commanded to draw their head-coverings over the collars, so that this would conceal what used to show. In the word "daraba" there is intensity in the act of placing, which is attaching.

The majority read "bi-khumurihinna" with a moving mim; Talhah ibn Musarrif read it with sukun.

The majority read "juyubihinna" with a damma on the jim; Ibn Kathir and some Kufans read it with a kasra; and many of the earlier grammarians do not permit this reading.

Al-Zajjaj said: it is permissible to replace the damma with a kasra; as for what is reported from Hamzah of combining damma and kasra, it is impossible, and no one can pronounce it except by indication. The majority have explained "juyub" by what we have mentioned, and this is the literal meaning.

Muqatil said: the meaning of "'ala juyubihinna" is "over their breasts," so there is an omitted modifier in the verse, namely: over the places of their collars.

Then He, glory be to Him, repeated the prohibition against displaying adornment for the sake of the exception He is about to mention, saying: ﴿And not to display their adornment except to their husbands﴾. "Ba'l" in the speech of the Arabs means husband and master. He put the husbands first, because they are the ones intended by the adornment; and because every part of the wife's body and of the concubine is lawful to them. Similar is His saying: ﴿And those who guard their private parts, except from their wives or what their right hands possess, for they are not blameworthy﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 5–6]. Then, when He, glory be to Him, had excepted the husband, He followed it with the exception of mahrams, saying: ﴿or their fathers, or the fathers of their husbands﴾ up to His saying ﴿or the sons of their sisters﴾. He permitted women to display adornment to these because of the frequency of association and the absence of fear of temptation, since human nature has aversion toward close relatives.

It is narrated from al-Hasan and al-Husayn, may Allah be pleased with them both, that they would not look at the Mothers of the Believers, on the view that the sons of the husbands were not mentioned in the verse concerning the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ), which is His saying: ﴿There is no blame upon them concerning their fathers﴾ [al-Ahzab: 55]. The "sons of their husbands" means the male children of the husbands. His saying "or their sons" includes the sons' sons however low they go, and the sons of their daughters however low they go; likewise the fathers of the husbands, the fathers of the fathers, and the fathers of the mothers however high they go; likewise the sons of the husbands however low they go; and likewise the sons of brothers and sisters.

The majority held that the paternal uncle and maternal uncle are like the rest of the mahrams in the permissibility of looking at what is permitted for them. There is no mention of foster-relationship in the verse, but it is like kinship.

Al-Sha'bi and 'Ikrimah said: the paternal uncle and the maternal uncle are not mahrams. The meaning of "or their women" (aw nisa'ihinna) is those who are particular to them and who are close to them by service or companionship, and this includes the female slaves; excluded from it are the women of the disbelievers, whether of the protected people (ahl al-dhimmah) or others, so it is not lawful for them to display their adornment to them, because they do not refrain from describing them to men.

On this question there is disagreement among the scholars, and the attribution of "women" to them indicates that this is specific to believing women.

﴿or what their right hands possess﴾ — the apparent meaning of the verse includes male and female slaves without distinction between whether they are Muslims or disbelievers; this is the view of a group of scholars, and 'A'ishah, Umm Salamah, Ibn 'Abbas and Malik held it.

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: do not let this verse deceive you: "or what their right hands possess" was only meant for the female slaves, and was not meant for the male slaves.

Al-Sha'bi used to dislike that a male slave look at the hair of his mistress; this is the view of 'Ata', Mujahid, al-Hasan and Ibn Sirin, and it is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, and Abu Hanifah and Ibn Jurayj held it. ﴿or male attendants who have no need [of women]﴾ — the majority read "ghayri" in the genitive. Abu Bakr and Ibn 'Amir read it in the accusative, as an exception; it is also said: in the accusative as a detachment (al-qat'). "Al-tabi'in" means those who follow a people and obtain some of their food, having no concern except that and no need for women; this was said by Mujahid, 'Ikrimah and al-Sha'bi. "Min al-rijal" is in the accusative position as a circumstantial qualifier (hal).

The root of "irbah," "arab" and "ma'rabah" is need, and the plural is "ma'arib," meaning needs. From it is His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿and in it are other needs (ma'arib)﴾, and from it is the saying of Tarafah:

"When a man utters folly, sin and obscenity, he advances one day, then his needs are lost."

It has been said: by "ghayr uli al-irbah min al-rijal" is meant the fools who have no need for women; it has been said: the simpleton; it has been said: the impotent; it has been said: the eunuch; it has been said: the effeminate; it has been said: the old man. There is no basis for this specification; rather, the verse means its apparent sense: those who follow the household and have no need for women and never experience that in any state. Thus whoever has this description is included, and whoever else is excluded. ﴿or children who have not yet attained knowledge of women's private nakedness﴾ — "tifl" is applied to the singular, dual and plural; or what is meant here is the category placed in the position of the plural, indicated by its being described with a plural description. In Ubayy's codex it reads "aw al-atfal" in the plural. A person is called "tifl" as long as he has not reached puberty (ihtilam). The meaning of "lam yazharu" is "did not become aware," from "zuhur" in the sense of "ittila'," as stated by Ibn Qutaybah.

It has been said: its meaning is: they have not reached the limit of desire for intercourse, as stated by al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj; one says "zahartu 'ala kadha" when I overcame it and subdued it.

The meaning: they have not become aware of women's private parts and uncovered them for intercourse, or they have not reached the limit of desire for intercourse.

The majority's reading is "'awrat" with a sukun on the waw, for lightening; this is the dialect of the majority of the Arabs. Ibn 'Amir in one narration read it with a fatha. Ibn Abi Ishaq and al-A'mash also read it thus. This reading is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, and it is the dialect of Hudhayl ibn Mudrikah; from it is the saying of the poet, which al-Farra' recited:

A brother of fair-skinned women, who goes out in the morning and returns, a companion for stroking the shoulders, a swift one.

The scholars differed over whether it is obligatory to cover what lies beyond the face and the two palms of young children. It was said that it is not obligatory, since there is no legal obligation (taklif) upon them, and this is the sound view. It was also said that it is obligatory, since a woman may feel desire for them.

Likewise, they differed concerning the 'awrah (the parts of the body that must be covered) of the elderly man whose desire has ceased. The better view is that the sanctity (hurmah) remains as it was. Therefore, it is not permissible to look at his 'awrah, nor is it permissible for him to expose it.

The scholars differed about the limit of the 'awrah. Al-Qurtubi said: The Muslims have agreed that the two private parts (saw'atan) are 'awrah for both man and woman, and that the entire body of a woman is 'awrah except her face and her hands, though there is disagreement on this. Most scholars said: The 'awrah of a man is from his navel to his knee. ﴿And let them not stamp their feet so that what they conceal of their adornment may be known﴾. That is, a woman should not strike her foot when she walks so that the sound of her anklet may be heard by men who hear it, and they thereby know that she wears an anklet.

Al-Zajjaj said: The hearing of this adornment is more stirring of desire than its display.

Then He guided His servants to repentance from acts of disobedience, and said, glorified is He: ﴿And turn to Allah in repentance, all of you, O believers﴾. In this is the command to repent, and there is no disagreement among the Muslims that it is obligatory and that it is one of the obligations of the religion.

The discussion of repentance has already been presented in Surat al-Nisa'.

Then He mentioned what encourages them to repent, saying: ﴿So that you may succeed﴾. That is, that you may attain the happiness of this world and the Hereafter. It was said that what is meant by repentance here is repentance from what they used to do in the Jahiliyyah (the period of ignorance before Islam). The first view is preferable, because it is established in the Sunnah that Islam wipes out what came before it.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, who said: "A man passed by during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on one of the roads of Madinah. He looked at a woman, and she looked at him. Satan whispered to both of them that neither of them had looked at the other except out of admiration for him. Then, while the man was walking alongside a wall and looking at her, the wall met him and split his nose. He said: 'By Allah, I will not wash off the blood until I come to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and inform him of my matter.' He came to him and related his story to him. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'This is the punishment for your sin.' And Allah revealed: ﴿Say to the believing men that they should lower their gaze﴾, the verse."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿Say to the believing men that they should lower their gaze﴾, that he said: That is, from their desires, that which Allah dislikes.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Buraydah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do not follow a glance with another glance, for the first is for you, but the second is not for you." In Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i, from Jarir al-Bajali, who said: "I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about a sudden glance, and he commanded me to turn my gaze away." In the Two Sahihs and others, from the hadith of Abu Sa'id, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Beware of sitting on the roads.' They said: 'O Messenger of Allah, we have no choice but to sit in our gatherings and converse in them.' He said: 'If you refuse, then give the road its due.' They said: 'And what is its due, O Messenger of Allah?' He said: 'Lowering the gaze, removing harm, returning the greeting, enjoining what is right, and forbidding what is wrong.'"

Al-Bukhari, the authors of the Sunan and others narrated from Bahz ibn Hakim, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: "I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, our 'awrat (private parts), what of them do we show and what do we leave?' He said: 'Guard your 'awrah except from your wife or what your right hand possesses.' I said: 'O Prophet of Allah, when people are among one another?' He said: 'If you are able that no one sees it, then let no one see it.' I said: 'When one of us is alone?' He said: 'Allah is more deserving that He be shown shame than people.'"

In the Two Sahihs and others, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah has prescribed for the son of Adam his share of adultery, which he will inevitably attain. The adultery of the eyes is the gaze, the adultery of the tongue is speech, the adultery of the ears is listening, the adultery of the hands is grasping, the adultery of the feet is walking, the soul wishes and desires, and the private part either confirms that or denies it."

Al-Hakim narrated and declared it sound, from Hudhayfah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A glance is one of the arrows of Iblis, poisoned. Whoever abandons it out of fear of Allah, Allah will reward him with a faith whose sweetness he will find in his heart." The hadiths on this subject are numerous.

(p-1010) Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Muqatil, who said: "It has reached us, and Allah knows best, that Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah al-Ansari related that Asma' bint Yazid was in a palm grove belonging to the Banu Harithah, and women would enter upon her without wearing their waist-wrappers, so what was on their feet would show, meaning the anklets, and their breasts and their braids would show. Asma' said: 'How ugly this is!' So Allah revealed that: ﴿And say to the believing women that they should lower their gaze﴾, the verse." In this report, along with its being mursal (lacking a companion in its chain), there is Muqatil.

'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, who declared it sound, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, regarding His words: ﴿And not to reveal their adornment﴾, he said: The adornment is the bracelet, the armlet, the anklet, the earring, and the necklace. ﴿Except what appears thereof﴾, he said: The garments and the outer cloak.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him, who said: The adornment is of two kinds: an apparent adornment and a hidden adornment, which none sees except the husband. As for the apparent adornment, it is the garments. As for the hidden adornment, it is the kohl, the bracelet and the ring.

The wording of Ibn Jarir is: "As for what is apparent of it, it is the garments, and what is hidden, the two anklets, the two earrings and the two bracelets."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Anas regarding His words: ﴿Except what appears thereof﴾, he said: The kohl and the ring.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿And not to reveal their adornment except what appears thereof﴾, he said: The kohl, the ring, the earring and the necklace.

'Abd al-Razzaq and 'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from him, who said: It is the dyeing of the palm and the ring.

Ibn Abi Shaybah and 'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Ibn 'Umar, who said: The apparent adornment is the face and the two palms.

They both (Ibn Abi Shaybah and 'Abd ibn Humayd) narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: ﴿Except what appears thereof﴾ is her face, her two palms and the ring. They both also narrated from him, who said: It is the area of the face and the inner part of the palm.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from 'A'ishah that she was asked about the apparent adornment, and she said: The bangle, the plain ring, and she gathered the edge of her sleeve.

Abu Dawud, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from 'A'ishah: "Asma' bint Abi Bakr entered upon the Prophet (ﷺ) wearing thin garments, so he turned away from her and said: 'O Asma', when a woman reaches menstruation, it is not fitting that anything of her be seen except this,' and he pointed to his face and his palm."

Abu Dawud and Abu Hatim al-Razi said: This is mursal, because it comes through Khalid ibn Duraik from 'A'ishah, and he did not hear from her.

Al-Bukhari, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from 'A'ishah, who said: "May Allah have mercy on the first emigrant women. When Allah revealed: ﴿And let them draw their head-coverings over their bosoms﴾, they split their thickest cloaks and covered themselves with them."

Ibn Jarir, al-Hakim, who declared it sound, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from her with the wording: "The women took their waist-wrappers and split them at the edges, and covered themselves with them."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words: ﴿And not to reveal their adornment except what appears thereof﴾, and the apparent adornment is the face, the kohl of the eyes, the dyeing of the palm and the ring. So this is what she displays in her house to whoever enters upon her.

Then He said: ﴿And not to reveal their adornment except to their husbands or their fathers﴾, the verse. The adornment that she reveals to these is her earring, her necklace and her bracelet. As for her anklet, her upper-arm ornament, her neck and her hair, she reveals these only to her husband.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated through al-Kalbi from Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿or their women﴾, he said: They are the Muslim women. She should not reveal it to a Jewish or Christian woman. It is the neck, the earring and the girdle, and whatever is forbidden for anyone to see except a mahram (a relative whom marriage is forbidden to).

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab that he wrote to Abu 'Ubaydah: "To proceed: it has reached me that some women of the Muslim women enter the bathhouses with the women of the people of polytheism. So prohibit those under your authority from that, for it is not lawful for a woman who believes in Allah and the Last Day to let anyone see her 'awrah except the people of her religion."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "There is no harm in a slave seeing the hair of his mistress."

Abu Dawud, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Anas: "The Prophet (ﷺ) came to Fatimah with a slave who had been given to her, and Fatimah was wearing a garment which, if her head was covered with it, did not reach her feet, and if she covered her feet with it, did not reach her head. When the Prophet (ﷺ) saw what she was facing, he said: 'There is no harm for you. He is only your father and your slave.'" Its chain in the Sunan of Abu Dawud is thus: "Muhammad ibn 'Isa narrated to us, Abu Jumay' Salim ibn Dinar narrated to us, from Thabit, from Anas," and so he mentioned it.

'Abd al-Razzaq and Ahmad narrated from Umm Salamah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If one of you has a mukatab (a slave contracted to buy his freedom), and he has the means to pay, then let her veil herself from him." The chain of Ahmad is thus: "Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah narrated to us, from al-Zuhri, from Nabhan, that Umm Salamah," and so he mentioned it.

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words: ﴿Or male attendants who have no physical desire﴾, he said: This is the one whom women are not shy before.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding the verse, he said: This is the man who follows the people and is dull-witted, not concerned with women and not desiring women.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him, regarding the verse, he said: In earlier times a man would follow a man, and he was not jealous over him, and a woman would not fear to remove her head-covering in his presence. He is the fool who has no need for women.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him also regarding the verse, he said: He is the effeminate man whose member does not stand.

'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from 'A'ishah, who said: "There was an effeminate man who used to enter upon the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ), and they used to count him among those without physical desire. The Prophet (ﷺ) entered one day while he was with one of his wives, and he was describing a woman. He said: 'When she comes forward, she comes with four (folds), and when she turns away, she turns away with eight.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Do I not see that this one knows what is here? Let him not enter upon you again.' So they forbade him."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words: ﴿And not to stamp their feet﴾, which is that she strikes one anklet against the other in front of men, or that she has anklets on her feet and moves them in front of men. So Allah forbade that, for it is one of the works of Satan.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 24, verses 30–31 (part 1 of 2):

.
When He, glory be to Him, mentioned the ruling on seeking permission (istidhan), He followed it with mention of the ruling on looking in general, so that lowering the gaze on the part of the one seeking permission falls within it, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Permission was only enjoined for the sake of the gaze." He specified the believers, although it is forbidden for others too, because cutting off the means to fornication, of which looking is one, is most incumbent upon them than upon others, and they are more deserving of it than anyone else.

It has been said: in the verse there is evidence that the disbelievers are not addressed by the legal rulings (shar'iyyat), as some scholars maintain. In the speech there is an ellipsis, and the implied meaning is ﴿Say to the believing men﴾ — "lower" (ghuddu), "they should lower" (yaghuddu). The meaning of lowering the gaze is closing the eyelid over the eye so that sight is prevented. From it is the saying of Jarir:

"So lower your glance, for you are from Numayr; you have not reached Ka'b, nor Kilab."

And the saying of 'Antarah:

"I lower my glance whenever my neighbour appears to me, until my neighbour conceals her dwelling."

The "min" in His saying ﴿of their gaze﴾ is partitive (tab'id), and this is the view of most scholars, who explained it as meaning: lowering the gaze from what is forbidden and confining it to what is permitted. It has been said: the partitive sense is that the one who looks is excused for the first glance that falls upon him without intention. Al-Akhfash said it is extra (za'ida), but Sibawayh rejected this. It has been said it is for explaining the category (li-bayan al-jins), as stated by Abu al-Baqa', and this was objected to on the grounds that no vague noun had preceded it that would be explained by "min." It has been said it is for the beginning of the goal (ibtida' al-ghayah), as stated by Ibn 'Atiyyah. It has been said: al-ghadd means reduction; one says "ghadda fulan min fulan," meaning he belittled him.
