So when the eye is not allowed to perform its function, it is lowered and diminished, and thus "min" is connected to the verb "ghadd" and is not one of the four meanings mentioned.

In this verse there is evidence for the prohibition of looking at anyone whom it is not permitted to look at. The meaning of ﴿and guard their private parts﴾ is that it is obligatory for them to guard them from what is forbidden to them.

It has been said: the intended meaning is covering their private parts from being seen by one for whom seeing them is not lawful, and there is no barrier to intending both meanings, for all of it falls under guarding the private parts.

It has been said that the reason for using "min" with the eyes but not with the private parts is that the matter of gaze is broader, for nothing is forbidden of it except what is excluded, whereas guarding the private parts is restricted, for nothing of them is lawful except what is excluded.

It has been said: the reason is that lowering the gaze entirely is almost impossible, unlike guarding the private parts, which is possible in every respect. The reference of "that" (dhalika) in His saying is to what was mentioned of lowering the gaze and guarding, and it is a subject (mubtada'), whose predicate is ﴿is purer for them﴾, meaning cleaner for them from the filth of doubt and more pure than being involved in this base act. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Aware of what they do﴾ — nothing of their doing is hidden from Him.

In this there is a warning for whoever does not lower his gaze and guard his private parts.

﴿And say to the believing women that they should lower their gaze from their eyes⦆ — He, glory be to Him, specified the females with this address for emphasis, since they enter under the address to the believers by way of predominance (taghlib), as in the rest of the Qur'anic addresses. The doubling appears in "yaghdudna" but does not appear in "yaghuddu," because the final consonant of the verb in the first is vowelled, while in the second it is quiescent; both are in the position of jussive as an answer to the imperative. He, glory be to Him, began with lowering the gaze in both places before guarding the private parts, because looking is a means to failing to guard the private parts, and the means precedes that to which it leads. The meaning of "yaghdudna min absarihinna" is the same as the meaning of "yaghuddu min absarihim," so it is used as evidence for the prohibition of women looking at what is forbidden to them. Likewise, it is obligatory for them to guard their private parts in the manner already mentioned for the men's guarding of theirs. ﴿And not to display their adornment﴾ — that is, what they adorn themselves with, of jewellery and other things. In the prohibition against displaying the places of adornment on their bodies there is a fortiori.

Then He, glory be to Him, made an exception to this prohibition, saying: ﴿except what appears thereof﴾. People differed concerning the apparent adornment and what it is. Ibn Mas'ud and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the apparent adornment is the clothing, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr added the face. 'Ata' and al-Awza'i said: the face and the palms. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah and al-Miswar ibn Makhramah said: the apparent adornment is kohl, siwak, dye up to the middle of the shin, and the like, for it is permissible for the woman to display it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said that the woman displays nothing of her adornment and conceals all of her adornment, and the exception applies to what appears of it by necessity. You are not unaware that the apparent wording of the Qur'anic text is a prohibition against displaying adornment except what appears of it, such as the outer garment, the veil and the like, and of the jewellery on the hands and feet and the like; and if by adornment is meant its places, then the exception refers to what it is hard for the woman to cover, such as the two palms and the two feet and the like.

Likewise, when the prohibition against displaying adornment entails the prohibition against displaying its places by implication of the address, the exception is taken as we have stated for both cases. As for when adornment includes both the places of adornment and what women adorn themselves with, the matter is clear, and the exception applies to all of it.

Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir: adornment is of two kinds: natural (khilqiyyah) and acquired (muktasabah). The natural is the face, for it is the root of adornment; the acquired adornment is what the woman strives for in beautifying her creation, such as clothing, jewellery, kohl and dye. From this is His saying ﴿Take your adornment﴾ [al-A'raf: 31], and the saying of the poet:

"They take their adornment, the finest you see; and when they are left bare, they are the best of the bare ones."

﴿And let them draw their veils over their bosoms﴾ — the majority read the lam of command with sukun. Abu 'Amr read it with kasra according to the original, since the original of the lam of command is kasra; this reading is reported from Ibn 'Abbas. "Khumur" is the plural of "khimar," which is what a woman covers her head with, and from it come "ikhtamarat al-mar'ah" and "takhammarat."

"Juyub" is the plural of "jayb," which is the opening of the shift and the shirt, derived from "jawb," meaning cutting.

The exegetes said: the women of the Jahiliyyah used to let their veils hang behind them, while their collars in front were wide, so their necks and necklaces would be exposed; so they were commanded to draw their head-coverings over the collars, so that this would conceal what used to show. In the word "daraba" there is intensity in the act of placing, which is attaching.

The majority read "bi-khumurihinna" with a moving mim; Talhah ibn Musarrif read it with sukun.

The majority read "juyubihinna" with a damma on the jim; Ibn Kathir and some Kufans read it with a kasra; and many of the earlier grammarians do not permit this reading.

Al-Zajjaj said: it is permissible to replace the damma with a kasra; as for what is reported from Hamzah of combining damma and kasra, it is impossible, and no one can pronounce it except by indication. The majority have explained "juyub" by what we have mentioned, and this is the literal meaning.

Muqatil said: the meaning of "'ala juyubihinna" is "over their breasts," so there is an omitted modifier in the verse, namely: over the places of their collars.

Then He, glory be to Him, repeated the prohibition against displaying adornment for the sake of the exception He is about to mention, saying: ﴿And not to display their adornment except to their husbands﴾. "Ba'l" in the speech of the Arabs means husband and master. He put the husbands first, because they are the ones intended by the adornment; and because every part of the wife's body and of the concubine is lawful to them. Similar is His saying: ﴿And those who guard their private parts, except from their wives or what their right hands possess, for they are not blameworthy﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 5–6]. Then, when He, glory be to Him, had excepted the husband, He followed it with the exception of mahrams, saying: ﴿or their fathers, or the fathers of their husbands﴾ up to His saying ﴿or the sons of their sisters﴾. He permitted women to display adornment to these because of the frequency of association and the absence of fear of temptation, since human nature has aversion toward close relatives.

It is narrated from al-Hasan and al-Husayn, may Allah be pleased with them both, that they would not look at the Mothers of the Believers, on the view that the sons of the husbands were not mentioned in the verse concerning the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ), which is His saying: ﴿There is no blame upon them concerning their fathers﴾ [al-Ahzab: 55]. The "sons of their husbands" means the male children of the husbands. His saying "or their sons" includes the sons' sons however low they go, and the sons of their daughters however low they go; likewise the fathers of the husbands, the fathers of the fathers, and the fathers of the mothers however high they go; likewise the sons of the husbands however low they go; and likewise the sons of brothers and sisters.

The majority held that the paternal uncle and maternal uncle are like the rest of the mahrams in the permissibility of looking at what is permitted for them. There is no mention of foster-relationship in the verse, but it is like kinship.

Al-Sha'bi and 'Ikrimah said: the paternal uncle and the maternal uncle are not mahrams. The meaning of "or their women" (aw nisa'ihinna) is those who are particular to them and who are close to them by service or companionship, and this includes the female slaves; excluded from it are the women of the disbelievers, whether of the protected people (ahl al-dhimmah) or others, so it is not lawful for them to display their adornment to them, because they do not refrain from describing them to men.

On this question there is disagreement among the scholars, and the attribution of "women" to them indicates that this is specific to believing women.

﴿or what their right hands possess﴾ — the apparent meaning of the verse includes male and female slaves without distinction between whether they are Muslims or disbelievers; this is the view of a group of scholars, and 'A'ishah, Umm Salamah, Ibn 'Abbas and Malik held it.

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: do not let this verse deceive you: "or what their right hands possess" was only meant for the female slaves, and was not meant for the male slaves.

Al-Sha'bi used to dislike that a male slave look at the hair of his mistress; this is the view of 'Ata', Mujahid, al-Hasan and Ibn Sirin, and it is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, and Abu Hanifah and Ibn Jurayj held it. ﴿or male attendants who have no need [of women]﴾ — the majority read "ghayri" in the genitive. Abu Bakr and Ibn 'Amir read it in the accusative, as an exception; it is also said: in the accusative as a detachment (al-qat'). "Al-tabi'in" means those who follow a people and obtain some of their food, having no concern except that and no need for women; this was said by Mujahid, 'Ikrimah and al-Sha'bi. "Min al-rijal" is in the accusative position as a circumstantial qualifier (hal).

The root of "irbah," "arab" and "ma'rabah" is need, and the plural is "ma'arib," meaning needs. From it is His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿and in it are other needs (ma'arib)﴾, and from it is the saying of Tarafah:

"When a man utters folly, sin and obscenity, he advances one day, then his needs are lost."

It has been said: by "ghayr uli al-irbah min al-rijal" is meant the fools who have no need for women; it has been said: the simpleton; it has been said: the impotent; it has been said: the eunuch; it has been said: the effeminate; it has been said: the old man. There is no basis for this specification; rather, the verse means its apparent sense: those who follow the household and have no need for women and never experience that in any state. Thus whoever has this description is included, and whoever else is excluded. ﴿or children who have not yet attained knowledge of women's private nakedness﴾ — "tifl" is applied to the singular, dual and plural; or what is meant here is the category placed in the position of the plural, indicated by its being described with a plural description. In Ubayy's codex it reads "aw al-atfal" in the plural. A person is called "tifl" as long as he has not reached puberty (ihtilam). The meaning of "lam yazharu" is "did not become aware," from "zuhur" in the sense of "ittila'," as stated by Ibn Qutaybah.

It has been said: its meaning is: they have not reached the limit of desire for intercourse, as stated by al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj; one says "zahartu 'ala kadha" when I overcame it and subdued it.

The meaning: they have not become aware of women's private parts and uncovered them for intercourse, or they have not reached the limit of desire for intercourse.

The majority's reading is "'awrat" with a sukun on the waw, for lightening; this is the dialect of the majority of the Arabs. Ibn 'Amir in one narration read it with a fatha. Ibn Abi Ishaq and al-A'mash also read it thus. This reading is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, and it is the dialect of Hudhayl ibn Mudrikah; from it is the saying of the poet, which al-Farra' recited:

A brother of fair-skinned women, who goes out in the morning and returns, a companion for stroking the shoulders, a swift one.

The scholars differed over whether it is obligatory to cover what lies beyond the face and the two palms of young children. It was said that it is not obligatory, since there is no legal obligation (taklif) upon them, and this is the sound view. It was also said that it is obligatory, since a woman may feel desire for them.

Likewise, they differed concerning the 'awrah (the parts of the body that must be covered) of the elderly man whose desire has ceased. The better view is that the sanctity (hurmah) remains as it was. Therefore, it is not permissible to look at his 'awrah, nor is it permissible for him to expose it.

The scholars differed about the limit of the 'awrah. Al-Qurtubi said: The Muslims have agreed that the two private parts (saw'atan) are 'awrah for both man and woman, and that the entire body of a woman is 'awrah except her face and her hands, though there is disagreement on this. Most scholars said: The 'awrah of a man is from his navel to his knee. ﴿And let them not stamp their feet so that what they conceal of their adornment may be known﴾. That is, a woman should not strike her foot when she walks so that the sound of her anklet may be heard by men who hear it, and they thereby know that she wears an anklet.

Al-Zajjaj said: The hearing of this adornment is more stirring of desire than its display.

Then He guided His servants to repentance from acts of disobedience, and said, glorified is He: ﴿And turn to Allah in repentance, all of you, O believers﴾. In this is the command to repent, and there is no disagreement among the Muslims that it is obligatory and that it is one of the obligations of the religion.

The discussion of repentance has already been presented in Surat al-Nisa'.

Then He mentioned what encourages them to repent, saying: ﴿So that you may succeed﴾. That is, that you may attain the happiness of this world and the Hereafter. It was said that what is meant by repentance here is repentance from what they used to do in the Jahiliyyah (the period of ignorance before Islam). The first view is preferable, because it is established in the Sunnah that Islam wipes out what came before it.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, who said: "A man passed by during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on one of the roads of Madinah. He looked at a woman, and she looked at him. Satan whispered to both of them that neither of them had looked at the other except out of admiration for him. Then, while the man was walking alongside a wall and looking at her, the wall met him and split his nose. He said: 'By Allah, I will not wash off the blood until I come to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and inform him of my matter.' He came to him and related his story to him. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'This is the punishment for your sin.' And Allah revealed: ﴿Say to the believing men that they should lower their gaze﴾, the verse."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿Say to the believing men that they should lower their gaze﴾, that he said: That is, from their desires, that which Allah dislikes.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Buraydah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do not follow a glance with another glance, for the first is for you, but the second is not for you." In Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i, from Jarir al-Bajali, who said: "I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about a sudden glance, and he commanded me to turn my gaze away." In the Two Sahihs and others, from the hadith of Abu Sa'id, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Beware of sitting on the roads.' They said: 'O Messenger of Allah, we have no choice but to sit in our gatherings and converse in them.' He said: 'If you refuse, then give the road its due.' They said: 'And what is its due, O Messenger of Allah?' He said: 'Lowering the gaze, removing harm, returning the greeting, enjoining what is right, and forbidding what is wrong.'"

Al-Bukhari, the authors of the Sunan and others narrated from Bahz ibn Hakim, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: "I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, our 'awrat (private parts), what of them do we show and what do we leave?' He said: 'Guard your 'awrah except from your wife or what your right hand possesses.' I said: 'O Prophet of Allah, when people are among one another?' He said: 'If you are able that no one sees it, then let no one see it.' I said: 'When one of us is alone?' He said: 'Allah is more deserving that He be shown shame than people.'"

In the Two Sahihs and others, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah has prescribed for the son of Adam his share of adultery, which he will inevitably attain. The adultery of the eyes is the gaze, the adultery of the tongue is speech, the adultery of the ears is listening, the adultery of the hands is grasping, the adultery of the feet is walking, the soul wishes and desires, and the private part either confirms that or denies it."

Al-Hakim narrated and declared it sound, from Hudhayfah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A glance is one of the arrows of Iblis, poisoned. Whoever abandons it out of fear of Allah, Allah will reward him with a faith whose sweetness he will find in his heart." The hadiths on this subject are numerous.

(p-1010) Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Muqatil, who said: "It has reached us, and Allah knows best, that Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah al-Ansari related that Asma' bint Yazid was in a palm grove belonging to the Banu Harithah, and women would enter upon her without wearing their waist-wrappers, so what was on their feet would show, meaning the anklets, and their breasts and their braids would show. Asma' said: 'How ugly this is!' So Allah revealed that: ﴿And say to the believing women that they should lower their gaze﴾, the verse." In this report, along with its being mursal (lacking a companion in its chain), there is Muqatil.

'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, who declared it sound, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, regarding His words: ﴿And not to reveal their adornment﴾, he said: The adornment is the bracelet, the armlet, the anklet, the earring, and the necklace. ﴿Except what appears thereof﴾, he said: The garments and the outer cloak.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him, who said: The adornment is of two kinds: an apparent adornment and a hidden adornment, which none sees except the husband. As for the apparent adornment, it is the garments. As for the hidden adornment, it is the kohl, the bracelet and the ring.

The wording of Ibn Jarir is: "As for what is apparent of it, it is the garments, and what is hidden, the two anklets, the two earrings and the two bracelets."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Anas regarding His words: ﴿Except what appears thereof﴾, he said: The kohl and the ring.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿And not to reveal their adornment except what appears thereof﴾, he said: The kohl, the ring, the earring and the necklace.

'Abd al-Razzaq and 'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from him, who said: It is the dyeing of the palm and the ring.

Ibn Abi Shaybah and 'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Ibn 'Umar, who said: The apparent adornment is the face and the two palms.

They both (Ibn Abi Shaybah and 'Abd ibn Humayd) narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: ﴿Except what appears thereof﴾ is her face, her two palms and the ring. They both also narrated from him, who said: It is the area of the face and the inner part of the palm.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from 'A'ishah that she was asked about the apparent adornment, and she said: The bangle, the plain ring, and she gathered the edge of her sleeve.

Abu Dawud, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from 'A'ishah: "Asma' bint Abi Bakr entered upon the Prophet (ﷺ) wearing thin garments, so he turned away from her and said: 'O Asma', when a woman reaches menstruation, it is not fitting that anything of her be seen except this,' and he pointed to his face and his palm."

Abu Dawud and Abu Hatim al-Razi said: This is mursal, because it comes through Khalid ibn Duraik from 'A'ishah, and he did not hear from her.

Al-Bukhari, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from 'A'ishah, who said: "May Allah have mercy on the first emigrant women. When Allah revealed: ﴿And let them draw their head-coverings over their bosoms﴾, they split their thickest cloaks and covered themselves with them."

Ibn Jarir, al-Hakim, who declared it sound, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from her with the wording: "The women took their waist-wrappers and split them at the edges, and covered themselves with them."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words: ﴿And not to reveal their adornment except what appears thereof﴾, and the apparent adornment is the face, the kohl of the eyes, the dyeing of the palm and the ring. So this is what she displays in her house to whoever enters upon her.

Then He said: ﴿And not to reveal their adornment except to their husbands or their fathers﴾, the verse. The adornment that she reveals to these is her earring, her necklace and her bracelet. As for her anklet, her upper-arm ornament, her neck and her hair, she reveals these only to her husband.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated through al-Kalbi from Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿or their women﴾, he said: They are the Muslim women. She should not reveal it to a Jewish or Christian woman. It is the neck, the earring and the girdle, and whatever is forbidden for anyone to see except a mahram (a relative whom marriage is forbidden to).

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab that he wrote to Abu 'Ubaydah: "To proceed: it has reached me that some women of the Muslim women enter the bathhouses with the women of the people of polytheism. So prohibit those under your authority from that, for it is not lawful for a woman who believes in Allah and the Last Day to let anyone see her 'awrah except the people of her religion."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "There is no harm in a slave seeing the hair of his mistress."

Abu Dawud, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Anas: "The Prophet (ﷺ) came to Fatimah with a slave who had been given to her, and Fatimah was wearing a garment which, if her head was covered with it, did not reach her feet, and if she covered her feet with it, did not reach her head. When the Prophet (ﷺ) saw what she was facing, he said: 'There is no harm for you. He is only your father and your slave.'" Its chain in the Sunan of Abu Dawud is thus: "Muhammad ibn 'Isa narrated to us, Abu Jumay' Salim ibn Dinar narrated to us, from Thabit, from Anas," and so he mentioned it.

'Abd al-Razzaq and Ahmad narrated from Umm Salamah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If one of you has a mukatab (a slave contracted to buy his freedom), and he has the means to pay, then let her veil herself from him." The chain of Ahmad is thus: "Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah narrated to us, from al-Zuhri, from Nabhan, that Umm Salamah," and so he mentioned it.

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words: ﴿Or male attendants who have no physical desire﴾, he said: This is the one whom women are not shy before.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding the verse, he said: This is the man who follows the people and is dull-witted, not concerned with women and not desiring women.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him, regarding the verse, he said: In earlier times a man would follow a man, and he was not jealous over him, and a woman would not fear to remove her head-covering in his presence. He is the fool who has no need for women.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him also regarding the verse, he said: He is the effeminate man whose member does not stand.

'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from 'A'ishah, who said: "There was an effeminate man who used to enter upon the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ), and they used to count him among those without physical desire. The Prophet (ﷺ) entered one day while he was with one of his wives, and he was describing a woman. He said: 'When she comes forward, she comes with four (folds), and when she turns away, she turns away with eight.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Do I not see that this one knows what is here? Let him not enter upon you again.' So they forbade him."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words: ﴿And not to stamp their feet﴾, which is that she strikes one anklet against the other in front of men, or that she has anklets on her feet and moves them in front of men. So Allah forbade that, for it is one of the works of Satan.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 24, verses 32–34 (part 1 of 2):

When Allah, glorified is He, commanded lowering the gaze and guarding the private parts, He then directed people, after that, to what is lawful for the servants of marriage (nikah), through which the desire is satisfied, the impulses toward fornication (zina) are calmed, and after which lowering the gaze from what is forbidden and guarding the private part from what is not lawful become easier. So He said: ﴿And marry the unmarried (al-ayama) among you.﴾ The ayyim (unmarried person) is the one who has no spouse, whether a virgin or previously married. Its plural is ayama, and the original form is ayaymu, with the yā' doubled. It includes both man and woman.

Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i said: The lexicographers agreed that the ayyim, in its original sense, is the woman who has no husband, whether a virgin or previously married.

Abu 'Ubayd said: It is said "rajul ayyim" (an unmarried man) and "imra'ah ayyim" (an unmarried woman), but it is mostly used of women, and for men it is like a borrowed usage. From this is the saying of Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt:

*By Allah, how excellent are the sons of 'Ali: one among them is unmarried, and another is married.*

From it also is the saying of another:

*I have been left bereft (lovelorn) until every friend blamed me, hoping that Sulayma would become a widow as I have become bereft.*

The address in the verse is to the guardians (awliya'), and it has been said it is to the husbands. The first is more preferred, and in it is evidence that a woman may not give herself in marriage, though Abu Hanifa disagreed on this.

The scholars differed concerning marriage: is it permissible (mubah), recommended (mustahabb), or obligatory (wajib)? Al-Shafi'i and others held the first view; Malik and Abu Hanifa held the second; and some scholars held the third, with distinctions among them: they said that if a person fears falling into sin for himself, it is obligatory upon him, and otherwise it is not.

The apparent position is that those who held permissibility and recommendation do not dispute its obligation when that fear exists. In general, when that fear is absent, it is among the emphasized sunan (sunnah practices), based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) in the sound hadith, after encouraging marriage: "Whoever turns away from my sunnah is not of me." But this applies with the ability to marry, and to bear its expenses, as will come shortly. The meaning of the ayama here is the free men and free women. As for the slaves, He clarified that by His saying: ﴿And the righteous among your male servants and your female servants.﴾ The majority read ﴿'ibadikum﴾ (your servants), and al-Hasan read ('abidikum) (your male slaves). Al-Farra' said: It is also permissible to read (wa-ima'akum) (and your female slaves) in the accusative, by referring it back to al-Salihin (the righteous). And righteousness (al-salah) is faith (iman).

He, glorified is He, mentioned righteousness regarding the slaves but not the free people, because righteousness is generally found among the free, unlike the slaves. In this is evidence that a slave does not marry himself off; rather, his owner marries him.

The majority held that it is permissible for a master to compel his male or female slave to marry. Malik said: It is not permissible.

Then He, glorified is He, returned to speaking about the free people, and said: ﴿If they are poor, Allah will enrich them from His bounty.﴾ That is, do not refrain from marrying off free people because of the poverty of the man or the woman, or of one of them, for if they are poor, Allah, glorified is He, will enrich them and bestow His favor upon them through it.

Al-Zajjaj said: Allah urged marriage and informed that it is a cause for the removal of poverty. But it does not necessarily follow that this is attained by every poor person who marries, for that is restricted by Allah's will. Indeed, many poor people exist in reality who do not attain wealth when they marry.

It has been said: The meaning is that He enriches him with the richness of the self (contentment). It has also been said: The meaning is: if they are poor in need of marriage, Allah will enrich them from His bounty with what is lawful, so that they may abstain from fornication.

The first interpretation is preferable, and what supports it is His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And if you fear poverty, Allah will enrich you from His bounty, if He wills﴾ [al-Tawbah: 28]. So the unrestricted statement here is interpreted by the restricted statement there. The clause ﴿And Allah is All-Encompassing (wasi'), All-Knowing﴾ confirms what precedes it and establishes it. The meaning is that He, glorified is He, possesses boundless capacity; the enrichment of whomever He enriches among His servants does not diminish the vastness of His dominion. He is All-Knowing of the interests of His creation; He enriches whom He wills and impoverishes whom He wills.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned the condition of those unable to marry, after explaining the permissibility of marrying them off, as guidance to what is better. So He said: ﴿And let those who find no means of marriage keep chaste (wa-l-yasta'fif)...﴾ The verb istа'affa means seeking to be chaste. That is: let those who do not find the means of marriage (nikah), namely wealth, seek chastity from fornication and what is unlawful.

It has been said: Here "marriage" refers to what the woman is married with of dower and maintenance, like al-lihaf (blanket, a name for what one is wrapped in) and al-libas (clothing, a name for what is worn). He, glorified is He, restricted this prohibition by that limit, which is: ﴿until Allah enriches them from His bounty﴾, that is, He provides them with sustenance by which they become independent and are enabled through it to marry. In this verse there is something that indicates the restriction of the first clause: "If they are poor, Allah will enrich them," by will, as we have mentioned. For if it were a definite promise that certainly will be fulfilled, then wealth and marriage would be inseparable, and then the command to chastity in the state of poverty would have little benefit, since he would certainly become rich upon marrying. So in marrying while poor there would be an attainment of wealth. Unless it is said: This command to chastity is for the one unable to obtain the beginnings of marriage, and that does not contradict his becoming rich after he marries, for it has truly been said of him that he did not find marriage while he lacked its causes, the greatest of which is wealth.

Then, when He, glorified is He, encouraged marrying off the righteous among the male and female slaves, He directed owners to a method by which the slave may become one of the free. So He said: ﴿And those who seek a deed of manumission (al-kitab) from among those whom your right hands possess...﴾ The relative pronoun (alladhina) is in the nominative position as the subject (mubtada'), and it is permissible that it is in the accusative position, by implying a verb that is explained by what follows it: that is, "and contract with those who seek the deed (kitab)." Al-kitab is the verbal noun of kataba (to contract), like al-mukatabah. One says: "kataba yukatibu kitaban wa-mukatabatan," just as one says "qatala yuqatilu qitalan wa-muqatalatan."

It has been said: Here al-kitab is the name of a thing, the document in which something is written. That is because when they contracted with a slave, they wrote for him and for themselves a document concerning that. So the meaning is "those who seek the document of manumission contract."

The meaning of al-mukatabah in the Shari'ah: that a man contracts with his slave for a sum of money that he pays in installments; when he pays it, he is free. The apparent meaning of His saying: ﴿So contract with them (fa-katibuhum)﴾ is that if the slave asks his master for the contract, it becomes obligatory upon him to contract with him under the condition stated after it, which is: ﴿if you know good in them.﴾ The "good" (khayr) is the ability to pay what was contracted for, even if he has no wealth. It has been said: It is wealth only, as Mujahid, al-Hasan, 'Ata', al-Dahhak, Tawus and Muqatil held. The first view was held by Ibn 'Umar and Ibn Zayd, and was chosen by Malik, al-Shafi'i, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj.

Al-Farra' said: It means: if you hope among them for fulfillment and payment of the money.

Al-Zajjaj said: Since He said "in them," the more apparent sense is earning, fulfillment, and the performance of trust (amanah).

Al-Nakha'i said: The good is religion and trustworthiness. Something similar was narrated from al-Hasan. 'Ubaydah al-Salmani said: It is establishing the prayer.

Al-Tahawi said: The view of the one who said it is wealth is not sound according to us, because the slave is the wealth of his master, so how can he have wealth of his own? He said: The meaning according to us is: if you know in them religion and truthfulness.

Abu 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: Whoever does not say that the good here is wealth denies that one may say "if you know in them wealth"; rather, one says "I know in him good, righteousness and trustworthiness," and one does not say "I know in him wealth."

This is the summary of the disagreement among the scholars concerning the good mentioned in this verse.

Once this is established for you, know that the apparent implication of the command mentioned in the verse, that it is obligatory, was held by 'Ikrimah, Masruq, 'Umar ibn Dinar, al-Dahhak, and the people of the apparent meaning (Ahl al-Zahir). They said: It is obligatory upon the master to contract with his slave if he asks for that and the master knows good in him.

The majority of scholars said: This is not obligatory. They relied on the consensus that if a slave asks his master to sell him to someone else, the master is not obligated to do so and cannot be compelled to, so likewise the contract of manumission, since it is an exchange (mu'awadah).

But it is not hidden from you that this is a feeble proof and a refuted doubt. The truth is what the earlier scholars said, and 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, Ibn 'Abbas said so, and Ibn Jarir chose it.

Then He, glorified is He, commanded the masters to show kindness to those under contract, and said: ﴿And give them from the wealth of Allah which He has given you.﴾ In this verse there is a command to the owners to help the contracted slaves with the sum of the contract, either by giving them some of the wealth or by remitting part of what they were contracted for. The apparent meaning of the verse is that no specific amount is set. It has been said: a third; it has been said: a quarter; it has been said: a tenth. Perhaps the reason for specifying the masters with this command is that the discussion concerns them, and the context of speech is with them, for they are the ones commanded to contract.

Al-Hasan, al-Nakha'i and Buraydah said: The address in His saying "and give them" is to all people. Zayd ibn Aslam said: The address is to the rulers, that they should give the contracted slaves their share from the money of charity (sadaqah), as in His saying: ﴿and for the captives (fi al-riqab)﴾. For the contracted slave there are well-known rulings when he has paid some of the contract money.

Then, when He, glorified is He, had directed masters to marry the righteous among the slaves, He forbade the Muslims from what the people of the Jahiliyyah used to do: compelling their slave women to fornication. So He said: ﴿And do not compel your slave girls to prostitution (al-bigha').﴾ The meaning of "fatayat" (slave girls) here is the female slaves, although the words fata and fatah may be applied to free people in other places.

Al-bigha' is fornication, the verbal noun of baghat al-mar'ah tabghi bighaa'an, when a woman commits zina. This term is specific to women's fornication, so it is not said of a man who commits zina that he is baghiy. Allah, glorified is He, restricted this prohibition by His saying: ﴿if they desire chastity (in tahassunan)﴾, because compulsion is only conceivable when they desire chastity, for one who does not desire chastity cannot be described as "compelled to fornication." The meaning of "tahassun" here is: abstinence and marriage. It has been said that this condition refers back to the unmarried.

Al-Zajjaj and al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl said: There is inversion and transposition in the speech; that is: "And marry the unmarried and the righteous among your servants and your female servants, if they desire chastity." It has been said: this condition is cancelled (mulgha). It has been said: this condition is according to what they were upon, for they used to compel them while they desired abstinence, and the prohibition is not restricted to the situation where they desire abstinence.

It has been said: this condition came out in the manner of what is usual (kharaja makhraja al-ghalib), because it is usual that compulsion occurs only when they desire chastity, so it does not necessarily follow that compulsion is permissible when they do not desire chastity. This view is the strongest of these views, for a slave woman may be one who desires neither the lawful nor the unlawful, as in the case of one who has no desire for marriage, or a young girl; she is described as "compelled to fornication" even though she does not desire chastity. So what has been said, that compulsion is only conceivable when chastity is desired, is not complete, unless it is said that the meaning of "tahassun" here is merely abstinence, and that it does not apply to one who wants marriage, that she desires chastity, and that is far-fetched. For the scholar Ibn 'Abbas said: The meaning of "tahassun" is abstinence and marriage, and others followed him in this.

Then He, glorified is He, gave the reason for this prohibition by His saying: ﴿so that you may seek the goods of worldly life (ʿaraḍ al-ḥayat al-dunya)﴾. This is what the slave woman earns through her private part. This reason also came out in the manner of what is usual, and the meaning is that this worldly gain is what usually led them to compel slave women to prostitution; for a man's compelling his slave woman to prostitution, without any benefit to him at all, is not something sensible people do. So this reasoning does not indicate that it is permissible for him to compel her if he is not seeking through her compulsion the goods of worldly life.

Some say that this reasoning for the prohibition of coercion (ikrah) is based on the fact that this was their custom, and not that it is the basis for the prohibition of coercing them. This view agrees with the first meaning and does not contradict it. ﴿And whoever coerces them, then indeed Allah, after their coercion, is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ This confirms and emphasizes what precedes it. The meaning is that the punishment for coercion falls upon the coercers, not upon the coerced women, as indicated by the reading (qira'a) of Ibn Mas'ud, Jabir ibn Abd Allah and Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "Indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful to them" (lahunna). Some say this interpretation is remote, because a woman forced into adultery is not sinful. The answer given is that even if she is coerced, she may not be entirely free, during the act of adultery, of some trace of compliance, either by the natural human disposition, or because the coercion falls short of the degree of compulsion that removes choice. Some say the meaning is: ﴿indeed Allah, after their coercion, is Forgiving and Merciful to them﴾, either absolutely, or on condition of repentance.

When Allah, glorified is He, had finished explaining those rulings, He began to describe the Qur'an with three attributes. The first is that it is ﴿clear signs﴾, meaning clear in themselves or made clear, so the verses mentioned in this surah are included primarily.

The second attribute is that it is ﴿an example from those who passed away before you﴾, meaning an example (p-1013) drawn from the amazing stories of those who passed away and from the parables struck for them in earlier scriptures. The wonder at the story of Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, is like the wonder at the story of Yusuf and Maryam and what they were accused of, after which their innocence and freedom from it was made clear, peace of Allah be upon them both.

The third attribute is that it is ﴿an admonition for the God-fearing﴾, through which only the God-fearing benefit, so they follow its commands and refrain from its prohibitions.

As for those who are not God-fearing, Allah has sealed their hearts and placed a veil over their eyes, so that they do not hear admonitions, do not take heed from the stories of those who passed away, and do not understand what the clear verses contain.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words: ﴿And marry the single among you﴾ to the end of the verse, that he said: Allah, glorified is He, commanded marriage and encouraged them to it, and commanded them to marry off their free people and their slaves, and promised them wealth in that, saying: ﴿If they are poor, Allah will enrich them from His bounty.﴾

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, who said: Obey Allah regarding what He has commanded you concerning marriage; He will fulfil for you what He has promised you of wealth. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿If they are poor, Allah will enrich them from His bounty.﴾

Abd al-Razzaq in al-Musannaf and Abd ibn Humayd reported from Qatada, who said: It was related to us that Umar ibn al-Khattab said: I have never seen a man who does not seek wealth through marriage, when Allah has promised in it what He has promised, saying: ﴿If they are poor, Allah will enrich them from His bounty.﴾

Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Abi Shaybah reported from him something similar by another route.

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn Mas'ud something similar.

Al-Bazzar, al-Daraqutni in al-Ilal, al-Hakim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Daylami reported through the route of Urwa, from Aisha, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Marry women, for they will bring you wealth."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it sound), al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim (who graded it sound) and al-Bayhaqi in al-Sunan reported from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Three are a right upon Allah to help them: the one who marries seeking chastity, the mukatab (slave seeking contractual manumission) who seeks to pay, and the one who fights in the way of Allah." There are many hadiths encouraging marriage in general, but this is not the place to mention them.

Al-Khatib in his History reported from Ibn Abbas regarding His words: ﴿And let those who cannot find marriage keep themselves chaste﴾, that he said: Let whoever cannot find (the means to) marry marry, for Allah will enrich him.

Ibn al-Sakan in Ma'rifat al-Sahaba reported "from Abd Allah ibn Subayh, from his father, who said: I was a slave of Huwaytib ibn Abd al-Uzza. I asked him for mukatabah, but he refused, so there was revealed: ﴿And those who seek the writing (of manumission) among those whom your right hands possess, write it for them if you know any good in them﴾ to the end of the verse."

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported from Anas ibn Malik, who said: Sirin asked me for mukatabah, and I refused him. So he went to Umar ibn al-Khattab, who turned towards me with the whip and said: "Write for him," and recited: ﴿So write for them if you know any good in them﴾. So I wrote for him.

Ibn Kathir said: its chain is sound.

Abu Dawud in al-Marasil and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan reported from Yahya ibn Abi Kathir, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "﴿So write for them if you know any good in them﴾ means: if you know in them a trade (hirfa), and do not leave them as a burden upon people."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi reported from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿if you know any good in them﴾, that he said: "Wealth."

Ibn Mardawayh reported something similar from Ali.

Al-Bayhaqi reported from Ibn Abbas regarding the verse, that he said: "Trustworthiness and fulfilment."

He also reported from him, that he said: "If you know that your mukatab will pay you."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi reported from him regarding the verse, that he said: "If you know a means for them (to earn), and do not place their maintenance upon the Muslims." ﴿And give them from the wealth of Allah which He has given you﴾ means: relieve them of some of their obligation in the mukatabah.

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi reported from Nafi', who said: Ibn Umar disliked contracting mukatabah with his slave if he had no trade, and he would say: "He will feed me from people's refuse."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: Ibn Abbas said regarding His words: ﴿And give them from the wealth of Allah﴾ to the end of the verse: He commanded the believers to designate (a portion) for the slaves.

Ali ibn Abi Talib said: Allah commanded the master to forgo for the mukatab a quarter of his price. This is a teaching from Allah, not an obligation, but there is reward in it.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Ruyani in his Musnad and al-Diya' al-Maqdisi in al-Mukhtara reported from Buraydah regarding the verse, that he said: "He urged people to give it to him."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Muslim, al-Bazzar, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi reported through the route of Abu Sufyan, from Jabir ibn Abd Allah, who said: Abd Allah ibn Ubayy used to say to a slave girl of his: "Go and seek something for us," and she was unwilling. So Allah revealed: (﴿And do not compel your slave girls to prostitution, if they desire chastity, to seek the transient gain of worldly life. And whoever compels them, then indeed Allah, after their compulsion, is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾) He used to recite it this way.

Muslim in his Sahih mentioned from Jabir that a slave girl of Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, called Musayka, and another called Umayma, he would force them into adultery, so they complained of that to the Prophet (ﷺ), and Allah revealed: ﴿And do not compel your slave girls﴾ to the end of the verse.

Al-Bazzar and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Anas something similar to the first hadith of Jabir.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ali ibn Abi Talib regarding the verse, that he said: "The people of the Jahiliyya used to force their female slaves into prostitution, and they were forbidden from that in Islam."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn Abbas, who said: "In the Jahiliyya they used to compel their female slaves to adultery, taking their wages, so the verse was revealed."

It has been reported that the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade the earnings of a prostitute (mahr al-baghi), the earnings of a cupper (kasb al-hajjam), and the fee of a soothsayer (hulwan al-kahin).

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 24, verses 32–34 (part 1 of 2):

When Allah, glorified is He, commanded lowering the gaze and guarding the private parts, He then directed people, after that, to what is lawful for the servants of marriage (nikah), through which the desire is satisfied, the impulses toward fornication (zina) are calmed, and after which lowering the gaze from what is forbidden and guarding the private part from what is not lawful become easier. So He said: ﴿And marry the unmarried (al-ayama) among you.﴾ The ayyim (unmarried person) is the one who has no spouse, whether a virgin or previously married. Its plural is ayama, and the original form is ayaymu, with the yā' doubled. It includes both man and woman.

Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i said: The lexicographers agreed that the ayyim, in its original sense, is the woman who has no husband, whether a virgin or previously married.

Abu 'Ubayd said: It is said "rajul ayyim" (an unmarried man) and "imra'ah ayyim" (an unmarried woman), but it is mostly used of women, and for men it is like a borrowed usage. From this is the saying of Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt:

*By Allah, how excellent are the sons of 'Ali: one among them is unmarried, and another is married.*

From it also is the saying of another:

*I have been left bereft (lovelorn) until every friend blamed me, hoping that Sulayma would become a widow as I have become bereft.*

The address in the verse is to the guardians (awliya'), and it has been said it is to the husbands. The first is more preferred, and in it is evidence that a woman may not give herself in marriage, though Abu Hanifa disagreed on this.

The scholars differed concerning marriage: is it permissible (mubah), recommended (mustahabb), or obligatory (wajib)? Al-Shafi'i and others held the first view; Malik and Abu Hanifa held the second; and some scholars held the third, with distinctions among them: they said that if a person fears falling into sin for himself, it is obligatory upon him, and otherwise it is not.

The apparent position is that those who held permissibility and recommendation do not dispute its obligation when that fear exists. In general, when that fear is absent, it is among the emphasized sunan (sunnah practices), based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) in the sound hadith, after encouraging marriage: "Whoever turns away from my sunnah is not of me." But this applies with the ability to marry, and to bear its expenses, as will come shortly. The meaning of the ayama here is the free men and free women. As for the slaves, He clarified that by His saying: ﴿And the righteous among your male servants and your female servants.﴾ The majority read ﴿'ibadikum﴾ (your servants), and al-Hasan read ('abidikum) (your male slaves). Al-Farra' said: It is also permissible to read (wa-ima'akum) (and your female slaves) in the accusative, by referring it back to al-Salihin (the righteous). And righteousness (al-salah) is faith (iman).

He, glorified is He, mentioned righteousness regarding the slaves but not the free people, because righteousness is generally found among the free, unlike the slaves. In this is evidence that a slave does not marry himself off; rather, his owner marries him.

The majority held that it is permissible for a master to compel his male or female slave to marry. Malik said: It is not permissible.

Then He, glorified is He, returned to speaking about the free people, and said: ﴿If they are poor, Allah will enrich them from His bounty.﴾ That is, do not refrain from marrying off free people because of the poverty of the man or the woman, or of one of them, for if they are poor, Allah, glorified is He, will enrich them and bestow His favor upon them through it.

Al-Zajjaj said: Allah urged marriage and informed that it is a cause for the removal of poverty. But it does not necessarily follow that this is attained by every poor person who marries, for that is restricted by Allah's will. Indeed, many poor people exist in reality who do not attain wealth when they marry.

It has been said: The meaning is that He enriches him with the richness of the self (contentment). It has also been said: The meaning is: if they are poor in need of marriage, Allah will enrich them from His bounty with what is lawful, so that they may abstain from fornication.

The first interpretation is preferable, and what supports it is His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And if you fear poverty, Allah will enrich you from His bounty, if He wills﴾ [al-Tawbah: 28]. So the unrestricted statement here is interpreted by the restricted statement there. The clause ﴿And Allah is All-Encompassing (wasi'), All-Knowing﴾ confirms what precedes it and establishes it. The meaning is that He, glorified is He, possesses boundless capacity; the enrichment of whomever He enriches among His servants does not diminish the vastness of His dominion. He is All-Knowing of the interests of His creation; He enriches whom He wills and impoverishes whom He wills.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned the condition of those unable to marry, after explaining the permissibility of marrying them off, as guidance to what is better. So He said: ﴿And let those who find no means of marriage keep chaste (wa-l-yasta'fif)...﴾ The verb istа'affa means seeking to be chaste. That is: let those who do not find the means of marriage (nikah), namely wealth, seek chastity from fornication and what is unlawful.

It has been said: Here "marriage" refers to what the woman is married with of dower and maintenance, like al-lihaf (blanket, a name for what one is wrapped in) and al-libas (clothing, a name for what is worn). He, glorified is He, restricted this prohibition by that limit, which is: ﴿until Allah enriches them from His bounty﴾, that is, He provides them with sustenance by which they become independent and are enabled through it to marry. In this verse there is something that indicates the restriction of the first clause: "If they are poor, Allah will enrich them," by will, as we have mentioned. For if it were a definite promise that certainly will be fulfilled, then wealth and marriage would be inseparable, and then the command to chastity in the state of poverty would have little benefit, since he would certainly become rich upon marrying. So in marrying while poor there would be an attainment of wealth. Unless it is said: This command to chastity is for the one unable to obtain the beginnings of marriage, and that does not contradict his becoming rich after he marries, for it has truly been said of him that he did not find marriage while he lacked its causes, the greatest of which is wealth.

Then, when He, glorified is He, encouraged marrying off the righteous among the male and female slaves, He directed owners to a method by which the slave may become one of the free. So He said: ﴿And those who seek a deed of manumission (al-kitab) from among those whom your right hands possess...﴾ The relative pronoun (alladhina) is in the nominative position as the subject (mubtada'), and it is permissible that it is in the accusative position, by implying a verb that is explained by what follows it: that is, "and contract with those who seek the deed (kitab)." Al-kitab is the verbal noun of kataba (to contract), like al-mukatabah. One says: "kataba yukatibu kitaban wa-mukatabatan," just as one says "qatala yuqatilu qitalan wa-muqatalatan."

It has been said: Here al-kitab is the name of a thing, the document in which something is written. That is because when they contracted with a slave, they wrote for him and for themselves a document concerning that. So the meaning is "those who seek the document of manumission contract."

The meaning of al-mukatabah in the Shari'ah: that a man contracts with his slave for a sum of money that he pays in installments; when he pays it, he is free. The apparent meaning of His saying: ﴿So contract with them (fa-katibuhum)﴾ is that if the slave asks his master for the contract, it becomes obligatory upon him to contract with him under the condition stated after it, which is: ﴿if you know good in them.﴾ The "good" (khayr) is the ability to pay what was contracted for, even if he has no wealth. It has been said: It is wealth only, as Mujahid, al-Hasan, 'Ata', al-Dahhak, Tawus and Muqatil held. The first view was held by Ibn 'Umar and Ibn Zayd, and was chosen by Malik, al-Shafi'i, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj.

Al-Farra' said: It means: if you hope among them for fulfillment and payment of the money.

Al-Zajjaj said: Since He said "in them," the more apparent sense is earning, fulfillment, and the performance of trust (amanah).

Al-Nakha'i said: The good is religion and trustworthiness. Something similar was narrated from al-Hasan. 'Ubaydah al-Salmani said: It is establishing the prayer.

Al-Tahawi said: The view of the one who said it is wealth is not sound according to us, because the slave is the wealth of his master, so how can he have wealth of his own? He said: The meaning according to us is: if you know in them religion and truthfulness.

Abu 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: Whoever does not say that the good here is wealth denies that one may say "if you know in them wealth"; rather, one says "I know in him good, righteousness and trustworthiness," and one does not say "I know in him wealth."

This is the summary of the disagreement among the scholars concerning the good mentioned in this verse.

Once this is established for you, know that the apparent implication of the command mentioned in the verse, that it is obligatory, was held by 'Ikrimah, Masruq, 'Umar ibn Dinar, al-Dahhak, and the people of the apparent meaning (Ahl al-Zahir). They said: It is obligatory upon the master to contract with his slave if he asks for that and the master knows good in him.

The majority of scholars said: This is not obligatory. They relied on the consensus that if a slave asks his master to sell him to someone else, the master is not obligated to do so and cannot be compelled to, so likewise the contract of manumission, since it is an exchange (mu'awadah).

But it is not hidden from you that this is a feeble proof and a refuted doubt. The truth is what the earlier scholars said, and 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, Ibn 'Abbas said so, and Ibn Jarir chose it.

Then He, glorified is He, commanded the masters to show kindness to those under contract, and said: ﴿And give them from the wealth of Allah which He has given you.﴾ In this verse there is a command to the owners to help the contracted slaves with the sum of the contract, either by giving them some of the wealth or by remitting part of what they were contracted for. The apparent meaning of the verse is that no specific amount is set. It has been said: a third; it has been said: a quarter; it has been said: a tenth. Perhaps the reason for specifying the masters with this command is that the discussion concerns them, and the context of speech is with them, for they are the ones commanded to contract.

Al-Hasan, al-Nakha'i and Buraydah said: The address in His saying "and give them" is to all people. Zayd ibn Aslam said: The address is to the rulers, that they should give the contracted slaves their share from the money of charity (sadaqah), as in His saying: ﴿and for the captives (fi al-riqab)﴾. For the contracted slave there are well-known rulings when he has paid some of the contract money.

Then, when He, glorified is He, had directed masters to marry the righteous among the slaves, He forbade the Muslims from what the people of the Jahiliyyah used to do: compelling their slave women to fornication. So He said: ﴿And do not compel your slave girls to prostitution (al-bigha').﴾ The meaning of "fatayat" (slave girls) here is the female slaves, although the words fata and fatah may be applied to free people in other places.

Al-bigha' is fornication, the verbal noun of baghat al-mar'ah tabghi bighaa'an, when a woman commits zina. This term is specific to women's fornication, so it is not said of a man who commits zina that he is baghiy. Allah, glorified is He, restricted this prohibition by His saying: ﴿if they desire chastity (in tahassunan)﴾, because compulsion is only conceivable when they desire chastity, for one who does not desire chastity cannot be described as "compelled to fornication." The meaning of "tahassun" here is: abstinence and marriage. It has been said that this condition refers back to the unmarried.

Al-Zajjaj and al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl said: There is inversion and transposition in the speech; that is: "And marry the unmarried and the righteous among your servants and your female servants, if they desire chastity." It has been said: this condition is cancelled (mulgha). It has been said: this condition is according to what they were upon, for they used to compel them while they desired abstinence, and the prohibition is not restricted to the situation where they desire abstinence.

It has been said: this condition came out in the manner of what is usual (kharaja makhraja al-ghalib), because it is usual that compulsion occurs only when they desire chastity, so it does not necessarily follow that compulsion is permissible when they do not desire chastity. This view is the strongest of these views, for a slave woman may be one who desires neither the lawful nor the unlawful, as in the case of one who has no desire for marriage, or a young girl; she is described as "compelled to fornication" even though she does not desire chastity. So what has been said, that compulsion is only conceivable when chastity is desired, is not complete, unless it is said that the meaning of "tahassun" here is merely abstinence, and that it does not apply to one who wants marriage, that she desires chastity, and that is far-fetched. For the scholar Ibn 'Abbas said: The meaning of "tahassun" is abstinence and marriage, and others followed him in this.

Then He, glorified is He, gave the reason for this prohibition by His saying: ﴿so that you may seek the goods of worldly life (ʿaraḍ al-ḥayat al-dunya)﴾. This is what the slave woman earns through her private part. This reason also came out in the manner of what is usual, and the meaning is that this worldly gain is what usually led them to compel slave women to prostitution; for a man's compelling his slave woman to prostitution, without any benefit to him at all, is not something sensible people do. So this reasoning does not indicate that it is permissible for him to compel her if he is not seeking through her compulsion the goods of worldly life.

Some say that this reasoning for the prohibition of coercion (ikrah) is based on the fact that this was their custom, and not that it is the basis for the prohibition of coercing them. This view agrees with the first meaning and does not contradict it. ﴿And whoever coerces them, then indeed Allah, after their coercion, is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ This confirms and emphasizes what precedes it. The meaning is that the punishment for coercion falls upon the coercers, not upon the coerced women, as indicated by the reading (qira'a) of Ibn Mas'ud, Jabir ibn Abd Allah and Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "Indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful to them" (lahunna). Some say this interpretation is remote, because a woman forced into adultery is not sinful. The answer given is that even if she is coerced, she may not be entirely free, during the act of adultery, of some trace of compliance, either by the natural human disposition, or because the coercion falls short of the degree of compulsion that removes choice. Some say the meaning is: ﴿indeed Allah, after their coercion, is Forgiving and Merciful to them﴾, either absolutely, or on condition of repentance.

When Allah, glorified is He, had finished explaining those rulings, He began to describe the Qur'an with three attributes. The first is that it is ﴿clear signs﴾, meaning clear in themselves or made clear, so the verses mentioned in this surah are included primarily.

The second attribute is that it is ﴿an example from those who passed away before you﴾, meaning an example (p-1013) drawn from the amazing stories of those who passed away and from the parables struck for them in earlier scriptures. The wonder at the story of Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, is like the wonder at the story of Yusuf and Maryam and what they were accused of, after which their innocence and freedom from it was made clear, peace of Allah be upon them both.

The third attribute is that it is ﴿an admonition for the God-fearing﴾, through which only the God-fearing benefit, so they follow its commands and refrain from its prohibitions.

As for those who are not God-fearing, Allah has sealed their hearts and placed a veil over their eyes, so that they do not hear admonitions, do not take heed from the stories of those who passed away, and do not understand what the clear verses contain.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words: ﴿And marry the single among you﴾ to the end of the verse, that he said: Allah, glorified is He, commanded marriage and encouraged them to it, and commanded them to marry off their free people and their slaves, and promised them wealth in that, saying: ﴿If they are poor, Allah will enrich them from His bounty.﴾

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, who said: Obey Allah regarding what He has commanded you concerning marriage; He will fulfil for you what He has promised you of wealth. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿If they are poor, Allah will enrich them from His bounty.﴾

Abd al-Razzaq in al-Musannaf and Abd ibn Humayd reported from Qatada, who said: It was related to us that Umar ibn al-Khattab said: I have never seen a man who does not seek wealth through marriage, when Allah has promised in it what He has promised, saying: ﴿If they are poor, Allah will enrich them from His bounty.﴾

Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Abi Shaybah reported from him something similar by another route.

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn Mas'ud something similar.

Al-Bazzar, al-Daraqutni in al-Ilal, al-Hakim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Daylami reported through the route of Urwa, from Aisha, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Marry women, for they will bring you wealth."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it sound), al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim (who graded it sound) and al-Bayhaqi in al-Sunan reported from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Three are a right upon Allah to help them: the one who marries seeking chastity, the mukatab (slave seeking contractual manumission) who seeks to pay, and the one who fights in the way of Allah." There are many hadiths encouraging marriage in general, but this is not the place to mention them.

Al-Khatib in his History reported from Ibn Abbas regarding His words: ﴿And let those who cannot find marriage keep themselves chaste﴾, that he said: Let whoever cannot find (the means to) marry marry, for Allah will enrich him.

Ibn al-Sakan in Ma'rifat al-Sahaba reported "from Abd Allah ibn Subayh, from his father, who said: I was a slave of Huwaytib ibn Abd al-Uzza. I asked him for mukatabah, but he refused, so there was revealed: ﴿And those who seek the writing (of manumission) among those whom your right hands possess, write it for them if you know any good in them﴾ to the end of the verse."

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported from Anas ibn Malik, who said: Sirin asked me for mukatabah, and I refused him. So he went to Umar ibn al-Khattab, who turned towards me with the whip and said: "Write for him," and recited: ﴿So write for them if you know any good in them﴾. So I wrote for him.

Ibn Kathir said: its chain is sound.

Abu Dawud in al-Marasil and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan reported from Yahya ibn Abi Kathir, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "﴿So write for them if you know any good in them﴾ means: if you know in them a trade (hirfa), and do not leave them as a burden upon people."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi reported from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿if you know any good in them﴾, that he said: "Wealth."

Ibn Mardawayh reported something similar from Ali.

Al-Bayhaqi reported from Ibn Abbas regarding the verse, that he said: "Trustworthiness and fulfilment."

He also reported from him, that he said: "If you know that your mukatab will pay you."

So Allah revealed: (﴿And do not compel your slave girls to prostitution, if they desire chastity, to seek the transient gain of worldly life. And whoever compels them, then indeed Allah, after their compulsion, is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾) He used to recite it this way.

Al-Zajjaj said: Allah urged marriage and informed that it is a cause for the removal of poverty. But it does not necessarily follow that this is attained by every poor person who marries, for that is restricted by Allah's will. Indeed, many poor people exist in reality who do not attain wealth when they marry.

It has been said: The meaning is that He enriches him with the richness of the self (contentment). It has also been said: The meaning is: if they are poor in need of marriage, Allah will enrich them from His bounty with what is lawful, so that they may abstain from fornication.

The first interpretation is preferable, and what supports it is His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And if you fear poverty, Allah will enrich you from His bounty, if He wills﴾ [al-Tawbah: 28]. So the unrestricted statement here is interpreted by the restricted statement there. The clause ﴿And Allah is All-Encompassing (wasi'), All-Knowing﴾ confirms what precedes it and establishes it. The meaning is that He, glorified is He, possesses boundless capacity; the enrichment of whomever He enriches among His servants does not diminish the vastness of His dominion. He is All-Knowing of the interests of His creation; He enriches whom He wills and impoverishes whom He wills.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned the condition of those unable to marry, after explaining the permissibility of marrying them off, as guidance to what is better. So He said: ﴿And let those who find no means of marriage keep chaste (wa-l-yasta'fif)...﴾ The verb istа'affa means seeking to be chaste. That is: let those who do not find the means of marriage (nikah), namely wealth, seek chastity from fornication and what is unlawful.

It has been said: Here "marriage" refers to what the woman is married with of dower and maintenance, like al-lihaf (blanket, a name for what one is wrapped in) and al-libas (clothing, a name for what is worn). He, glorified is He, restricted this prohibition by that limit, which is: ﴿until Allah enriches them from His bounty﴾, that is, He provides them with sustenance by which they become independent and are enabled through it to marry. In this verse there is something that indicates the restriction of the first clause: "If they are poor, Allah will enrich them," by will, as we have mentioned. For if it were a definite promise that certainly will be fulfilled, then wealth and marriage would be inseparable, and then the command to chastity in the state of poverty would have little benefit, since he would certainly become rich upon marrying. So in marrying while poor there would be an attainment of wealth. Unless it is said: This command to chastity is for the one unable to obtain the beginnings of marriage, and that does not contradict his becoming rich after he marries, for it has truly been said of him that he did not find marriage while he lacked its causes, the greatest of which is wealth.

Then, when He, glorified is He, encouraged marrying off the righteous among the male and female slaves, He directed owners to a method by which the slave may become one of the free. So He said: ﴿And those who seek a deed of manumission (al-kitab) from among those whom your right hands possess...﴾ The relative pronoun (alladhina) is in the nominative position as the subject (mubtada'), and it is permissible that it is in the accusative position, by implying a verb that is explained by what follows it: that is, "and contract with those who seek the deed (kitab)." Al-kitab is the verbal noun of kataba (to contract), like al-mukatabah. One says: "kataba yukatibu kitaban wa-mukatabatan," just as one says "qatala yuqatilu qitalan wa-muqatalatan."

It has been said: Here al-kitab is the name of a thing, the document in which something is written. That is because when they contracted with a slave, they wrote for him and for themselves a document concerning that. So the meaning is "those who seek the document of manumission contract."

The meaning of al-mukatabah in the Shari'ah: that a man contracts with his slave for a sum of money that he pays in installments; when he pays it, he is free. The apparent meaning of His saying: ﴿So contract with them (fa-katibuhum)﴾ is that if the slave asks his master for the contract, it becomes obligatory upon him to contract with him under the condition stated after it, which is: ﴿if you know good in them.﴾ The "good" (khayr) is the ability to pay what was contracted for, even if he has no wealth. It has been said: It is wealth only, as Mujahid, al-Hasan, 'Ata', al-Dahhak, Tawus and Muqatil held. The first view was held by Ibn 'Umar and Ibn Zayd, and was chosen by Malik, al-Shafi'i, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj.

Al-Farra' said: It means: if you hope among them for fulfillment and payment of the money.

Al-Zajjaj said: Since He said "in them," the more apparent sense is earning, fulfillment, and the performance of trust (amanah).

Al-Nakha'i said: The good is religion and trustworthiness. Something similar was narrated from al-Hasan. 'Ubaydah al-Salmani said: It is establishing the prayer.

Al-Tahawi said: The view of the one who said it is wealth is not sound according to us, because the slave is the wealth of his master, so how can he have wealth of his own? He said: The meaning according to us is: if you know in them religion and truthfulness.

Abu 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: Whoever does not say that the good here is wealth denies that one may say "if you know in them wealth"; rather, one says "I know in him good, righteousness and trustworthiness," and one does not say "I know in him wealth."

This is the summary of the disagreement among the scholars concerning the good mentioned in this verse.

Once this is established for you, know that the apparent implication of the command mentioned in the verse, that it is obligatory, was held by 'Ikrimah, Masruq, 'Umar ibn Dinar, al-Dahhak, and the people of the apparent meaning (Ahl al-Zahir). They said: It is obligatory upon the master to contract with his slave if he asks for that and the master knows good in him.

The majority of scholars said: This is not obligatory. They relied on the consensus that if a slave asks his master to sell him to someone else, the master is not obligated to do so and cannot be compelled to, so likewise the contract of manumission, since it is an exchange (mu'awadah).

But it is not hidden from you that this is a feeble proof and a refuted doubt. The truth is what the earlier scholars said, and 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, Ibn 'Abbas said so, and Ibn Jarir chose it.

Then He, glorified is He, commanded the masters to show kindness to those under contract, and said: ﴿And give them from the wealth of Allah which He has given you.﴾ In this verse there is a command to the owners to help the contracted slaves with the sum of the contract, either by giving them some of the wealth or by remitting part of what they were contracted for. The apparent meaning of the verse is that no specific amount is set. It has been said: a third; it has been said: a quarter; it has been said: a tenth. Perhaps the reason for specifying the masters with this command is that the discussion concerns them, and the context of speech is with them, for they are the ones commanded to contract.

Al-Hasan, al-Nakha'i and Buraydah said: The address in His saying "and give them" is to all people. Zayd ibn Aslam said: The address is to the rulers, that they should give the contracted slaves their share from the money of charity (sadaqah), as in His saying: ﴿and for the captives (fi al-riqab)﴾. For the contracted slave there are well-known rulings when he has paid some of the contract money.

Then, when He, glorified is He, had directed masters to marry the righteous among the slaves, He forbade the Muslims from what the people of the Jahiliyyah used to do: compelling their slave women to fornication. So He said: ﴿And do not compel your slave girls to prostitution (al-bigha').﴾ The meaning of "fatayat" (slave girls) here is the female slaves, although the words fata and fatah may be applied to free people in other places.

Al-bigha' is fornication, the verbal noun of baghat al-mar'ah tabghi bighaa'an, when a woman commits zina. This term is specific to women's fornication, so it is not said of a man who commits zina that he is baghiy. Allah, glorified is He, restricted this prohibition by His saying: ﴿if they desire chastity (in tahassunan)﴾, because compulsion is only conceivable when they desire chastity, for one who does not desire chastity cannot be described as "compelled to fornication." The meaning of "tahassun" here is: abstinence and marriage. It has been said that this condition refers back to the unmarried.

Al-Zajjaj and al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl said: There is inversion and transposition in the speech; that is: "And marry the unmarried and the righteous among your servants and your female servants, if they desire chastity." It has been said: this condition is cancelled (mulgha). It has been said: this condition is according to what they were upon, for they used to compel them while they desired abstinence, and the prohibition is not restricted to the situation where they desire abstinence.

It has been said: this condition came out in the manner of what is usual (kharaja makhraja al-ghalib), because it is usual that compulsion occurs only when they desire chastity, so it does not necessarily follow that compulsion is permissible when they do not desire chastity. This view is the strongest of these views, for a slave woman may be one who desires neither the lawful nor the unlawful, as in the case of one who has no desire for marriage, or a young girl; she is described as "compelled to fornication" even though she does not desire chastity. So what has been said, that compulsion is only conceivable when chastity is desired, is not complete, unless it is said that the meaning of "tahassun" here is merely abstinence, and that it does not apply to one who wants marriage, that she desires chastity, and that is far-fetched. For the scholar Ibn 'Abbas said: The meaning of "tahassun" is abstinence and marriage, and others followed him in this.

Then He, glorified is He, gave the reason for this prohibition by His saying: ﴿so that you may seek the goods of worldly life (ʿaraḍ al-ḥayat al-dunya)﴾. This is what the slave woman earns through her private part.
