Al-Hasan said: This tree is not one of the trees of this world, but it is a parable that Allah struck for His light; had it been in this world, it would be either eastern or western.

Al-Tha'labi said: The Qur'an has made clear that it is from the trees of this world, because His saying "an olive tree" is an apposition (*badal*) of His saying "a tree."

Ibn Zayd said: It is from the trees of al-Sham (Greater Syria), for al-Sham is neither eastern nor western, and al-Sham is the blessed land.

It has been read *tūqadu* with the feminine *tā'* (second person ta), with the pronoun referring to the glass and not the lamp, and the Kufans read this way.

Shaybah, Nafiʿ, Ayyub, Salam, Ibn ʿAmir, the people of al-Sham, and Hafs read *yūqadu* with a *yāʾ* underneath, with a damma, a light *qāf*, and a damma on the *dāl*.

Al-Hasan, al-Sulami, Abu ʿUmar ibn al-ʿAla', and Abu Jaʿfar read *tawaqqada* with a *tā'* (feminine) on top, with a fatha, a fatha on the *wāw*, a doubled *qāf*, and a fatha on the *dāl*, as a past tense verb from *tawaqqada yatawaqqadu*. The pronoun in these two readings refers to the lamp.

Al-Nahhas said: These two readings are close in meaning, because both refer to the lamp, and it is more appropriate to this description (p-1015) because it is what gives light and shines, and the glass is only a container for it.

Nasr ibn ʿAsim read like the reading of Abu ʿAmr and those with him, except that he put a damma on the *dāl*, as a present tense verb, and its original form is *tatawaqqadu*.

Then He described the olive tree with another description, saying: ﴿its oil nearly gives light even if no fire touches it﴾. The majority read *tamassuhu* with a *tā'* on top, because fire is feminine. Abu ʿUbayd said: He knows only this reading.

Abu Hatim reported that al-Suddi narrated from Abu Malik from Ibn ʿAbbas that he read *yamassuhu* with a *yāʾ* underneath, because the feminine of fire is not real.

The meaning is that this oil, in its clarity and its brightness, nearly gives light by itself, without fire touching it at all. The *nūrun* (light) is in the nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "it is light." And ﴿upon light﴾ is connected to an omitted word which is an adjective of "light," emphasizing it, and the meaning is: it is light existing upon light. Mujahid said: the intended meaning is the fire upon the oil.

Al-Kalbi said: The lamp is light, and the glass is light. Al-Suddi said: the light of faith and the light of the Qur'an.

﴿Allah guides to His light whomever He wills﴾ from among His servants, meaning a special guidance that delivers to the desired goal, and the intended meaning of guidance here is not mere indication.

﴿Allah strikes parables for the people﴾, meaning He makes things clear by their likenesses and similar examples, bringing them near to understanding and facilitating their comprehension; for the presentation of the intelligible in the form of the sensible and depicting it with its image adds to its clarity and explanation.

﴿Allah is All-Knowing of everything﴾, nothing is hidden from Him of things, whether intelligible or sensible, apparent or hidden.

There has been disagreement about His saying: ﴿in houses which Allah has permitted to be raised﴾, regarding what it is connected to. It was said it is connected to what precedes it, meaning: like a niche in some of the houses of Allah, which are the mosques. As if it were said: the parable of His light is as you see in the mosque, the light of the niche whose description is such and such. It was said: it is connected to "lamp." Ibn al-Anbari said: I heard Abu al-ʿAbbas say: it is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) for the lamp, the glass, and the star, as if it were said: and it is in houses. It was said: it is connected to "is lit," meaning it is lit in houses. It has also been said it is connected to what follows it, which is "glorifies," meaning men glorify Him in houses. On this view, His saying "in it" is a repetition, like your saying: Zayd is sitting in the house, in it.

It was said: it is separate from what precedes it, as if Allah said: in houses which Allah has permitted to be raised.

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi said: Reports have come with this, that whoever sits in the mosques is sitting with his Lord.

It has been said, on the supposition that it is connected to niche, lamp, or "is lit," what is the reason for singularizing the niche and the lamp while pluralizing the house? A single niche or single lamp is only in a single house. The answer is that this is from the kind of address which begins with the singular and ends with the plural, like His saying, glorified is He: ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women﴾ [al-Talaq: 1] and similar.

It was said: the meaning of "in houses" is: in each one of the houses, as if He said: in every house, or in each one of the houses.

People differed regarding the houses, in several views. The first is that they are the mosques, which is the view of Mujahid, al-Hasan, and others.

The second is that what is meant by them is the houses of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), narrated from al-Hasan.

The third is that they are the houses of the Prophet (ﷺ), narrated from Mujahid.

The fourth is that they are all the houses, said by ʿIkrimah.

The fifth is that they are the four mosques: the Kaʿbah, the mosque of Quba', the mosque of Madinah, and the mosque of Bayt al-Maqdis, said by Ibn Zayd.

The first view is more apparent because of His saying: ﴿He is glorified in them morning and evening by men﴾. The *bāʾ* in *bayt* may be pronounced with a damma or a kasra, both of which are established in the language. The meaning of "Allah has permitted it to be raised" is: He commanded and decreed. The meaning of "raised" is "built," said by Mujahid, ʿIkrimah, and others, and from it is His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And when Ibrahim was raising the foundations of the House﴾. Al-Hasan al-Basri and others said: the meaning of "raised" is exalted, its status raised, and purified from impurities and filth. Al-Zajjaj preferred this. It was said: the intended meaning of raising here is the combination of both matters. The meaning of ﴿His name is mentioned in them﴾ is every remembrance of Allah, mighty and majestic is He. It was said: it is monotheism. It was said: the intended meaning is recitation of the Qur'an. The first is preferable.

﴿He is glorified in them morning and evening by men﴾. Ibn ʿAmir and Abu Bakr read *yusabbaha* with a fatha on the *bāʾ*, in the passive form. The rest read it with a kasra on it, in the active form, except Ibn Wathhab and Abu Haywah, who read with a *tā'* on top and a kasra on the *bāʾ*. According to the first reading, the element standing in place of the subject is one of the three prepositional phrases, and "men" is nominative in one of two ways: either by an implied verb, as if it were an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: who glorifies Him? So it was said: men glorify Him. The second is that "men" is raised as the predicate of an omitted subject. According to the second reading, "men" is the subject of "glorifies." According to the third reading, the subject is also "men," and the verb was made feminine because a broken plural is treated in some cases as feminine.

The tafsir has been divided over what this glorification (*tasbih*) is. Most scholars understood it as the obligatory prayers. They said that *al-ghuduww* is the Dawn Prayer (*salat al-subh*) and *al-asal* is the Noon and Afternoon Prayers and the two Night Prayers (*al-'ishaiyn*), since the term *al-asal* includes them. The meaning of *bil-ghuduww wal-asal* is "in the morning and in the evening." It was also said that it refers to the Dawn and Afternoon Prayers, and that it refers to the Forenoon Prayer (*salat al-duha*). It was also said that the glorification here has its literal meaning (*ma'nahu al-haqiqi*), which is declaring Allah far exalted above whatever is unfitting for Him in His essence, His attributes, and His actions. This is supported by the mention of prayer and zakat after it. This view is preferable to what came before it, because it is the literal meaning, and there is evidence against what the earlier scholars held. This is what we have mentioned.

﴿Neither trade nor commerce distracts them from the remembrance of Allah.﴾ This clause describes the men (*rijal*). That is, trade and selling do not occupy them away from remembrance. Trade is singled out because it is the thing that most occupies a person away from remembrance.

Al-Farra' said: "Trade (*tijara*) is for those who import goods (*ahl al-jalab*), and selling (*bay'*) is what a man sells with his own hands." Some scholars restricted *tijara* here to buying (*al-shira'*), because selling is mentioned after it. Al-Waqidi said something similar to al-Farra's view, saying: "The merchants (*al-tujjar*) are the importers who travel, and the sellers (*al-ba'a*) are the ones who stay put." The meaning of *'an dhikr Allah* is what was mentioned earlier in His words, ﴿and that His name may be remembered therein﴾. It was also said that it refers to the call to prayer (*al-adhan*). It was also said that it means remembering Him by His Most Beautiful Names, that is, affirming His oneness and glorifying Him.

It was also said that it refers to the prayer itself, but this is refuted by the mention of prayer after remembrance here. The meaning of *iqam al-salah* (establishing the prayer) is performing it at its appointed times without delay. The *ta'* (ة) is dropped from *iqam*, because the genitive construction (*idafa*) takes the place of the *ta'* in three words, which a poet gathered in his verse:

> Three words have their *ta'*s dropped when they are made genitive (*mudafa*), according to all the grammarians:
> *Abu 'udhriha* (when you wish), *layta shi'ri*, and *iqam al-salah*.

(p. 1016)

Al-Farra' cited, as evidence for the omission mentioned in this verse, the poet's words:

> Indeed the companions (*al-khalit*) hastened to part, and they left, and they broke with you the promise of the matter they had promised.

That is, *'idat al-amr* (the promise of the matter). This line shows that omission with the genitive construction is not restricted to those three places.

Al-Zajjaj said: "The *ha'* was dropped because one says *aqamta al-salata iqamatan*, and the original was *iqwaman*. But the *waw* was changed into an *alif*, so two *alifs* came together, and one of them was dropped to avoid two consecutive unvoweled letters. So it became *aqamtu al-salata iqaman*, and then the *ha'* was inserted as a replacement for what was dropped, and the genitive construction here takes the place of the dropped *ha'*. This is a consensus among the grammarians." End of quote.

Whoever understood *dhikr Allah* as the obligatory prayer has been forced to understand *iqam al-salah* as performing it at its times, to avoid repetition. But there is no need for that. Rather, *dhikr* is understood in its literal meaning, as we have already mentioned.

The zakat mentioned here is the obligatory zakat. It was also said that the zakat means obedience to Allah and sincerity, since not every believer has wealth.

﴿They fear a Day﴾, that is, the Day of Resurrection. Its grammatical status (*intisabuhu*) is that it is an object of the verb (*maf'ul*), not a time adverb for it. Then He described this Day with His words: ﴿in which hearts and eyes will be turned about﴾, that is, they will be agitated and transformed. It was said that the meaning of the turning of hearts is that they are pulled from their places up to the throats, so they neither return to their places nor leave. The meaning of the turning of eyes is that they will become blind after having been seeing.

It was also said that the turning of hearts means that they will fluctuate between hope for salvation and fear of destruction. As for the turning of eyes, it is their looking in every direction from which they will be seized and toward which they will go.

It was also said that the meaning is the transformation of their hearts and eyes from the doubt they were in to certainty. A similar verse is His words: ﴿So We removed your veil, and your sight today is sharp﴾. What he used to see in this world as error, he will see in the Hereafter as right guidance. It was also said that the meaning is the turning over on the embers of Hell, and it was said other than this.

﴿That Allah may reward them with the best of what they did.﴾ This is connected to an omitted element, that is: they do what they do of glorification, remembrance, establishing the prayer, and giving zakat, ﴿that Allah may reward them with the best of what they did﴾. That is, the best reward for their deeds, according to what He promised them of multiplication of that to ten times its like and to seven hundred times. It was also said that what is meant in this verse is what He bestows on them of favor beyond what they deserve. The first view is better, because of His words: ﴿and increase them from His bounty﴾, since what is meant there is bestowing on them more than the promised reward. ﴿And Allah provides for whom He wills without account﴾, that is, without being called to account for what He gave him, or because His giving, glory be to Him, has no end. This sentence confirms what preceded it, namely the promise of increase.

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth﴾, that he said: "He manages the affair in them: their stars, their sun, and their moon." Al-Firyabi reported from him, regarding His words ﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth. The likeness of His light﴾ that is given to the believer, "is like a niche (*mishkat*)." And about the explanation of ﴿an olive tree neither eastern nor western﴾, he said: "It is the one on the slope of a mountain, which the sun does not touch when it rises or when it sets." ﴿Its oil would almost glow even if no fire touched it. Light upon light﴾. That is the likeness of the heart of the believer: light upon light.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Anbari reported in *al-Masahif* from al-Sha'bi that he said: "In the recitation of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, it is: *mathalu nuri al-mu'min kamishkat* (the likeness of the light of the believer is like a niche)."

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, reported from Ibn 'Abbas regarding the verse that he said: "It says: the likeness of the light of one who believes in Allah is like a niche, which is a window (*kuwwa*)."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him regarding ﴿the likeness of His light﴾ that he said: "It is an error by the scribe. He is far too great for His light to be the likeness of a niche." He said: "The likeness of the light of the believer is like a niche."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wal-sifat* reported from him as well, regarding ﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth﴾, that he said: "He is the guide of the people of the heavens and the earth." ﴿The likeness of His light﴾: "the likeness of His guidance in the heart of the believer is like a niche." He says: "The place of the wick, as the pure oil almost glows before fire touches it. When fire touches it, its light increases upon its light. So the heart of the believer acts with guidance before knowledge comes to it, and when knowledge comes to it, its guidance increases upon guidance and its light upon light." In its chain is 'Ali ibn Abi Talha, about whom there is criticism.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ubayy ibn Ka'b regarding ﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth. The likeness of His light﴾, that he said: "It is the believer in whose chest faith and the Qur'an have been placed, so Allah gave his likeness. He said: ﴿the light of the heavens and the earth, the likeness of His light﴾, so He began with His own light. Then He mentioned the light of the believer, and said: the likeness of the light of the one who believes in Him." Ubayy ibn Ka'b used to recite it as *mathalu nuri man amana bihi* (the likeness of the light of the one who believes in Him). "So it is the believer, in whose chest faith and the Qur'an have been placed like a niche." He said: "The believer's chest is the niche. ﴿In it is a lamp, the lamp﴾ is the light, which is the Qur'an and the faith placed in his chest. ﴿In a glass﴾, and the glass is his heart. ﴿As if it were a star of brilliance﴾, that is, a shining star. ﴿Lit from a blessed tree﴾. The blessed tree is the root of the blessing: sincerity to Allah alone and worshipping Him with no partner. ﴿An olive tree neither eastern nor western﴾." He said: "Its likeness is like the likeness of a tree intertwined with other trees, green and lush, which the sun does not touch in any condition, neither when it rises nor when it sets. Likewise, this believer has been protected from being led astray by any of the trials."

Ibn Abi Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas that "the Jews said to Muhammad: 'How does the light of Allah emerge from beyond the sky?' So Allah struck the likeness of that light of His, and said: ﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth. The likeness of His light is like a niche.﴾" The niche is a window of the house, in which is a lamp, which is the lamp that is in the glass. It is a likeness that Allah struck for His obedience, so He called His obedience light, then named it different kinds. ﴿Neither eastern nor western﴾: he said: "It is the middle of the tree, which the sun does not reach when it rises or sets, and that is the finest oil." ﴿Its oil would almost glow﴾ without fire. ﴿Light upon light﴾, meaning by that the faith and knowledge of the servant. ﴿Allah guides to His light whom He wills﴾, and that is the likeness of the believer.

(p. 1017) Al-Tabarani, Ibn 'Adi, Ibn Mardawayh, and Ibn 'Asakir reported from Ibn 'Umar regarding His words ﴿like a niche in which is a lamp﴾ that he said: "The niche is the inside of Muhammad (ﷺ), the glass is his heart, and the lamp is the light that is in his heart. ﴿Lit from a blessed tree﴾: the tree is Ibrahim. ﴿An olive tree neither eastern nor western﴾: neither Jewish nor Christian." Then he recited: ﴿Ibrahim was neither a Jew nor a Christian, but he was a upright Muslim, and he was not of the polytheists.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 67].

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Shamr ibn 'Atiyya that he said: "Ibn 'Abbas came to Ka'b al-Ahbar and said: 'Tell me about the words of Allah: ﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth. The likeness of His light﴾.' He said: 'The likeness of the light of Muhammad (ﷺ) is like a niche.' He said: 'The niche is the window which Allah struck as an example of a lamp, in which is a lamp, and the lamp is his heart. ﴿The lamp is in a glass﴾, and the glass is his chest. ﴿As if it were a star of brilliance﴾: he likened the chest of Muhammad (ﷺ) to a shining star. Then the lamp returned to his heart, and He said: ﴿lit from a blessed tree, an olive, neither eastern nor western, whose oil would almost glow﴾.' He said: 'Muhammad (ﷺ) almost makes it clear to people, even if he did not speak, that he is a Prophet, just as the oil almost glows even if no fire touches it.'"

I say: explaining the Qur'anic text in this way, and in similar ways, of what came earlier from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Ibn 'Abbas, and Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them, is not in accordance with what the Arabic language requires. Nor was anything authentically reported from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that would permit departing from the Arabic meaning toward these meanings, which resemble riddles and obscurity. But these Companions and those who agreed with them among those who came after them found it unlikely that the light of Allah, glory be to Him, be likened to the light of a lamp in a niche. That is why Ibn 'Abbas said: "He is far too great for His light to be like the light of a niche," as we quoted from him earlier. But there is no basis for this unlikelihood. We have already mentioned at the beginning of the discussion what removes the difficulty and clarifies what is meant in the best way and most eloquent style, in accordance with what the Arabic language requires and what the words of eloquent speakers convey. So there is no reason to depart from the apparent meaning, neither from the Book, nor from the Sunnah, nor from the language.

As for what was reported from Ka'b al-Ahbar concerning this, as we have mentioned, if it was the cause of those honored Companions departing from the apparent meaning in explaining the verse, then someone like Ka'b, may Allah have mercy on him, is not one to be followed in such matters. We have already pointed out earlier that when the tafsir of a Companion is based on narrations from the People of the Book, as happens often, it does not constitute a proof, and it is not permissible to depart from the Arabic explanation because of it. However, if the recitation of Ubayy ibn Ka'b is authentic, it would be the basis for these tafsirs that differ from the apparent meaning, and would be like an explanatory addition clarifying the intended meaning. But if it is not authentic, then adhering to what is required by the recitation of the majority (*al-jumhur*), namely the seven readers (*al-sab'a*) and others before and after them, is what is necessary.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿in houses which Allah has permitted to be raised﴾, that he said: "They are the mosques, which are honored and where idle talk is forbidden. The name of Allah is remembered in them, and His Book is recited in them. ﴿Therein He is glorified morning and evening﴾: the prayer of the morning and the prayer of the afternoon. These two are the first prayers that Allah made obligatory, so He loved to mention them and to remind His servants of them."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 24, verse 35–38 (part 3 of 3):

There have been reported many hadiths concerning the exalting of mosques, keeping them free from filth and idle talk, and cleaning and perfuming them, but this is not the place to mention them.

Ibn Abi Shaybah and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Indeed, the prayer of ad-duha (the forenoon prayer) is in the Qur'an, and none dives into it except a diver, in His saying: ﴿In houses which Allah has permitted to be raised, and His name is remembered therein; He is glorified therein morning and evening﴾."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayrah: "From the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, concerning His saying: ﴿Men whom neither trade nor sale diverts from the remembrance of Allah﴾, he said: 'They are those who travel through the earth seeking of Allah's bounty.'"

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Daylami narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri: "From the Prophet ﷺ, concerning His saying: ﴿Neither trade nor sale diverts them from the remembrance of Allah﴾, he said: 'They are those who seek of Allah's bounty.'"

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning the verse, he said: "They were men who sought of Allah's bounty, buying and selling. When they heard the call to prayer, they would drop what was in their hands and go to the mosque and pray."

Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab narrated from him concerning the verse, he said: "Allah struck this parable, His saying: ﴿As a niche﴾, for those people whom neither trade nor sale diverts from the remembrance of Allah. They were the most active in trade and the most engaged in selling, but their trade and their selling did not divert them from the remembrance of Allah."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated also from him, concerning "from the remembrance of Allah", he said: "From attending the prayer."

'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Umar that he was in the marketplace when the prayer was established, so they closed their shops and entered the mosque. Ibn 'Umar said: "Concerning them this was revealed: ﴿Men whom neither trade nor sale diverts from the remembrance of Allah﴾."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, al-Tabarani and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he saw some people from the market who heard the adhan and left their goods, so he said: "These are the ones concerning whom Allah said: ﴿Neither trade nor sale diverts them from the remembrance of Allah﴾."

Hannad ibn al-Sarri in al-Zuhd, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab and Muhammad ibn Nasr in al-Salah narrated from Asma' bint Yazid, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "On the Day of Resurrection Allah will gather the people in one plain; the caller will make them hear him and the sight will reach them. A herald will stand and call: 'Where are those who used to praise Allah in ease and in hardship?' They will stand, and they are few, and they will enter Paradise without reckoning. Then he will return and call: 'Where are those whose sides used to forsake their beds?' They will stand, and they are few, and they will enter Paradise without reckoning. Then he will return and call: 'Let those stand whom neither trade nor sale diverted from the remembrance of Allah.' They will stand, and they are few, and they will enter Paradise without reckoning. Then the rest of the people will stand and be reckoned."

al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab narrated from 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir, traced to the Prophet ﷺ, a similar report.

(p-1014) When Allah, glorified is He, had made clear the rulings that He had made clear, He followed that with His being in the utmost perfection, and so He said: ﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth﴾. This sentence is a fresh statement (mustaʾnafah) confirming what came before it. The noble Name is the subject (mubtada'), and "the light of the heavens and the earth" is its predicate (khabar). This is either by omitting a modifier, meaning "the possessor of the light of the heavens and the earth," or because the intended meaning is an exaggeration in describing Him, glorified is He, as being Light, on account of the perfection of His majesty, the manifestation of His justice, and the extent of His rulings. This is like saying "So-and-so is the light of the land," "the moon of the age," or "the sun of the era." From this is the saying of al-Nabighah:

*For you are a sun, and the kings are stars; when it rises, no star remains among them.*

And the saying of another:

*Why did you not head, from among the lands, to the most excellent one, the moon of the tribes, Khalid ibn Yazid?*

And from this is the saying of the poet:

*When ʿAbd Allah travels from Marw by night, its light and its beauty have traveled away from it.*

And the saying of another:

*A lineage as if upon it, from the sun of forenoon, is light, and from the dawn's brightness, a pillar.*

The meaning of *nūr* (light) in the language is *ḍiyāʾ* (radiance), which makes things clear and lets the eyes see the reality of what they see. So it is permissible to apply the term "light" to Allah, glorified is He, by way of praise, and because He originated the things that are illuminated, and originated their lights and their light. This meaning is supported by the reading of Zayd ibn ʿAli, Abu Jaʿfar, and ʿAbd al-ʿAziz al-Makki: ﴿Allah has illuminated the heavens and the earth﴾, in the form of the past tense verb, whose subject is a pronoun referring to Allah, and "the heavens" is its object. So the meaning of ﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth﴾ is that He, glorified is He, made them both luminous, by the rightness of the states of their inhabitants and the perfection of His management, mighty and majestic is He, of those who are in them, just as one says "the king is the light of the land." This is what al-Hasan, Mujahid, al-Azhari, al-Dahhak, al-Qurazi, Ibn ʿArafa, Ibn Jarir, and others said. Similar to it is the saying of the poet:

*You are for us a light, rain, a protection, and a plant for whoever hopes for your generosity, and abundance.*

Hisham al-Jawaliqi and a group of the *Mujassimah* (anthropomorphists) said: He, glorified is He, is light unlike lights, and a body unlike bodies. His saying ﴿the parable of His light﴾ is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is ﴿like a niche﴾, meaning the description of His light, which overflows from Him and appears upon things, is like a niche. The *mishkāh* (niche) is a recess in the wall that does not pass through. This is what al-Wahidi reported from all the commentators, and al-Qurtubi reported it from their majority.

The reason for specifying the niche is that it is the most comprehensive container for the light that is in it, whether from a lamp or other. The original meaning of *mishkāh* is the vessel in which a thing is placed. It was said: the *mishkāh* is the pillar of the lamp in which the wick is. Mujahid said: it is the lamp-stand. The first view is preferable, and from this is the saying of the poet:

*As if his two eyes were two niches in a hole.*

Then He said: ﴿in it is a lamp﴾, which is the lantern, ﴿the lamp is in a glass﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: The light in the glass and the fire's radiance are clearer in it than in anything else, and its radiance increases in the glass. The reason for this is that glass is a transparent body in which light appears in its most perfect appearance.

Then He described the glass, saying: ﴿the glass is as if it were a glittering star﴾, meaning one attributed to pearl (*durrī*), because it has in it such clarity and beauty that resemble pearl.

Al-Dahhak said: *al-kawkab al-durriyy* is Venus.

Abu ʿAmr (Abu ʿUmar) read *dirrīy* with a kasra on the *dāl*. Abu ʿAmr said: I have not heard any Bedouin say anything but *kaʾannahu kawkabun dirriyyun* with a kasra on the *dāl*. They took it from *darʾat al-nujūm*, meaning the stars when they are propelled.

Hamzah read it with a damma on the *dāl* and with hamza, but al-Farraʾ, al-Zajjaj, and al-Mubarrad rejected this. Abu ʿUbayd said: If you put a damma on the *dāl*, you must not use hamza, because it is not in the speech of the Arabs.

The *darārī* (stars) are the well-known stars such as Jupiter, Venus, Mars, and what resembles them of the fixed stars.

Then He described the lamp by His saying: ﴿it is lit from a blessed tree﴾. Here "from" (*min*) is for origin, meaning the beginning of kindling the lamp is from it. It was said that it is by way of an omitted modifier, meaning "it is lit from the oil of a blessed tree." The blessed tree is one of many benefits. It was said: it is that which grows abundantly. The olive is among the greatest of fruits in growth. From this is the saying of Abu Talib lamenting Musafir ibn Abi ʿAmr ibn Umayyah ibn ʿAbd Shams:

*Would that I knew, Musafir ibn Abi ʿAmr,*
*and would that the grieving one would say it: May the stranger, the dead, be blessed, as the shoot of the pomegranate and the olive were blessed.*

It was said that among its blessings is that its branches are green from its bottom up to its top. It is food, oil, tanning material, and fuel, and there is nothing in it that does not have a benefit. Then He described it as ﴿neither eastern nor western﴾. The commentators differed on the meaning of this description. ʿIkrimah, Qatadah, and others said: the eastern is the one that the sun reaches when it rises, and does not reach when it sets. The western is the one that the sun reaches when it sets, and does not reach when it rises.

This olive tree is in an open desert, such that nothing screens it from the sun, neither at its rising nor at its setting. Whatever olive is like this, its fruit is better.

It was said: The meaning is that it is a tree within a grove that has surrounded it, so it is not exposed from the east, nor from the west. Ibn Jarir reported this from Ibn ʿAbbas.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: This is not authentically from Ibn ʿAbbas, because the fruit with this description spoils, and this is observed in existence. Al-Farraʾ and al-Zajjaj preferred the first view.

Al-Hasan said: This tree is not one of the trees of this world, but it is a parable that Allah struck for His light; had it been in this world, it would be either eastern or western.

Al-Tha'labi said: The Qur'an has made clear that it is from the trees of this world, because His saying "an olive tree" is an apposition (*badal*) of His saying "a tree."

Ibn Zayd said: It is from the trees of al-Sham (Greater Syria), for al-Sham is neither eastern nor western, and al-Sham is the blessed land.

It has been read *tūqadu* with the feminine *tā'* (second person ta), with the pronoun referring to the glass and not the lamp, and the Kufans read this way.

Shaybah, Nafiʿ, Ayyub, Salam, Ibn ʿAmir, the people of al-Sham, and Hafs read *yūqadu* with a *yāʾ* underneath, with a damma, a light *qāf*, and a damma on the *dāl*.

Al-Hasan, al-Sulami, Abu ʿUmar ibn al-ʿAla', and Abu Jaʿfar read *tawaqqada* with a *tā'* (feminine) on top, with a fatha, a fatha on the *wāw*, a doubled *qāf*, and a fatha on the *dāl*, as a past tense verb from *tawaqqada yatawaqqadu*. The pronoun in these two readings refers to the lamp.

Al-Nahhas said: These two readings are close in meaning, because both refer to the lamp, and it is more appropriate to this description (p-1015) because it is what gives light and shines, and the glass is only a container for it.

Nasr ibn ʿAsim read like the reading of Abu ʿAmr and those with him, except that he put a damma on the *dāl*, as a present tense verb, and its original form is *tatawaqqadu*.

Then He described the olive tree with another description, saying: ﴿its oil nearly gives light even if no fire touches it﴾. The majority read *tamassuhu* with a *tā'* on top, because fire is feminine. Abu ʿUbayd said: He knows only this reading.

Abu Hatim reported that al-Suddi narrated from Abu Malik from Ibn ʿAbbas that he read *yamassuhu* with a *yāʾ* underneath, because the feminine of fire is not real.

The meaning is that this oil, in its clarity and its brightness, nearly gives light by itself, without fire touching it at all. The *nūrun* (light) is in the nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "it is light." And ﴿upon light﴾ is connected to an omitted word which is an adjective of "light," emphasizing it, and the meaning is: it is light existing upon light. Mujahid said: the intended meaning is the fire upon the oil.

Al-Kalbi said: The lamp is light, and the glass is light. Al-Suddi said: the light of faith and the light of the Qur'an.

﴿Allah guides to His light whomever He wills﴾ from among His servants, meaning a special guidance that delivers to the desired goal, and the intended meaning of guidance here is not mere indication.

﴿Allah strikes parables for the people﴾, meaning He makes things clear by their likenesses and similar examples, bringing them near to understanding and facilitating their comprehension; for the presentation of the intelligible in the form of the sensible and depicting it with its image adds to its clarity and explanation.

﴿Allah is All-Knowing of everything﴾, nothing is hidden from Him of things, whether intelligible or sensible, apparent or hidden.

There has been disagreement about His saying: ﴿in houses which Allah has permitted to be raised﴾, regarding what it is connected to. It was said it is connected to what precedes it, meaning: like a niche in some of the houses of Allah, which are the mosques. As if it were said: the parable of His light is as you see in the mosque, the light of the niche whose description is such and such. It was said: it is connected to "lamp." Ibn al-Anbari said: I heard Abu al-ʿAbbas say: it is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) for the lamp, the glass, and the star, as if it were said: and it is in houses. It was said: it is connected to "is lit," meaning it is lit in houses. It has also been said it is connected to what follows it, which is "glorifies," meaning men glorify Him in houses. On this view, His saying "in it" is a repetition, like your saying: Zayd is sitting in the house, in it.

It was said: it is separate from what precedes it, as if Allah said: in houses which Allah has permitted to be raised.

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi said: Reports have come with this, that whoever sits in the mosques is sitting with his Lord.

It has been said, on the supposition that it is connected to niche, lamp, or "is lit," what is the reason for singularizing the niche and the lamp while pluralizing the house? A single niche or single lamp is only in a single house. The answer is that this is from the kind of address which begins with the singular and ends with the plural, like His saying, glorified is He: ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women﴾ [al-Talaq: 1] and similar.

It was said: the meaning of "in houses" is: in each one of the houses, as if He said: in every house, or in each one of the houses.

People differed regarding the houses, in several views. The first is that they are the mosques, which is the view of Mujahid, al-Hasan, and others.

The second is that what is meant by them is the houses of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), narrated from al-Hasan.

The third is that they are the houses of the Prophet (ﷺ), narrated from Mujahid.

The fourth is that they are all the houses, said by ʿIkrimah.

The fifth is that they are the four mosques: the Kaʿbah, the mosque of Quba', the mosque of Madinah, and the mosque of Bayt al-Maqdis, said by Ibn Zayd.

The first view is more apparent because of His saying: ﴿He is glorified in them morning and evening by men﴾. The *bāʾ* in *bayt* may be pronounced with a damma or a kasra, both of which are established in the language. The meaning of "Allah has permitted it to be raised" is: He commanded and decreed. The meaning of "raised" is "built," said by Mujahid, ʿIkrimah, and others, and from it is His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And when Ibrahim was raising the foundations of the House﴾. Al-Hasan al-Basri and others said: the meaning of "raised" is exalted, its status raised, and purified from impurities and filth. Al-Zajjaj preferred this. It was said: the intended meaning of raising here is the combination of both matters. The meaning of ﴿His name is mentioned in them﴾ is every remembrance of Allah, mighty and majestic is He. It was said: it is monotheism. It was said: the intended meaning is recitation of the Qur'an. The first is preferable.

﴿He is glorified in them morning and evening by men﴾. Ibn ʿAmir and Abu Bakr read *yusabbaha* with a fatha on the *bāʾ*, in the passive form. The rest read it with a kasra on it, in the active form, except Ibn Wathhab and Abu Haywah, who read with a *tā'* on top and a kasra on the *bāʾ*. According to the first reading, the element standing in place of the subject is one of the three prepositional phrases, and "men" is nominative in one of two ways: either by an implied verb, as if it were an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: who glorifies Him? So it was said: men glorify Him. The second is that "men" is raised as the predicate of an omitted subject. According to the second reading, "men" is the subject of "glorifies." According to the third reading, the subject is also "men," and the verb was made feminine because a broken plural is treated in some cases as feminine.

The tafsir has been divided over what this glorification (*tasbih*) is. Most scholars understood it as the obligatory prayers. They said that *al-ghuduww* is the Dawn Prayer (*salat al-subh*) and *al-asal* is the Noon and Afternoon Prayers and the two Night Prayers (*al-'ishaiyn*), since the term *al-asal* includes them. The meaning of *bil-ghuduww wal-asal* is "in the morning and in the evening." It was also said that it refers to the Dawn and Afternoon Prayers, and that it refers to the Forenoon Prayer (*salat al-duha*). It was also said that the glorification here has its literal meaning (*ma'nahu al-haqiqi*), which is declaring Allah far exalted above whatever is unfitting for Him in His essence, His attributes, and His actions. This is supported by the mention of prayer and zakat after it. This view is preferable to what came before it, because it is the literal meaning, and there is evidence against what the earlier scholars held. This is what we have mentioned.

﴿Neither trade nor commerce distracts them from the remembrance of Allah.﴾ This clause describes the men (*rijal*). That is, trade and selling do not occupy them away from remembrance. Trade is singled out because it is the thing that most occupies a person away from remembrance.

Al-Farra' said: "Trade (*tijara*) is for those who import goods (*ahl al-jalab*), and selling (*bay'*) is what a man sells with his own hands." Some scholars restricted *tijara* here to buying (*al-shira'*), because selling is mentioned after it. Al-Waqidi said something similar to al-Farra's view, saying: "The merchants (*al-tujjar*) are the importers who travel, and the sellers (*al-ba'a*) are the ones who stay put." The meaning of *'an dhikr Allah* is what was mentioned earlier in His words, ﴿and that His name may be remembered therein﴾. It was also said that it refers to the call to prayer (*al-adhan*). It was also said that it means remembering Him by His Most Beautiful Names, that is, affirming His oneness and glorifying Him.

It was also said that it refers to the prayer itself, but this is refuted by the mention of prayer after remembrance here. The meaning of *iqam al-salah* (establishing the prayer) is performing it at its appointed times without delay. The *ta'* (ة) is dropped from *iqam*, because the genitive construction (*idafa*) takes the place of the *ta'* in three words, which a poet gathered in his verse:

> Three words have their *ta'*s dropped when they are made genitive (*mudafa*), according to all the grammarians:
> *Abu 'udhriha* (when you wish), *layta shi'ri*, and *iqam al-salah*.

(p. 1016)

Al-Farra' cited, as evidence for the omission mentioned in this verse, the poet's words:

> Indeed the companions (*al-khalit*) hastened to part, and they left, and they broke with you the promise of the matter they had promised.

That is, *'idat al-amr* (the promise of the matter). This line shows that omission with the genitive construction is not restricted to those three places.

Al-Zajjaj said: "The *ha'* was dropped because one says *aqamta al-salata iqamatan*, and the original was *iqwaman*. But the *waw* was changed into an *alif*, so two *alifs* came together, and one of them was dropped to avoid two consecutive unvoweled letters. So it became *aqamtu al-salata iqaman*, and then the *ha'* was inserted as a replacement for what was dropped, and the genitive construction here takes the place of the dropped *ha'*. This is a consensus among the grammarians." End of quote.

Whoever understood *dhikr Allah* as the obligatory prayer has been forced to understand *iqam al-salah* as performing it at its times, to avoid repetition. But there is no need for that. Rather, *dhikr* is understood in its literal meaning, as we have already mentioned.

The zakat mentioned here is the obligatory zakat. It was also said that the zakat means obedience to Allah and sincerity, since not every believer has wealth.

﴿They fear a Day﴾, that is, the Day of Resurrection. Its grammatical status (*intisabuhu*) is that it is an object of the verb (*maf'ul*), not a time adverb for it. Then He described this Day with His words: ﴿in which hearts and eyes will be turned about﴾, that is, they will be agitated and transformed. It was said that the meaning of the turning of hearts is that they are pulled from their places up to the throats, so they neither return to their places nor leave. The meaning of the turning of eyes is that they will become blind after having been seeing.

It was also said that the turning of hearts means that they will fluctuate between hope for salvation and fear of destruction. As for the turning of eyes, it is their looking in every direction from which they will be seized and toward which they will go.

It was also said that the meaning is the transformation of their hearts and eyes from the doubt they were in to certainty. A similar verse is His words: ﴿So We removed your veil, and your sight today is sharp﴾. What he used to see in this world as error, he will see in the Hereafter as right guidance. It was also said that the meaning is the turning over on the embers of Hell, and it was said other than this.

﴿That Allah may reward them with the best of what they did.﴾ This is connected to an omitted element, that is: they do what they do of glorification, remembrance, establishing the prayer, and giving zakat, ﴿that Allah may reward them with the best of what they did﴾. That is, the best reward for their deeds, according to what He promised them of multiplication of that to ten times its like and to seven hundred times. It was also said that what is meant in this verse is what He bestows on them of favor beyond what they deserve. The first view is better, because of His words: ﴿and increase them from His bounty﴾, since what is meant there is bestowing on them more than the promised reward. ﴿And Allah provides for whom He wills without account﴾, that is, without being called to account for what He gave him, or because His giving, glory be to Him, has no end. This sentence confirms what preceded it, namely the promise of increase.

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth﴾, that he said: "He manages the affair in them: their stars, their sun, and their moon." Al-Firyabi reported from him, regarding His words ﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth. The likeness of His light﴾ that is given to the believer, "is like a niche (*mishkat*)." And about the explanation of ﴿an olive tree neither eastern nor western﴾, he said: "It is the one on the slope of a mountain, which the sun does not touch when it rises or when it sets." ﴿Its oil would almost glow even if no fire touched it. Light upon light﴾. That is the likeness of the heart of the believer: light upon light.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Anbari reported in *al-Masahif* from al-Sha'bi that he said: "In the recitation of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, it is: *mathalu nuri al-mu'min kamishkat* (the likeness of the light of the believer is like a niche)."

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, reported from Ibn 'Abbas regarding the verse that he said: "It says: the likeness of the light of one who believes in Allah is like a niche, which is a window (*kuwwa*)."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him regarding ﴿the likeness of His light﴾ that he said: "It is an error by the scribe. He is far too great for His light to be the likeness of a niche." He said: "The likeness of the light of the believer is like a niche."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wal-sifat* reported from him as well, regarding ﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth﴾, that he said: "He is the guide of the people of the heavens and the earth." ﴿The likeness of His light﴾: "the likeness of His guidance in the heart of the believer is like a niche." He says: "The place of the wick, as the pure oil almost glows before fire touches it. When fire touches it, its light increases upon its light. So the heart of the believer acts with guidance before knowledge comes to it, and when knowledge comes to it, its guidance increases upon guidance and its light upon light." In its chain is 'Ali ibn Abi Talha, about whom there is criticism.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ubayy ibn Ka'b regarding ﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth. The likeness of His light﴾, that he said: "It is the believer in whose chest faith and the Qur'an have been placed, so Allah gave his likeness. He said: ﴿the light of the heavens and the earth, the likeness of His light﴾, so He began with His own light. Then He mentioned the light of the believer, and said: the likeness of the light of the one who believes in Him." Ubayy ibn Ka'b used to recite it as *mathalu nuri man amana bihi* (the likeness of the light of the one who believes in Him). "So it is the believer, in whose chest faith and the Qur'an have been placed like a niche." He said: "The believer's chest is the niche. ﴿In it is a lamp, the lamp﴾ is the light, which is the Qur'an and the faith placed in his chest. ﴿In a glass﴾, and the glass is his heart. ﴿As if it were a star of brilliance﴾, that is, a shining star. ﴿Lit from a blessed tree﴾. The blessed tree is the root of the blessing: sincerity to Allah alone and worshipping Him with no partner. ﴿An olive tree neither eastern nor western﴾." He said: "Its likeness is like the likeness of a tree intertwined with other trees, green and lush, which the sun does not touch in any condition, neither when it rises nor when it sets. Likewise, this believer has been protected from being led astray by any of the trials."

Ibn Abi Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas that "the Jews said to Muhammad: 'How does the light of Allah emerge from beyond the sky?' So Allah struck the likeness of that light of His, and said: ﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth. The likeness of His light is like a niche.﴾" The niche is a window of the house, in which is a lamp, which is the lamp that is in the glass. It is a likeness that Allah struck for His obedience, so He called His obedience light, then named it different kinds. ﴿Neither eastern nor western﴾: he said: "It is the middle of the tree, which the sun does not reach when it rises or sets, and that is the finest oil." ﴿Its oil would almost glow﴾ without fire. ﴿Light upon light﴾, meaning by that the faith and knowledge of the servant. ﴿Allah guides to His light whom He wills﴾, and that is the likeness of the believer.

(p. 1017) Al-Tabarani, Ibn 'Adi, Ibn Mardawayh, and Ibn 'Asakir reported from Ibn 'Umar regarding His words ﴿like a niche in which is a lamp﴾ that he said: "The niche is the inside of Muhammad (ﷺ), the glass is his heart, and the lamp is the light that is in his heart. ﴿Lit from a blessed tree﴾: the tree is Ibrahim. ﴿An olive tree neither eastern nor western﴾: neither Jewish nor Christian." Then he recited: ﴿Ibrahim was neither a Jew nor a Christian, but he was a upright Muslim, and he was not of the polytheists.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 67].

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Shamr ibn 'Atiyya that he said: "Ibn 'Abbas came to Ka'b al-Ahbar and said: 'Tell me about the words of Allah: ﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth. The likeness of His light﴾.' He said: 'The likeness of the light of Muhammad (ﷺ) is like a niche.' He said: 'The niche is the window which Allah struck as an example of a lamp, in which is a lamp, and the lamp is his heart. ﴿The lamp is in a glass﴾, and the glass is his chest. ﴿As if it were a star of brilliance﴾: he likened the chest of Muhammad (ﷺ) to a shining star. Then the lamp returned to his heart, and He said: ﴿lit from a blessed tree, an olive, neither eastern nor western, whose oil would almost glow﴾.' He said: 'Muhammad (ﷺ) almost makes it clear to people, even if he did not speak, that he is a Prophet, just as the oil almost glows even if no fire touches it.'"

I say: explaining the Qur'anic text in this way, and in similar ways, of what came earlier from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Ibn 'Abbas, and Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them, is not in accordance with what the Arabic language requires. Nor was anything authentically reported from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that would permit departing from the Arabic meaning toward these meanings, which resemble riddles and obscurity. But these Companions and those who agreed with them among those who came after them found it unlikely that the light of Allah, glory be to Him, be likened to the light of a lamp in a niche. That is why Ibn 'Abbas said: "He is far too great for His light to be like the light of a niche," as we quoted from him earlier. But there is no basis for this unlikelihood. We have already mentioned at the beginning of the discussion what removes the difficulty and clarifies what is meant in the best way and most eloquent style, in accordance with what the Arabic language requires and what the words of eloquent speakers convey. So there is no reason to depart from the apparent meaning, neither from the Book, nor from the Sunnah, nor from the language.

As for what was reported from Ka'b al-Ahbar concerning this, as we have mentioned, if it was the cause of those honored Companions departing from the apparent meaning in explaining the verse, then someone like Ka'b, may Allah have mercy on him, is not one to be followed in such matters. We have already pointed out earlier that when the tafsir of a Companion is based on narrations from the People of the Book, as happens often, it does not constitute a proof, and it is not permissible to depart from the Arabic explanation because of it. However, if the recitation of Ubayy ibn Ka'b is authentic, it would be the basis for these tafsirs that differ from the apparent meaning, and would be like an explanatory addition clarifying the intended meaning. But if it is not authentic, then adhering to what is required by the recitation of the majority (*al-jumhur*), namely the seven readers (*al-sab'a*) and others before and after them, is what is necessary.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿in houses which Allah has permitted to be raised﴾, that he said: "They are the mosques, which are honored and where idle talk is forbidden. The name of Allah is remembered in them, and His Book is recited in them. ﴿Therein He is glorified morning and evening﴾: the prayer of the morning and the prayer of the afternoon. These two are the first prayers that Allah made obligatory, so He loved to mention them and to remind His servants of them."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 24, verse 35–38 (part 3 of 3):

There have been reported many hadiths concerning the exalting of mosques, keeping them free from filth and idle talk, and cleaning and perfuming them, but this is not the place to mention them.

Ibn Abi Shaybah and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Indeed, the prayer of ad-duha (the forenoon prayer) is in the Qur'an, and none dives into it except a diver, in His saying: ﴿In houses which Allah has permitted to be raised, and His name is remembered therein; He is glorified therein morning and evening﴾."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayrah: "From the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, concerning His saying: ﴿Men whom neither trade nor sale diverts from the remembrance of Allah﴾, he said: 'They are those who travel through the earth seeking of Allah's bounty.'"

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Daylami narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri: "From the Prophet ﷺ, concerning His saying: ﴿Neither trade nor sale diverts them from the remembrance of Allah﴾, he said: 'They are those who seek of Allah's bounty.'"

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning the verse, he said: "They were men who sought of Allah's bounty, buying and selling. When they heard the call to prayer, they would drop what was in their hands and go to the mosque and pray."

Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab narrated from him concerning the verse, he said: "Allah struck this parable, His saying: ﴿As a niche﴾, for those people whom neither trade nor sale diverts from the remembrance of Allah. They were the most active in trade and the most engaged in selling, but their trade and their selling did not divert them from the remembrance of Allah."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated also from him, concerning "from the remembrance of Allah", he said: "From attending the prayer."

'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Umar that he was in the marketplace when the prayer was established, so they closed their shops and entered the mosque. Ibn 'Umar said: "Concerning them this was revealed: ﴿Men whom neither trade nor sale diverts from the remembrance of Allah﴾."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, al-Tabarani and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he saw some people from the market who heard the adhan and left their goods, so he said: "These are the ones concerning whom Allah said: ﴿Neither trade nor sale diverts them from the remembrance of Allah﴾."

Hannad ibn al-Sarri in al-Zuhd, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab and Muhammad ibn Nasr in al-Salah narrated from Asma' bint Yazid, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "On the Day of Resurrection Allah will gather the people in one plain; the caller will make them hear him and the sight will reach them. A herald will stand and call: 'Where are those who used to praise Allah in ease and in hardship?' They will stand, and they are few, and they will enter Paradise without reckoning. Then he will return and call: 'Where are those whose sides used to forsake their beds?' They will stand, and they are few, and they will enter Paradise without reckoning. Then he will return and call: 'Let those stand whom neither trade nor sale diverted from the remembrance of Allah.' They will stand, and they are few, and they will enter Paradise without reckoning. Then the rest of the people will stand and be reckoned."

al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab narrated from 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir, traced to the Prophet ﷺ, a similar report.

(p-1018).
When He, glorified is He, mentioned the state of the believers and the outcome of their affair, He mentioned a parable for the disbelievers, saying: ﴿And those who disbelieve, their deeds are like a mirage in a level plain﴾. What is meant by "deeds" here are the deeds that are among the good works, such as charity, maintaining ties of kinship, freeing captives, maintaining the House (the Ka'bah), and providing water for the pilgrims. The "saraab" (mirage) is what is seen in the deserts from the shimmering of the sun when the heat of the day intensifies, in the form of water in the assumption of the one who sees it, and it is called saraab because it "yasrub", i.e., flows like water, except that it rises above the earth until it becomes as if it were between the sky and the earth. Imru' al-Qays said:
"Have I not wearied my mounts through every long, wide desert, glittering with mirage?"
And another said:
"When we restrained war, their covenants were like the gleam of a mirage in the plain, sparkling."
The word qî'ah (qi'ah) is the plural of qā' (qa'): it is the low-lying place where water settles, like jīrah and jār, as al-Harawi said.
Abu 'Ubayd said: qî'ah and qā' are one and the same.
al-Jawhari said: al-qā' is the level part of the earth, and its plural is uqū', aqwā' and qī'ān; the waw became a yā' because of the kasrah before it, and qî'ah is like qā'.
He said: Some say it is a plural.
﴿The thirsty one thinks it is water﴾: this is a second description of the mirage. "The thirsty" (al-ẓam'ān) is the one who is parched with thirst. The specification of the thinking to the thirsty, even though the one who is sated also sees it in that way, is to realize the comparison, which is built upon desire. ﴿Until, when he comes to it, he finds it to be nothing﴾: that is, when the thirsty one comes to that which he thought was water, he finds it to be nothing of what he estimated and supposed, nor anything else. The meaning is that the disbelievers rely upon their deeds, which they consider to be good, and hope for their reward; but when they come before Allah, glorified is He, they find nothing of them, because disbelief has nullified them and erased their trace. What is meant by His saying ﴿until, when he comes to it﴾, although it is nothing, is that he came to the place where he had been holding it.
Then He, glorified is He, mentioned what indicates an increase in the anguish of the disbelievers, and that the ultimate end of their affair is not merely the disappointment like the one who sees the mirage. He said: ﴿And he finds Allah with him, so He pays him his account in full, and Allah is swift in reckoning﴾: that is, he finds Allah lying in wait, so He pays him his account, i.e., the recompense of his deeds, as Imru' al-Qays said:
"So he turned back fleeing, hastening, and he was certain that he would meet the reckoning."
It was said: he finds Allah's promise of recompense for his deed; it was said: he finds Allah's command at His gathering; it was said: he finds His judgment and decree when He comes; it was said: at the work. The meanings are close.
Maslamah ibn Muharib read (biqī'āhu) with a round tā' (ha'), as one says rajul 'azhāh. It is related from him that he read (biqī'āt) with an extended tā'. It is said that the alif may be produced from prolonging the 'ayn in the first reading, and the plural of qī'ah in the second.
It is related from Nafi', Abu Ja'far and Shaybah that they read (al-ẓam'ān) without a hamzah, while the well-known reading from them is with the hamzah.
﴿Or like darkness﴾: this is coordinated with "like a mirage." Allah struck another parable for the deeds of the disbelievers, since they resemble the mirage described with those attributes, so they also resemble darkness.
al-Zajjaj said: Allah, glorified is He, informed that if the deeds of the disbelievers are likened to what exists, their likeness is that of the mirage; and if they are likened to what is seen, they are like these darknesses He described.
He also said: If you wish, liken them to the mirage, and if you wish, liken them to these darknesses; so "or" here is for permission, in accordance with what preceded in the discussion of ﴿or like a downpour﴾ [al-Baqarah: 19].
al-Jurjani said: the first verse is about the deeds of the disbelievers, and the second is about their disbelief; and the coupling of disbelief with their deeds is because it, too, is among their deeds.
al-Qushayri said: according to al-Zajjaj the parable applies to the deeds of the disbelievers, and according to al-Jurjani to the disbelief of the disbelievers.
﴿In a deep sea﴾: al-lujjah is the greater part of the water, its plural being lujaj, and it is that whose depth cannot be reached.
Then He, glorified is He, described this sea with another attribute, saying: ﴿Covered by waves﴾: that is, a wave rises over this sea and covers it and envelops it entirely. Then He described this wave, saying: ﴿above it are clouds﴾: that is, above that second wave are clouds. Thus there gathers over them the fear of the sea, its waves, and the clouds raised above it.
It was said: the meaning is: covered by a wave, after which a wave follows, so that the waves follow one another until it is as if one part of them is above another. The sea is most fearsome when its waves follow in succession; and when the presence of clouds above it is added to that, the fear increases in intensity, because they conceal the stars by which those in the sea are guided. Then, when those clouds rain and the wind blows, as is customary in most cases when rain falls, the worries accumulate and the sorrows follow one another, and the matter reaches the ultimate limit beyond which there is no limit. For this reason He, glorified is He, said: ﴿darkness, one above another﴾: that is, these are darknesses, or these are darknesses piled up and succeeding one another; so in this clause there is an explanation of the severity and magnitude of the matter.
Ibn Muhaysin and al-Bazzi read ﴿clouds of darkness﴾ with the idafah of "clouds" to "darkness." The reason for the idafah is that the cloud rises at the time of these darknesses, so it is attributed to them because of this association. The rest read it with a break and tanwin.
Among the strange interpretations is that He, glorified is He, intended by the darknesses: the deeds of the disbeliever; by the deep sea: his heart; by the wave above the wave: what covers his heart of ignorance, doubt and bewilderment; and by the clouds: the rust, the sealing and the stamping upon his heart. This is an interpretation far removed from the language of the Arabs.
Then He exaggerated about these mentioned darknesses by His saying: ﴿When he brings out his hand, he hardly can see it﴾. The doer of "brings out" is a pronoun referring to an implied subject indicated by the context, i.e., when the one present in these darknesses brings out (his hand), or the one who is afflicted by them.
al-Zajjaj and Abu 'Ubaydah said: the meaning is "he did not see it and did not nearly [see it]." al-Farra' said: "kād" (nearly) is superfluous.
The meaning is: when he brings out his hand, he does not see it, just as you say "I was not nearly knowing him." al-Mubarrad said: it means he does not see it except after great effort.
al-Nahhas said: the most correct of these statements in this regard is that the meaning is he does not come near to seeing it; so he does not see it, neither from a distance nor from close up.
The clause ﴿And whoever Allah does not grant light, for him there is no light﴾ confirms what precedes, namely that the deeds of the disbelievers are of this description. The meaning: whoever Allah does not grant guidance, for him there is no guidance.
al-Zajjaj said: that is in this world; the meaning is: whomever Allah does not guide will not be guided. It was said: the meaning is: whoever He does not give light by which he walks on the Day of Resurrection, for him there is no light by which he is guided to Paradise.
﴿Do you not see that Allah is glorified by whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾: the explanation of a similar verse has already preceded in Surat Subhan, and the address is to everyone who has the capacity for reflection, or to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who knew it through inference. The meaning of "Do you not see" is "Do you not know," and the interrogative particle is for affirmation: that is, you have known with certain knowledge resembling direct observation. Tasbih (glorification) is declaring Him free of imperfection in His essence, His acts and His attributes, from everything unbefitting to Him. The meaning of "whoever is in the heavens and the earth" is whoever dwells in them from among the rational and others. The glorification of non-rational beings is what is heard of their sounds and what is witnessed of the traces of the marvelous craftsmanship in them.
It was said: the tasbih here is prayer from the rational, and declaring Him free of imperfection from the others.
It has been said: this verse includes animals and inanimate objects, and that the traces of divine craftsmanship in inanimate objects speak and inform of His being described with attributes of majesty and perfection and of His being free of attributes of deficiency. In this there is a rebuke to the disbelievers and a reproach to them, in that they made inanimate objects, whose nature is to glorify Allah, partners to Him, worshipping them as they worship Him, mighty and majestic.
In sum, the tasbih should be understood as befitting each kind of created being, by way of the general use of metaphor.
The majority read ﴿and the birds, in ranks﴾ with raf' (nominative) for "the birds" and nasb (accusative) for "ranks," on the basis that "the birds" is coordinated with "whoever," and "ranks" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state.
al-A'raj read (wal-ṭayra) with nasb as an object with (ma'a) (accompaniment), and "ranks" is also a state. al-Zajjaj said: this is better than the nominative.
al-Hasan and Kharijah from Nafi' read (wal-ṭayru ṣāffāt) with raf' for both, as subject and predicate, and the object of "ranks" is omitted, i.e., "their wings." He singled out the birds for mention, although they are included under "whoever is in the heavens and the earth," because they do not remain steadily on the earth, and because they are abundant in staying aloft, and they are neither of the heaven nor of the earth; and because of the marvelous craftsmanship in them by which they are able at one time to fly and at another to walk, unlike other animals. He mentioned a state of the bird, namely that the glorification proceeds from them while they are in ranks with their wings, because this state is the most remarkable of their conditions; for their remaining in the air glorifying without moving their wings, and without settling on the earth, is among the greatest of Allah's workmanship, who perfected everything.
Then He increased the clarification, saying: ﴿Each knows its prayer and its glorification﴾: that is, each one of those mentioned; the pronoun in "knows" refers to "each." The meaning: each of these glorifiers of Allah knows the prayer of the one who prays and the glorification of the one who glorifies. It was said: the meaning is that each one who prays and glorifies knows the prayer of himself and the glorification of himself.
It was said: "prayer" here means glorification, and it is repeated for emphasis, since prayer is sometimes called glorification. It was said: what is meant by "prayer" here is supplication, i.e., each one knows its supplication and its glorification.
The benefit of the information that each one knows this is that its emanation from them is by way of spontaneity without deliberation; and in this there is an increase of indication of the wondrous craftsmanship of Allah, glorified is He, and the greatness of His station, that He made them glorify Him, knowing what proceeds from them, not ignorant of Him. ﴿And Allah is Knower of what they do﴾: this clause confirms what precedes, i.e., their obedience and their glorification are not hidden from Him. It is also permissible that the pronoun in "knows" refers to Allah, glorified is He; i.e., each one of these glorifying creatures, Allah knows its prayer and its glorification of Him. The first is more preferred, because the readers agree on the raf' of "each" (kullun); if the pronoun in "knows" referred to Allah, the nasb of "each" would have been more appropriate. Some exegetes mentioned that a group of readers read (ʿulima) in the passive voice.
Then He, glorified is He, made clear that the origin is from Him and the return is to Him, saying: ﴿And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾: that is, it belongs to Him, not to another, and to Him is the destination, not to another. "Maṣīr" (destination) is the return after death. The explanation of similar verses has already preceded in more than one place.
Then He, glorified is He, mentioned another proof from the heavenly phenomena, saying: ﴿Do you not see that Allah drives clouds gently﴾. The izjā' (driving) is driving slowly, little by little; from it is the saying of al-Nabighah:
"Indeed I came to you from my family and my homeland, driving the remnant of a soul in which there is no breath left."
And his saying also:
"A nightly traveler over it from Orion drove it, while al-Simak drove over it hardened hail."
The meaning is that He, glorified is He, drives the clouds with a gentle drive wherever He wills. ﴿Then He joins them together﴾: that is, joins their parts, gathering some of it to some and bringing it together after its dispersion, so that it becomes strong, connected and dense. The original form of "ta'lif" (joining) is with the hamzah.
Warsh and Qalun from Nafi' read (yu'allifu) with waw, as a lightening (of the hamzah). The cloud is singular in wording, but its meaning is plural; for this reason (bayn) was used with it, since its parts have the status of individual units.

Al-Farra' said: The pronoun in (baynahu) refers to the mass of clouds, as you would say "the trees, I sat among them" (al-shajar qad jalastu baynahu), because it is a collective noun, and the pronoun was made singular in consideration of the word's form. ﴿Then He makes it piled up﴾, meaning heaped up, one part riding upon another. Al-rakm is the gathering of a thing: one says rakama al-shay' yarkumuhu rakman, meaning he gathered it and cast part of it upon part. Irtakama al-shay' and tarakama mean it gathered together. Al-rukmah is clay that has been gathered, and al-rukam is sand piled in layers. ﴿Then you see the rain (al-wadq) coming out from within it﴾. Al-wadq is the rain according to the majority of the exegetes, and from it is the line of the poet:

"Neither a cloud has poured its rain, nor a land has sprouted its herbage."

And the line of Imru' al-Qays:

"Their tears are a downpour, a heavy rain, a continuous rain, a flood, a pouring, and a flowing."

It is said: the clouds poured (waddat al-sahab), so it is wadiqah, and the rain poured (wadaqa al-matar yadiqu), meaning it dripped and trickled. It is also said that al-wadq is lightning, and from it is the line of the poet:

"They raised a dust cloud and came out from it, like the emerging of the wadq from the openings of the clouds."

The first view is preferable. The meaning of ﴿from within it﴾ is from its openings, which are the outlets of the drops. The clause ﴿coming out from within it﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal), because the seeing here is visual seeing.

Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, al-Dahhak and Abu al-'Aliyah read (khallihi) in the singular. There has been disagreement over khilal: is it singular, like hijab, or plural, like jibal?

﴿And He sends down from the sky mountains containing hail﴾. What is meant by "from the sky" is from above, since "sky" may be applied to the direction of height. The meaning of "from hail" is partitive, and it is the object of "sends down". It is also said that the object is omitted, and the estimate is: He sends down from mountains in which there is hail, hail. It is also said that "min" in "min barad" is extra, and the estimate is: He sends down from the sky mountains in which there is hail. It is also said that the speech contains an omitted modifier, meaning: He sends down from the sky an amount equal to mountains, or like mountains, of hail, down to the earth.

Al-Akhfash said: "min" in "min jibal" and in "min barad" is extra in both places, and "al-jibal" and "al-barad" are in the accusative position, meaning: He sends down from the sky hail that is like mountains.

The summary is that "min" in "min al-sama'" is for the beginning of the limit (ibtida' al-ghayah) without disagreement. As for "min" in "min jibal", there are three possibilities. The first is that it is for the beginning of the limit, so it and its genitive are a substitute for the first, by repeating the governing particle, a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal). The second is that it is partitive, so in this case it and its genitive are in the accusative position as the object of the sending down, as if he said: He sends down some mountains. The third is that it is extra, meaning: He sends down from the sky mountains.

As for "min" in "min barad", there are four possibilities: the three mentioned earlier, and the fourth is that it is for explaining the kind, so the estimate in this way is: He sends down from the sky some mountains which are hail.

Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of the verse is: He sends down from the sky, from mountains, hail in them, as you say: "This is a ring in my hand of iron," meaning: a ring of iron in my hand, because if you say "this is a ring of iron" and "a ring made of iron," the meaning is one. End.

On this basis, "min barad" is in the genitive position as a qualifier of "jibal", just as "min hadid" is a qualifier of "khatam", and the object of "yunazzilu" is "min jibal". From the mountains being hail it follows that what is sent down is hail.

Abu al-Baqa' mentioned that the estimate is: some of mountains, so he omitted the modified noun and was content with the qualifier.

﴿So He strikes with it whom He wills﴾, meaning He strikes with what He sends down of hail whomever of His servants He wills to strike, ﴿and averts it from whom He wills﴾ among them; or He strikes with it the property of whom He wills and averts it from the property of whom He wills. This kind of thing has been discussed before in al-Baqarah.

﴿The flash of His lightning nearly takes away the sights﴾. Al-sana is the light, meaning the light of the lightning that is in the clouds nearly takes away the sights because of its intense glare and the increase of its brightness. This is like His saying: ﴿The lightning nearly snatches away their sight﴾ [al-Baqarah: 20]. Al-Shammakh said:

"And when it raises its light, it almost would not let anyone see its light except the one with sight."

Imru' al-Qays said:

"Its light shines like the lamps of a monk who has made the pressed oil cheap in the twisted wick."

Al-sana with short vowel is the light of lightning, and with the long vowel (sana') it is the elevation. So said al-Mubarrad and others.

Talhah ibn Musarrif and Yahya ibn Wathhab read (sana'u barqihi) with the long vowel, as an exaggeration in the intensity of light and its purity, so the name of elevation and nobility is applied to it.

Talhah and Yahya also read, with a damma on the ba' of (buraqihi) and a fatha on the ra', and said Ahmad ibn Yahya Tha'lab: on this reading it is the plural of barq.

Al-Nahhas said: al-buraqah is a quantity of lightning, and al-barqah is one flash.

Al-Jahdari and Ibn al-Qa'qa' read (yudhhibu) with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the ha', from the causative (al-idhhab). The rest read sana with the short vowel and barqihi with a fatha on the ba' and a sukun on the ra', and yadhhabu with a fatha on the ya' and ha', from dhahab. Al-Akhfash and Abu Hatim criticized the reading of al-Jahdari and Ibn al-Qa'qa'. The meaning of the lightning taking away the sights is that it snatches them because of the intensity of its illumination and the increase of its glitter. The ba' in "al-absar" according to the reading of the majority is for attachment, and according to the reading of the others it is extra.

﴿God causes the night and the day to alternate﴾, meaning He makes one follow the other. It is said: He increases one of them and decreases the other. It is said: He turns them by the variation of what He decrees in them of good and evil, benefit and harm. It is said: by heat and cold. It is said: what is meant is the change of the day by the darkness of clouds at one time and by the light of the sun at another, and the change of the night by the darkness of clouds at one time and by the light of the moon at another. The reference in His saying ﴿Surely in that is a lesson for those who have sight﴾ is to what has preceded. The meaning of "lesson" (ibrah) is the clear proof by which consideration is made, and what is meant by "those who have sight" is everyone who has a sight with which he sees.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned a third proof from the wonders of the creation of animals and the marvel of His workmanship, saying: ﴿And God created every creature (dabbah) from water﴾. Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (wallahu khaliqu kulli dabbah) as "creator"; the rest read "created" (khalaqa), and both meanings are sound. A dabbah is every living thing that crawls on the earth, from the verb dabba yadibbu, so he is a dabb; the ha' is for intensification. The meaning of "from water" is from a drop of semen, which is the sperm, so said the majority.

A group said: what is meant is ordinary water, because Adam was created from water and clay.
