Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿The flash of His lightning nearly takes away the sights﴾: he says: the light of its lightning.

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: every creature walks on four except the human being. I say: these birds, in their various kinds, walk on two legs, and so do others, like the ostrich, for it walks on two legs and is not one of the birds. So this universal statement attributed to him, may Allah be pleased with him, is not sound.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 24, verses 55–57 (part 1 of 3):

He, glorified is He, began to explain the states of those who have not been granted guidance to the Straight Path, so He said: ﴿They say: "We believe in Allah and the Messenger, and we obey."﴾ These are the hypocrites (munafiqun), who display faith and conceal disbelief, and who say with their mouths what is not in their hearts. As Allah related about them here, they ascribe to themselves belief in Allah and His Messenger and obedience to Allah and His Messenger, an ascription made merely with the tongue and not from sound conviction. For this reason He said: ﴿Then a group of them turn away﴾, meaning a group of these hypocrites who utter this statement, after that, that is, after what they had ascribed to themselves of the claim to faith and obedience had come from them. Then He, glorified and exalted is He, passed judgment on them that they are not believers, saying: ﴿And those are not believers﴾, meaning those who utter this statement are not believers in the true sense. The judgment of negating faith therefore covers all who utter it, and those who turned away are included in it by a primary inclusion.

It has been said that the reference of "those" (ulaika) is to those who turned away, but the first view is preferable.

The discourse contains two judgments: the first is a judgment upon some of them, that they turned away; the second is a judgment upon all of them, that they lack faith.

It has been said that by "those who turned away" is meant those who turned away from accepting his judgment, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace. It has also been said that what is meant is the leaders of the hypocrites. It has been said that what is meant by the turning away of this group is their return to the rest. What this verse may bear by the wording of its expression does not conflict with its having been revealed on a specific occasion, as will come its explanation.

Then He described these hypocrites by saying that a group of them turn away from answering the call to Allah and to His Messenger in their disputes. So He said: ﴿And when they are called to Allah and His Messenger, that he may judge between them﴾, meaning that the Messenger may judge between them. The pronoun therefore refers to him, because he is the one who directly issues the judgment, even though the judgment in reality belongs to Allah, glorified is He. Similar to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾. The "idha" in His saying ﴿Then when a group of them are turning away﴾ is the sudden "idha" (idha al-fuja'iyyah), meaning that a group of them suddenly turned away from being judged by Allah and His Messenger. Then He, glorified is He, mentioned that their turning away occurs only when the right is against them. As for when the right is theirs, they submit, because they know that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, judges only by the truth. So He said: ﴿But if the right is theirs, they come to him willingly submitting﴾. [p. 1022] Al-Zajjaj said: "al-idh'an" is hastening together with obedience. It is said: adh'ana li bi-haqqi, meaning he yielded to me in what I was seeking from him, and he began to hasten toward it. Mujahid said the same. Al-Akhfash and Ibn al-A'rabi said: "mudh' inin" means "acknowledging." Al-Naqqash said: "mudh'inin" means "humbled."

Then He divided the matter regarding their turning away from His judgment when the right is against them, so He said: ﴿Is there in their hearts a disease?﴾ This hamza is for rebuke and reproach toward them. "Disease" means hypocrisy, meaning: Was this turning away from them due to the hypocrisy present in their hearts? ﴿Or have they doubted?﴾, meaning they doubted the matter of his prophethood, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, and his justice in judgment. ﴿Or do they fear that Allah and His Messenger will wrong them?﴾ "Hayf" means inclination in judgment; it is said: "hafa fi qadiyyatihi," meaning he acted unjustly in what he decided. Then He turned away from these matters, which He introduced with the interrogative of denial, and said: ﴿Rather, those are the wrongdoers﴾, meaning it is not due to any of what has been mentioned, but rather due to their wrongdoing and obstinacy. For if the turning away were due to any of what has been mentioned, they would not have come to him submitting when the right was theirs.

In this verse is evidence for the obligation to respond to a judge who is knowledgeable of Allah's judgment and just in his ruling, because the scholars are the heirs of the prophets. Judgment by the judges of the Muslims who are knowledgeable of Allah's judgment, who know the Book and the Sunnah, and who are just in judging, is a judgment according to the judgment of Allah and the judgment of His Messenger. Therefore the one who calls for submitting disputes to them has called to Allah and to His Messenger, meaning to their judgment.

Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: "It is obligatory upon everyone who is summoned to the session of a ruler to respond, so long as he does not know that the ruler is an evildoer."

Al-Qurtubi said: "In this verse is evidence for the obligation to respond to one who summons to the ruler, because Allah, glorified is He, condemned with the most severe condemnation those who were called to His Messenger so that he might judge between them and their adversary, saying: ﴿Is there in their hearts a disease?﴾ to the end of the verse." End of quotation.

If the judge is deficient, not knowing the rulings of the Book and the Sunnah, and not comprehending the proofs of Allah and the meanings of His speech and the speech of His Messenger, but rather is ignorant with simple ignorance (jahl basit), meaning one who has no knowledge of any of that, or with compound ignorance (jahl murakkab), meaning one who has no knowledge of what we have mentioned, but has come to know some of the ijtihad of the mujtahids and has acquainted himself with some of the knowledge of opinion (ilm al-ra'y), then this one is in reality ignorant, and even if he believes he knows something of knowledge, his belief is false. Whoever is a judge of this sort, responding to him is not obligatory, because he is not one who knows the judgment of Allah and His Messenger so that he may judge according to it between the litigants who come to him. Rather, he is one of the judges of the false authority (taghut) and the rulers of falsehood. For what he has come to know of the knowledge of opinion was only permitted to be acted upon by the mujtahid to whom it is attributed when there is no evidence from the Book and the Sunnah, and it was not permitted for anyone else who comes after him.

When this has been established for you, and you have understood it in its proper understanding, you will know that taqlid (blind imitation), attributing oneself to one scholar of the scholars to the exclusion of others, and restricting oneself to everything that came from him of narration and opinion while neglecting whatever else there is, are among the greatest innovations (bid'ah) that have occurred in this Islamic religion, misguiding innovations and dreadful calamities. Surely we belong to Allah and to Him we return.

We have clarified this in our book that we named (al-Qawl al-Mufid fi Hukm al-Taqlid) and in our book that we named (Adab al-Talab wa Muntaha al-Arab). Whoever wishes to understand the reality of this innovation, which has spread through the Islamic lands, let him return to these two.

Then, having mentioned what the people of hypocrisy were upon, He followed it with what the believers must do when they are called to the judgment of Allah and His Messenger. So He said: ﴿The saying of the believers, when they are called to Allah and His Messenger that he may judge between them, is only that they say: "We hear and we obey."﴾ The majority read "qawla" in the accusative, taking it as the predicate of "kana" (khabar kana), with its subject being "an yaqulu" (that they say). 

Ali, al-Hasan and Ibn Abi Ishaq read "qawlu" in the nominative, taking it as the subject (ism), and "an" with what follows it as the predicate (khabar). I have preferred the first reading, on the basis of what the grammarians have established: that when two definite nouns are combined and one of them is more definite, the more definite one is made the subject (ism). As for Sibawayh, he allowed choice between any two definite nouns and did not make this distinction. We have already presented the discussion of the call to Allah and His Messenger for judgment between two litigants, and we mentioned who among the judges must be responded to and who need not be.

﴿That they say: "We hear and we obey"﴾, meaning that they should say this statement and no other statement. Although this is in the form of a report, what is meant by it is not merely that, but rather the teaching of the legal etiquette (adab shar'i) at this call from one of the two litigants to the other.

The meaning is: it is befitting for the believers to be such that when they hear the aforementioned summons, they respond with obedience and submission.

Muqatil and others said: they say, "We hear the statement of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, and we obey his command," even if that is in what they dislike and what harms them.

Then He, glorified is He, praised them by His saying: ﴿And those are the successful﴾, meaning the believers who uttered this statement are the successful, that is, the ones who attain the good of this world and the Hereafter.

Then He added to His praise of them another praise, saying: ﴿And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger, fears Allah and keeps his duty to Him, then those are the victorious﴾. This sentence confirms what came before it regarding the good state of the believers, and encourages those other than them to enter among their number, and to follow them in obeying Allah and His Messenger, in fearing Allah, glorified and exalted is He, and in being mindful of Him.

Hafs read "wa yattaqhi" with the qaf silent, on the intention of jussive (jazm). The rest read it with the qaf vowelled with a kasra, because the jussive of this verb is by deleting its last letter. Abu 'Amr and Abu Bakr silenced the ha'; Ya'qub and Qalun on the authority of Nafi' and al-Muthanna on the authority of Abu 'Amr and Hafs shortened the kasra; and the rest pronounced the kasra of the ha' fully.

Ibn al-Anbari said: The reading of Hafs follows the dialect of those who say: "lam ar Zaydan" and "lam ashtar ta'aman," dropping the yā' for the jussive and then silencing the letter that precedes it. From this is the saying of the poet:

"Sulaymā said: buy for us flour"

And the saying of another:

"I marvel at one born without a father,
and at one who has a child whom no two parents begot."

Its original form is "yalid" with a kasra on the lam and a sukun on the dal for the jussive. When he silenced the lam, two silent letters met. If he had moved the first, he would have returned to what the avoidance was meant to escape, so he moved the second, which is the dal.

It may be said that he moved the first in accordance with the original rule for meeting of two silent letters, and the sukun remained on the dal to show what this dialect's speakers do. The return to what the avoidance was meant to escape is not harmful, since this movement is different from that movement.

The reference of His saying ﴿Then those are the victorious﴾ is to those described by what was mentioned of obedience, fear, and God-consciousness, meaning they are the ones who are victorious with the worldly blessing [p. 1023] and the otherworldly blessing, not anyone else.

Then He, glorified is He, related about the hypocrites that when they disliked His judgment, they swore by Allah that if He commanded them to go out to the battle, they would go out. So He said: ﴿And they swore by Allah with their strongest oaths: "If you command them, they will surely go out."﴾, meaning, if you command them to go out for jihad, they will surely go out. And "jahda aymanihim" is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar mu'akkid) for the omitted verb that governs it, meaning: they swore by Allah, exerting their oaths with exertion.

The meaning of "jahda aymanihim" is the utmost of what they could swear, derived from their saying "jahada nafsahu," when he reaches its limit and the utmost of its capacity.

It has been said that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), the sense being: striving in their oaths, as in their saying: "do that with your utmost effort and capacity." Al-Zamakhshari combined the two possibilities and made them one.

The answer to the oath is His saying "they will surely go out." Since their statement was false and their oaths were sinful, Allah responded to them, saying: ﴿Say: "Do not swear."﴾, meaning respond to them, restraining them, and say to them, "Do not swear," that is, do not take oaths regarding what you claim of obedience and going out to jihad if you are commanded to it. Here the speech is complete.

Then He began, saying: ﴿Obedience is known﴾. The "ta'atun" is raised as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: your obedience is a known obedience, known to be an obedience of hypocrisy, not based on conviction. It may also be the subject (mubtada'), since it has been specified by the qualifying adjective, and the predicate is then omitted, meaning: a known obedience is more appropriate for you than your oaths. It may also be raised by an omitted verb, meaning: let there be obedience from you, or let it be found. In this there is weakness, because a verb is not omitted unless something indicating it has preceded.

Zayd ibn Ali and al-Tirmidhi read "ta'atan" in the accusative as a verbal noun for an omitted verb, meaning: obey with obedience.

﴿Indeed, Allah is Well-Acquainted with what you do﴾, of deeds, and with what you conceal of opposition to what your tongues utter. This sentence gives the reason for what came before it, namely that their obedience is the obedience of hypocrisy.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 24, verse 55–57 (part 2 of 3):

Then Allah, glorified is He, commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to order them to obey Allah and His Messenger, so He said: ﴿Say: Obey Allah and obey the Messenger﴾, an obedience that is outward and inward, with sincere belief and correct intention. This repetition by the Most High is to emphasise the obligation of obedience upon them, for His saying ﴿Say: Do not swear; known obedience﴾ is in the sense of a command to obey. It has also been said that the two are different: the first is a prohibition by way of rebuke and reproach, and the second is a command by way of imposing duty and obligation upon them. ﴿But if they turn away﴾ is an address to those who are commanded, and its original form is "fa-in tatawallaw", so one of the two tā's was dropped for lightness. In it there is a shift from addressing the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to addressing them directly, to emphasise the command upon them and to stress concern for guiding them to obedience and submission. The answer to the condition is His saying ﴿then upon him is what he has been charged with, and upon you is what you have been charged with﴾, meaning: know that upon the Prophet (ﷺ) is what he has been charged with of the duty of conveying, which he has done, and upon you is what you have been charged with, that is, what you have been commanded of obedience. This is a warning to them, as if He had said to them: If you turn away, then you have become bearers of a heavy burden. ﴿And if you obey him﴾ in what he commands you and forbids you, you will be guided to the truth, you will be rightly guided to good, and you will attain the reward. The clause ﴿And upon the Messenger is only the clear conveyance﴾ confirms what precedes it, and the lām is either for a specific reference, so that "the Messenger" means our Prophet (ﷺ), or for the category, so that it means every messenger. "Clear conveyance" means conveying that is plain or made clear.

It has been said that His saying ﴿But if they turn away﴾ may be in the past tense, with the wāw referring to the absent party, and this conditional clause would then be something the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was commanded to say to them, and there would be a shift in the speech from address to third person. The first view is more preferred. It is supported by the address in His saying ﴿and upon you is what you have been charged with﴾ and His saying ﴿and if you obey him, you will be guided﴾. It is also supported by al-Bazzi's reading "fa-in tawallaw" with a doubled tā', though this reading is weak because it involves joining two sukun letters.

﴿Allah has promised those of you who believe and do righteous deeds﴾. This clause confirms what precedes it, that their obedience to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is the cause of their guidance. This is a promise from Allah, glorified is He, to those who believe in Allah and do righteous deeds, that they will be made successors in the earth just as He made successors those who came before them from the nations. It is a promise that encompasses the whole community.

It has been said that it is specific to the Companions, but there is no basis for this, for belief and doing righteous deeds are not restricted to them; rather it is possible for this to occur from every individual of this community, and whoever acts by the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger has obeyed Allah and His Messenger. The lām in ﴿He will surely make them successors in the earth﴾ is the answer to an implied oath, or it is the answer to the promise, treating it as an oath because it is certain without doubt. The meaning of "He will surely make them successors in the earth" is: He will surely make them successors in it, who dispose of it as kings dispose of their possessions. Those who said it is restricted to the four Caliphs, or to the Emigrants, or that by "the earth" is meant the land of Makkah, have gone too far; you know that the consideration is the generality of the wording and not the specificity of the occasion. The apparent sense of His saying ﴿as He made successors those who came before them﴾ is that it applies to everyone whom Allah has made successor in His earth, so it is not restricted to the Children of Israel or to any one nation over others.

The majority read ﴿as He made successors﴾ with an open tā' (fataha) in the active voice. ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar, Abū Bakr and al-Mufaḍḍal from ʿĀṣim read it with a dammah in the passive voice. The place of the kāf is in the accusative as an adverbial of manner (maṣdar), meaning: a succession like that which He made. The clause ﴿and He will surely establish for them their religion which He has approved for them﴾ is joined to "He will surely make them successors" and falls under its ruling, being part of the answer. By "establishment" (tamkīn) here is meant firmness and confirmation, that is, Allah will make it firm and established, will widen for them in the lands, and will make their religion prevail over all religions. By "religion" here is meant Islam, as in His saying ﴿And I have approved for you Islam as a religion﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 3]. The Most High mentioned the succession for them first, which is making them kings, and mentioned the establishment second, and this conveys that this kingship is not temporary and passing, but firm and lasting, such that the kingdom belongs to them and to their descendants after them. The clause ﴿and He will surely change their state after their fear into security﴾ is joined to the one before it.

Ibn Kathīr, Ibn Muḥaysin, Yaʿqūb and Abū Bakr read ﴿yubdilannahum﴾ with lightness, from abdala. This is the reading of al-Ḥasan, and Abū Ḥātim preferred it. The others read it with doubling, from baddala, and Abū ʿUbayd preferred it. Both are dialects, and an increase in the structure indicates an increase in meaning, so the doubled reading is more preferred than the light reading.

Al-Naḥḥās said: Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā Thaʿlab claimed that there is a difference between the light and the heavy forms, that one says "baddaltuhu", meaning I changed it, and "abdaltuhu", meaning I removed it and put something else in its place. Al-Naḥḥās said: this view is correct.

The meaning is: He, glorified is He, will make for them, in place of what they were in of fear from enemies, security, and will remove from them the causes of the fear they were in, such that they fear none but Allah, glorified is He, and hope for none other than Him.

The Muslims, before the Hijrah and shortly after it, were in severe fear of the polytheists; they did not go out except armed, and they did not spend the evening or the morning except in constant watch for harm to come upon them from the disbelievers. Then they reached the utmost security and ease, Allah humbled for them the devils of the polytheists, opened the lands to them, paved the earth for them and established them in it. So to Allah belongs all praise.

The clause ﴿they worship Me﴾ is in the accusative place as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and it may be that it is a resumed clause, given in praise of them. The clause ﴿they do not associate anything with Me﴾ is in the accusative place as a circumstantial clause from the subject of "they worship Me", meaning: they worship Me, not associating anything with Me in worship. It has been said: its meaning is that they do not show off their worship of Me to anyone. It has been said: its meaning is that they do not fear other than Me. It has been said: its meaning is that they do not love other than Me.

﴿But whoever disbelieves after that, those are the defiantly disobedient﴾. That is: whoever disbelieves these blessings after that promise which is true, or whoever persists in disbelief, or whoever disbelieves after faith, then those who disbelieve are the defiantly disobedient, that is, the complete in defiance. Defiance is going out of obedience and transgression in disbelief.

The clause ﴿And establish the prayer﴾ is joined to an implied element indicated by what precedes it, as if it had been said to them: "So believe, do righteous deeds, and establish the prayer." It has also been said that it is joined to "And obey Allah". It has also been said that the estimate is: "So do not disbelieve, and establish the prayer."

The discussion of establishing the prayer and giving zakah has already been presented. He repeated the command to obey the Messenger for emphasis and singled it out for obedience, because his obedience is obedience to Allah. He did not mention what they are to obey him in, for the purpose of generality, as the omission indicates, according to what has been established in the science of rhetoric (ʿilm al-maʿānī), that such an omission indicates generality. ﴿So that you may be shown mercy﴾, that is: do what has been mentioned of establishing the prayer, giving zakah and obeying the Messenger, hoping that Allah, glorified is He, will show you mercy.

﴿Do not think that those who disbelieve can escape in the land﴾. Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamzah and Abū Ḥaywah read "lā taḥsabanna" with the yā' (third person), meaning: let not those who disbelieve think. The others read it with the tā' (second person), that is: do not think, O Muḥammad. The relative pronoun is the first object, and "muʿjizīn" is the second, since ḥasiba takes two objects, as said by al-Zajjāj, al-Farrā' and Abū ʿAlī.

As for the first reading, the first object is omitted, that is: let not those who disbelieve think that they themselves [can escape].

Al-Naḥḥās said: I do not know of any Basran or Kufan who does not criticise the reading of Ḥamzah. "Muʿjizīn" means "escaping" (fā'itīn). Its explanation and the explanation of what follows it have already been given.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted from Qatādah, concerning His saying ﴿And they say: We believe in Allah and in the Messenger﴾ to the end of the verse, that he said: "They are some hypocrites who displayed faith and obedience, while in that they were turning people away from the path of Allah, from obedience to Him and from striving alongside His Messenger (ﷺ)."

They also transmitted from al-Ḥasan, who said: "A man would have a dispute or contention with another man during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). When he was called to the Prophet (ﷺ) and he was in the right, he would submit and know that the Prophet (ﷺ) would judge in his favour with the truth. But when he wished to wrong, and was called to the Prophet (ﷺ), he would turn away and say: 'I will go to so-and-so.' So Allah, glorified is He, revealed: ﴿And when they are called to Allah and His Messenger﴾ up to His saying ﴿they are the wrongdoers﴾. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) then said: 'Whoever has a matter between himself and his brother, and he calls him to a judge from the judges of the Muslims and he does not respond, then he is a wrongdoer, with no right.'"

Ibn Kathīr, after transmitting this text, said in his words: "This is a strange ḥadīth, and it is mursal." Ibn al-ʿArabī said: "This ḥadīth is false. As for his saying 'then he is a wrongdoer', that is a correct statement; but as for his saying 'with no right', that is not sound. It may be that he means that he is in a state other than the truth." End of quotation.

I say: As for the ḥadīth being mursal, that is evident. But the claim that it is false requires proof. Three leading imams of ḥadīth, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim, transmitted it, as we mentioned. It is far-fetched in the extreme that they would all agree upon something false. Its isnād in Ibn Abī Ḥātim is thus: Ibn Abī Ḥātim said: "My father related to us, Mūsā ibn Ismāʿīl related to us, Mubārak related to us, al-Ḥasan related to us," and so he mentioned it. Among these there is no liar and no forger.

It is corroborated by what al-Ṭabarānī transmitted from al-Ḥasan, from Samurah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever is called to a ruler and does not respond, then he is a wrongdoer with no right." End of quotation.

And it is not hidden from you that the judges of justice and the rulers of the Sharīʿah, who are of the character we mentioned to you shortly before, are the rulers of religion who translate from the Book and the Sunnah, clarifying to people what has been sent down to them.

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "Some people came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, if you were to command us to leave our wealth, we would leave it.' So Allah revealed: ﴿And they swear by Allah with their most emphatic oaths﴾ to the end of the verse."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted from Muqātil concerning the verse, who said: "That concerns the matter of jihad. He commands them that they should not swear to anything; ﴿known obedience﴾ means he commanded that there should be from them known obedience to the Prophet (ﷺ) without their swearing."

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Mujāhid concerning ﴿known obedience﴾: "It means: their obedience is already known, that is, you are lying in it."

Muslim, al-Tirmidhī and others transmitted from ʿAlqamah ibn Wāʾil al-Ḥaḍramī, from his father, who said: "Zayd ibn Aslam came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'What do you think if there are rulers over us who take from us what is right and do not give us [our due]?' He said: 'Upon them is what they have been charged with, and upon you is what you have been charged with.'"

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Qāniʿ and al-Ṭabarānī transmitted from ʿAlqamah ibn Wāʾil al-Ḥaḍramī, from Salamah ibn Yazīd al-Juʿfī, who said: "I said, O Messenger of Allah," and then he mentioned something similar.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted from Ibn al-Zubayr, from Jābir, that he asked: "If there is over me a wicked imam, and I meet with him people of misguidance, should I fight them or not?" He said: "Fight the people of misguidance wherever you find them, and upon the imam is what he has been charged with, and upon you is what you have been charged with."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from al-Bara', regarding His words: ﴿Allah has promised those among you who believe﴾ the verse. He said: It was revealed concerning us while we were in great fear.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu al-ʿAliyah, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions were in Makkah for about ten years, calling to Allah alone, and to worshipping Him alone with no partner, secretly, while they were in fear and were not commanded to fight, until they were commanded to emigrate to Madinah. They came to Madinah, and Allah commanded them to fight. They were there in fear, spending their evenings and mornings in arms. They remained in that state for as long as Allah willed. Then a man among his Companions said: 'O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), will we be in this state of fear forever? Will there not come a day when we are safe and can lay down our arms?' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'You will not wait long before a man among you sits in a great assembly, wearing no iron armor.' Then Allah revealed: ﴿Allah has promised those among you who believe and do righteous deeds that He will surely make them successors in the earth﴾ to the end of the verse." Then Allah made His Prophet (ﷺ) victorious over the Arabian Peninsula, and they became secure and laid down their arms.

Then Allah took His Prophet (ﷺ) [in death], and they remained secure in the rule of Abu Bakr, ʿUmar and ʿUthman, until they fell into error and became ungrateful for the blessing. So Allah brought upon them the fear that had been lifted from them, and they adopted guards and police, and changed, so Allah changed what was with them.

Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il, and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtarah narrated from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, who said: When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) arrived in Madinah and the Ansar sheltered them, the Arabs shot at them with a single bow. They did not spend the night or morning except in arms. They said: "Do you think we will live to spend a night secure and at peace, fearing none but Allah?" Then the verse was revealed: ﴿Allah has promised those among you who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ the verse.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ﴿They worship Me, not associating anything with Me﴾, that he said: "They fear no one but Me."

al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Mujahid the like of this, and he said regarding ﴿And whoever disbelieves after that, those are the defiantly disobedient (al-fasiqun)﴾: the disobedient, the sinners.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd narrated from Abu al-ʿAliyah, who said: "It is ingratitude for this blessing, not disbelief in Allah."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd narrated from Qatadah regarding ﴿unable to escape [Allah] in the earth (mu'jizina fi al-ard)﴾, that he said: "Outrunning [Allah] in the earth."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 24, verses 55–57 (part 1 of 3):

He, glorified is He, began to explain the states of those who have not been granted guidance to the Straight Path, so He said: ﴿They say: "We believe in Allah and the Messenger, and we obey."﴾ These are the hypocrites (munafiqun), who display faith and conceal disbelief, and who say with their mouths what is not in their hearts. As Allah related about them here, they ascribe to themselves belief in Allah and His Messenger and obedience to Allah and His Messenger, an ascription made merely with the tongue and not from sound conviction. For this reason He said: ﴿Then a group of them turn away﴾, meaning a group of these hypocrites who utter this statement, after that, that is, after what they had ascribed to themselves of the claim to faith and obedience had come from them. Then He, glorified and exalted is He, passed judgment on them that they are not believers, saying: ﴿And those are not believers﴾, meaning those who utter this statement are not believers in the true sense. The judgment of negating faith therefore covers all who utter it, and those who turned away are included in it by a primary inclusion.

It has been said that the reference of "those" (ulaika) is to those who turned away, but the first view is preferable.

The discourse contains two judgments: the first is a judgment upon some of them, that they turned away; the second is a judgment upon all of them, that they lack faith.

It has been said that by "those who turned away" is meant those who turned away from accepting his judgment, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace. It has also been said that what is meant is the leaders of the hypocrites. It has been said that what is meant by the turning away of this group is their return to the rest. What this verse may bear by the wording of its expression does not conflict with its having been revealed on a specific occasion, as will come its explanation.

Then He described these hypocrites by saying that a group of them turn away from answering the call to Allah and to His Messenger in their disputes. So He said: ﴿And when they are called to Allah and His Messenger, that he may judge between them﴾, meaning that the Messenger may judge between them. The pronoun therefore refers to him, because he is the one who directly issues the judgment, even though the judgment in reality belongs to Allah, glorified is He. Similar to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾. The "idha" in His saying ﴿Then when a group of them are turning away﴾ is the sudden "idha" (idha al-fuja'iyyah), meaning that a group of them suddenly turned away from being judged by Allah and His Messenger. Then He, glorified is He, mentioned that their turning away occurs only when the right is against them. As for when the right is theirs, they submit, because they know that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, judges only by the truth. So He said: ﴿But if the right is theirs, they come to him willingly submitting﴾. [p. 1022] Al-Zajjaj said: "al-idh'an" is hastening together with obedience. It is said: adh'ana li bi-haqqi, meaning he yielded to me in what I was seeking from him, and he began to hasten toward it. Mujahid said the same. Al-Akhfash and Ibn al-A'rabi said: "mudh' inin" means "acknowledging." Al-Naqqash said: "mudh'inin" means "humbled."

Then He divided the matter regarding their turning away from His judgment when the right is against them, so He said: ﴿Is there in their hearts a disease?﴾ This hamza is for rebuke and reproach toward them. "Disease" means hypocrisy, meaning: Was this turning away from them due to the hypocrisy present in their hearts? ﴿Or have they doubted?﴾, meaning they doubted the matter of his prophethood, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, and his justice in judgment. ﴿Or do they fear that Allah and His Messenger will wrong them?﴾ "Hayf" means inclination in judgment; it is said: "hafa fi qadiyyatihi," meaning he acted unjustly in what he decided. Then He turned away from these matters, which He introduced with the interrogative of denial, and said: ﴿Rather, those are the wrongdoers﴾, meaning it is not due to any of what has been mentioned, but rather due to their wrongdoing and obstinacy. For if the turning away were due to any of what has been mentioned, they would not have come to him submitting when the right was theirs.

In this verse is evidence for the obligation to respond to a judge who is knowledgeable of Allah's judgment and just in his ruling, because the scholars are the heirs of the prophets. Judgment by the judges of the Muslims who are knowledgeable of Allah's judgment, who know the Book and the Sunnah, and who are just in judging, is a judgment according to the judgment of Allah and the judgment of His Messenger. Therefore the one who calls for submitting disputes to them has called to Allah and to His Messenger, meaning to their judgment.

Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: "It is obligatory upon everyone who is summoned to the session of a ruler to respond, so long as he does not know that the ruler is an evildoer."

Al-Qurtubi said: "In this verse is evidence for the obligation to respond to one who summons to the ruler, because Allah, glorified is He, condemned with the most severe condemnation those who were called to His Messenger so that he might judge between them and their adversary, saying: ﴿Is there in their hearts a disease?﴾ to the end of the verse." End of quotation.

If the judge is deficient, not knowing the rulings of the Book and the Sunnah, and not comprehending the proofs of Allah and the meanings of His speech and the speech of His Messenger, but rather is ignorant with simple ignorance (jahl basit), meaning one who has no knowledge of any of that, or with compound ignorance (jahl murakkab), meaning one who has no knowledge of what we have mentioned, but has come to know some of the ijtihad of the mujtahids and has acquainted himself with some of the knowledge of opinion (ilm al-ra'y), then this one is in reality ignorant, and even if he believes he knows something of knowledge, his belief is false. Whoever is a judge of this sort, responding to him is not obligatory, because he is not one who knows the judgment of Allah and His Messenger so that he may judge according to it between the litigants who come to him. Rather, he is one of the judges of the false authority (taghut) and the rulers of falsehood. For what he has come to know of the knowledge of opinion was only permitted to be acted upon by the mujtahid to whom it is attributed when there is no evidence from the Book and the Sunnah, and it was not permitted for anyone else who comes after him.

When this has been established for you, and you have understood it in its proper understanding, you will know that taqlid (blind imitation), attributing oneself to one scholar of the scholars to the exclusion of others, and restricting oneself to everything that came from him of narration and opinion while neglecting whatever else there is, are among the greatest innovations (bid'ah) that have occurred in this Islamic religion, misguiding innovations and dreadful calamities. Surely we belong to Allah and to Him we return.

We have clarified this in our book that we named (al-Qawl al-Mufid fi Hukm al-Taqlid) and in our book that we named (Adab al-Talab wa Muntaha al-Arab). Whoever wishes to understand the reality of this innovation, which has spread through the Islamic lands, let him return to these two.

Then, having mentioned what the people of hypocrisy were upon, He followed it with what the believers must do when they are called to the judgment of Allah and His Messenger. So He said: ﴿The saying of the believers, when they are called to Allah and His Messenger that he may judge between them, is only that they say: "We hear and we obey."﴾ The majority read "qawla" in the accusative, taking it as the predicate of "kana" (khabar kana), with its subject being "an yaqulu" (that they say). 

Ali, al-Hasan and Ibn Abi Ishaq read "qawlu" in the nominative, taking it as the subject (ism), and "an" with what follows it as the predicate (khabar). I have preferred the first reading, on the basis of what the grammarians have established: that when two definite nouns are combined and one of them is more definite, the more definite one is made the subject (ism). As for Sibawayh, he allowed choice between any two definite nouns and did not make this distinction. We have already presented the discussion of the call to Allah and His Messenger for judgment between two litigants, and we mentioned who among the judges must be responded to and who need not be.

﴿That they say: "We hear and we obey"﴾, meaning that they should say this statement and no other statement. Although this is in the form of a report, what is meant by it is not merely that, but rather the teaching of the legal etiquette (adab shar'i) at this call from one of the two litigants to the other.

The meaning is: it is befitting for the believers to be such that when they hear the aforementioned summons, they respond with obedience and submission.

Muqatil and others said: they say, "We hear the statement of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, and we obey his command," even if that is in what they dislike and what harms them.

Then He, glorified is He, praised them by His saying: ﴿And those are the successful﴾, meaning the believers who uttered this statement are the successful, that is, the ones who attain the good of this world and the Hereafter.

Then He added to His praise of them another praise, saying: ﴿And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger, fears Allah and keeps his duty to Him, then those are the victorious﴾. This sentence confirms what came before it regarding the good state of the believers, and encourages those other than them to enter among their number, and to follow them in obeying Allah and His Messenger, in fearing Allah, glorified and exalted is He, and in being mindful of Him.

Hafs read "wa yattaqhi" with the qaf silent, on the intention of jussive (jazm). The rest read it with the qaf vowelled with a kasra, because the jussive of this verb is by deleting its last letter. Abu 'Amr and Abu Bakr silenced the ha'; Ya'qub and Qalun on the authority of Nafi' and al-Muthanna on the authority of Abu 'Amr and Hafs shortened the kasra; and the rest pronounced the kasra of the ha' fully.

Ibn al-Anbari said: The reading of Hafs follows the dialect of those who say: "lam ar Zaydan" and "lam ashtar ta'aman," dropping the yā' for the jussive and then silencing the letter that precedes it. From this is the saying of the poet:

"Sulaymā said: buy for us flour"

And the saying of another:

"I marvel at one born without a father,
and at one who has a child whom no two parents begot."

Its original form is "yalid" with a kasra on the lam and a sukun on the dal for the jussive. When he silenced the lam, two silent letters met. If he had moved the first, he would have returned to what the avoidance was meant to escape, so he moved the second, which is the dal.

It may be said that he moved the first in accordance with the original rule for meeting of two silent letters, and the sukun remained on the dal to show what this dialect's speakers do. The return to what the avoidance was meant to escape is not harmful, since this movement is different from that movement.

The reference of His saying ﴿Then those are the victorious﴾ is to those described by what was mentioned of obedience, fear, and God-consciousness, meaning they are the ones who are victorious with the worldly blessing [p. 1023] and the otherworldly blessing, not anyone else.

Then He, glorified is He, related about the hypocrites that when they disliked His judgment, they swore by Allah that if He commanded them to go out to the battle, they would go out. So He said: ﴿And they swore by Allah with their strongest oaths: "If you command them, they will surely go out."﴾, meaning, if you command them to go out for jihad, they will surely go out. And "jahda aymanihim" is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar mu'akkid) for the omitted verb that governs it, meaning: they swore by Allah, exerting their oaths with exertion.

The meaning of "jahda aymanihim" is the utmost of what they could swear, derived from their saying "jahada nafsahu," when he reaches its limit and the utmost of its capacity.

It has been said that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), the sense being: striving in their oaths, as in their saying: "do that with your utmost effort and capacity." Al-Zamakhshari combined the two possibilities and made them one.

The answer to the oath is His saying "they will surely go out." Since their statement was false and their oaths were sinful, Allah responded to them, saying: ﴿Say: "Do not swear."﴾, meaning respond to them, restraining them, and say to them, "Do not swear," that is, do not take oaths regarding what you claim of obedience and going out to jihad if you are commanded to it. Here the speech is complete.

Then He began, saying: ﴿Obedience is known﴾. The "ta'atun" is raised as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: your obedience is a known obedience, known to be an obedience of hypocrisy, not based on conviction. It may also be the subject (mubtada'), since it has been specified by the qualifying adjective, and the predicate is then omitted, meaning: a known obedience is more appropriate for you than your oaths. It may also be raised by an omitted verb, meaning: let there be obedience from you, or let it be found. In this there is weakness, because a verb is not omitted unless something indicating it has preceded.

Zayd ibn Ali and al-Tirmidhi read "ta'atan" in the accusative as a verbal noun for an omitted verb, meaning: obey with obedience.

﴿Indeed, Allah is Well-Acquainted with what you do﴾, of deeds, and with what you conceal of opposition to what your tongues utter. This sentence gives the reason for what came before it, namely that their obedience is the obedience of hypocrisy.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 24, verse 55–57 (part 2 of 3):

Then Allah, glorified is He, commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to order them to obey Allah and His Messenger, so He said: ﴿Say: Obey Allah and obey the Messenger﴾, an obedience that is outward and inward, with sincere belief and correct intention. This repetition by the Most High is to emphasise the obligation of obedience upon them, for His saying ﴿Say: Do not swear; known obedience﴾ is in the sense of a command to obey. It has also been said that the two are different: the first is a prohibition by way of rebuke and reproach, and the second is a command by way of imposing duty and obligation upon them. ﴿But if they turn away﴾ is an address to those who are commanded, and its original form is "fa-in tatawallaw", so one of the two tā's was dropped for lightness. In it there is a shift from addressing the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to addressing them directly, to emphasise the command upon them and to stress concern for guiding them to obedience and submission. The answer to the condition is His saying ﴿then upon him is what he has been charged with, and upon you is what you have been charged with﴾, meaning: know that upon the Prophet (ﷺ) is what he has been charged with of the duty of conveying, which he has done, and upon you is what you have been charged with, that is, what you have been commanded of obedience. This is a warning to them, as if He had said to them: If you turn away, then you have become bearers of a heavy burden. ﴿And if you obey him﴾ in what he commands you and forbids you, you will be guided to the truth, you will be rightly guided to good, and you will attain the reward. The clause ﴿And upon the Messenger is only the clear conveyance﴾ confirms what precedes it, and the lām is either for a specific reference, so that "the Messenger" means our Prophet (ﷺ), or for the category, so that it means every messenger. "Clear conveyance" means conveying that is plain or made clear.

It has been said that His saying ﴿But if they turn away﴾ may be in the past tense, with the wāw referring to the absent party, and this conditional clause would then be something the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was commanded to say to them, and there would be a shift in the speech from address to third person. The first view is more preferred. It is supported by the address in His saying ﴿and upon you is what you have been charged with﴾ and His saying ﴿and if you obey him, you will be guided﴾. It is also supported by al-Bazzi's reading "fa-in tawallaw" with a doubled tā', though this reading is weak because it involves joining two sukun letters.

﴿Allah has promised those of you who believe and do righteous deeds﴾. This clause confirms what precedes it, that their obedience to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is the cause of their guidance. This is a promise from Allah, glorified is He, to those who believe in Allah and do righteous deeds, that they will be made successors in the earth just as He made successors those who came before them from the nations. It is a promise that encompasses the whole community.

It has been said that it is specific to the Companions, but there is no basis for this, for belief and doing righteous deeds are not restricted to them; rather it is possible for this to occur from every individual of this community, and whoever acts by the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger has obeyed Allah and His Messenger. The lām in ﴿He will surely make them successors in the earth﴾ is the answer to an implied oath, or it is the answer to the promise, treating it as an oath because it is certain without doubt. The meaning of "He will surely make them successors in the earth" is: He will surely make them successors in it, who dispose of it as kings dispose of their possessions. Those who said it is restricted to the four Caliphs, or to the Emigrants, or that by "the earth" is meant the land of Makkah, have gone too far; you know that the consideration is the generality of the wording and not the specificity of the occasion. The apparent sense of His saying ﴿as He made successors those who came before them﴾ is that it applies to everyone whom Allah has made successor in His earth, so it is not restricted to the Children of Israel or to any one nation over others.

The majority read ﴿as He made successors﴾ with an open tā' (fataha) in the active voice. ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar, Abū Bakr and al-Mufaḍḍal from ʿĀṣim read it with a dammah in the passive voice. The place of the kāf is in the accusative as an adverbial of manner (maṣdar), meaning: a succession like that which He made. The clause ﴿and He will surely establish for them their religion which He has approved for them﴾ is joined to "He will surely make them successors" and falls under its ruling, being part of the answer. By "establishment" (tamkīn) here is meant firmness and confirmation, that is, Allah will make it firm and established, will widen for them in the lands, and will make their religion prevail over all religions. By "religion" here is meant Islam, as in His saying ﴿And I have approved for you Islam as a religion﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 3]. The Most High mentioned the succession for them first, which is making them kings, and mentioned the establishment second, and this conveys that this kingship is not temporary and passing, but firm and lasting, such that the kingdom belongs to them and to their descendants after them. The clause ﴿and He will surely change their state after their fear into security﴾ is joined to the one before it.

Ibn Kathīr, Ibn Muḥaysin, Yaʿqūb and Abū Bakr read ﴿yubdilannahum﴾ with lightness, from abdala. This is the reading of al-Ḥasan, and Abū Ḥātim preferred it. The others read it with doubling, from baddala, and Abū ʿUbayd preferred it. Both are dialects, and an increase in the structure indicates an increase in meaning, so the doubled reading is more preferred than the light reading.

Al-Naḥḥās said: Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā Thaʿlab claimed that there is a difference between the light and the heavy forms, that one says "baddaltuhu", meaning I changed it, and "abdaltuhu", meaning I removed it and put something else in its place. Al-Naḥḥās said: this view is correct.

The meaning is: He, glorified is He, will make for them, in place of what they were in of fear from enemies, security, and will remove from them the causes of the fear they were in, such that they fear none but Allah, glorified is He, and hope for none other than Him.

The Muslims, before the Hijrah and shortly after it, were in severe fear of the polytheists; they did not go out except armed, and they did not spend the evening or the morning except in constant watch for harm to come upon them from the disbelievers. Then they reached the utmost security and ease, Allah humbled for them the devils of the polytheists, opened the lands to them, paved the earth for them and established them in it. So to Allah belongs all praise.

The clause ﴿they worship Me﴾ is in the accusative place as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and it may be that it is a resumed clause, given in praise of them. The clause ﴿they do not associate anything with Me﴾ is in the accusative place as a circumstantial clause from the subject of "they worship Me", meaning: they worship Me, not associating anything with Me in worship. It has been said: its meaning is that they do not show off their worship of Me to anyone. It has been said: its meaning is that they do not fear other than Me. It has been said: its meaning is that they do not love other than Me.

﴿But whoever disbelieves after that, those are the defiantly disobedient﴾. That is: whoever disbelieves these blessings after that promise which is true, or whoever persists in disbelief, or whoever disbelieves after faith, then those who disbelieve are the defiantly disobedient, that is, the complete in defiance. Defiance is going out of obedience and transgression in disbelief.

The clause ﴿And establish the prayer﴾ is joined to an implied element indicated by what precedes it, as if it had been said to them: "So believe, do righteous deeds, and establish the prayer." It has also been said that it is joined to "And obey Allah". It has also been said that the estimate is: "So do not disbelieve, and establish the prayer."

The discussion of establishing the prayer and giving zakah has already been presented. He repeated the command to obey the Messenger for emphasis and singled it out for obedience, because his obedience is obedience to Allah. He did not mention what they are to obey him in, for the purpose of generality, as the omission indicates, according to what has been established in the science of rhetoric (ʿilm al-maʿānī), that such an omission indicates generality. ﴿So that you may be shown mercy﴾, that is: do what has been mentioned of establishing the prayer, giving zakah and obeying the Messenger, hoping that Allah, glorified is He, will show you mercy.

﴿Do not think that those who disbelieve can escape in the land﴾. Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamzah and Abū Ḥaywah read "lā taḥsabanna" with the yā' (third person), meaning: let not those who disbelieve think. The others read it with the tā' (second person), that is: do not think, O Muḥammad. The relative pronoun is the first object, and "muʿjizīn" is the second, since ḥasiba takes two objects, as said by al-Zajjāj, al-Farrā' and Abū ʿAlī.

As for the first reading, the first object is omitted, that is: let not those who disbelieve think that they themselves [can escape].

Al-Naḥḥās said: I do not know of any Basran or Kufan who does not criticise the reading of Ḥamzah. "Muʿjizīn" means "escaping" (fā'itīn). Its explanation and the explanation of what follows it have already been given.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted from Qatādah, concerning His saying ﴿And they say: We believe in Allah and in the Messenger﴾ to the end of the verse, that he said: "They are some hypocrites who displayed faith and obedience, while in that they were turning people away from the path of Allah, from obedience to Him and from striving alongside His Messenger (ﷺ)."

They also transmitted from al-Ḥasan, who said: "A man would have a dispute or contention with another man during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). When he was called to the Prophet (ﷺ) and he was in the right, he would submit and know that the Prophet (ﷺ) would judge in his favour with the truth. But when he wished to wrong, and was called to the Prophet (ﷺ), he would turn away and say: 'I will go to so-and-so.' So Allah, glorified is He, revealed: ﴿And when they are called to Allah and His Messenger﴾ up to His saying ﴿they are the wrongdoers﴾. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) then said: 'Whoever has a matter between himself and his brother, and he calls him to a judge from the judges of the Muslims and he does not respond, then he is a wrongdoer, with no right.'"

Ibn Kathīr, after transmitting this text, said in his words: "This is a strange ḥadīth, and it is mursal." Ibn al-ʿArabī said: "This ḥadīth is false. As for his saying 'then he is a wrongdoer', that is a correct statement; but as for his saying 'with no right', that is not sound. It may be that he means that he is in a state other than the truth." End of quotation.

I say: As for the ḥadīth being mursal, that is evident. But the claim that it is false requires proof. Three leading imams of ḥadīth, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim, transmitted it, as we mentioned. It is far-fetched in the extreme that they would all agree upon something false. Its isnād in Ibn Abī Ḥātim is thus: Ibn Abī Ḥātim said: "My father related to us, Mūsā ibn Ismāʿīl related to us, Mubārak related to us, al-Ḥasan related to us," and so he mentioned it. Among these there is no liar and no forger.

It is corroborated by what al-Ṭabarānī transmitted from al-Ḥasan, from Samurah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever is called to a ruler and does not respond, then he is a wrongdoer with no right." End of quotation.

And it is not hidden from you that the judges of justice and the rulers of the Sharīʿah, who are of the character we mentioned to you shortly before, are the rulers of religion who translate from the Book and the Sunnah, clarifying to people what has been sent down to them.

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "Some people came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, if you were to command us to leave our wealth, we would leave it.' So Allah revealed: ﴿And they swear by Allah with their most emphatic oaths﴾ to the end of the verse."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted from Muqātil concerning the verse, who said: "That concerns the matter of jihad. He commands them that they should not swear to anything; ﴿known obedience﴾ means he commanded that there should be from them known obedience to the Prophet (ﷺ) without their swearing."

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Mujāhid concerning ﴿known obedience﴾: "It means: their obedience is already known, that is, you are lying in it."

Muslim, al-Tirmidhī and others transmitted from ʿAlqamah ibn Wāʾil al-Ḥaḍramī, from his father, who said: "Zayd ibn Aslam came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'What do you think if there are rulers over us who take from us what is right and do not give us [our due]?' He said: 'Upon them is what they have been charged with, and upon you is what you have been charged with.'"

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Qāniʿ and al-Ṭabarānī transmitted from ʿAlqamah ibn Wāʾil al-Ḥaḍramī, from Salamah ibn Yazīd al-Juʿfī, who said: "I said, O Messenger of Allah," and then he mentioned something similar.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted from Ibn al-Zubayr, from Jābir, that he asked: "If there is over me a wicked imam, and I meet with him people of misguidance, should I fight them or not?" He said: "Fight the people of misguidance wherever you find them, and upon the imam is what he has been charged with, and upon you is what you have been charged with."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from al-Bara', regarding His words: ﴿Allah has promised those among you who believe﴾ the verse. He said: It was revealed concerning us while we were in great fear.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu al-ʿAliyah, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions were in Makkah for about ten years, calling to Allah alone, and to worshipping Him alone with no partner, secretly, while they were in fear and were not commanded to fight, until they were commanded to emigrate to Madinah. They came to Madinah, and Allah commanded them to fight. They were there in fear, spending their evenings and mornings in arms. They remained in that state for as long as Allah willed. Then a man among his Companions said: 'O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), will we be in this state of fear forever? Will there not come a day when we are safe and can lay down our arms?' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'You will not wait long before a man among you sits in a great assembly, wearing no iron armor.' Then Allah revealed: ﴿Allah has promised those among you who believe and do righteous deeds that He will surely make them successors in the earth﴾ to the end of the verse." Then Allah made His Prophet (ﷺ) victorious over the Arabian Peninsula, and they became secure and laid down their arms.

Then Allah took His Prophet (ﷺ) [in death], and they remained secure in the rule of Abu Bakr, ʿUmar and ʿUthman, until they fell into error and became ungrateful for the blessing. So Allah brought upon them the fear that had been lifted from them, and they adopted guards and police, and changed, so Allah changed what was with them.

Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il, and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtarah narrated from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, who said: When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) arrived in Madinah and the Ansar sheltered them, the Arabs shot at them with a single bow. They did not spend the night or morning except in arms. They said: "Do you think we will live to spend a night secure and at peace, fearing none but Allah?" Then the verse was revealed: ﴿Allah has promised those among you who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ the verse.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ﴿They worship Me, not associating anything with Me﴾, that he said: "They fear no one but Me."

al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Mujahid the like of this, and he said regarding ﴿And whoever disbelieves after that, those are the defiantly disobedient (al-fasiqun)﴾: the disobedient, the sinners.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd narrated from Abu al-ʿAliyah, who said: "It is ingratitude for this blessing, not disbelief in Allah."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd narrated from Qatadah regarding ﴿unable to escape [Allah] in the earth (mu'jizina fi al-ard)﴾, that he said: "Outrunning [Allah] in the earth."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 24, verses 55–57 (part 1 of 3):

He, glorified is He, began to explain the states of those who have not been granted guidance to the Straight Path, so He said: ﴿They say: "We believe in Allah and the Messenger, and we obey."﴾ These are the hypocrites (munafiqun), who display faith and conceal disbelief, and who say with their mouths what is not in their hearts. As Allah related about them here, they ascribe to themselves belief in Allah and His Messenger and obedience to Allah and His Messenger, an ascription made merely with the tongue and not from sound conviction. For this reason He said: ﴿Then a group of them turn away﴾, meaning a group of these hypocrites who utter this statement, after that, that is, after what they had ascribed to themselves of the claim to faith and obedience had come from them. Then He, glorified and exalted is He, passed judgment on them that they are not believers, saying: ﴿And those are not believers﴾, meaning those who utter this statement are not believers in the true sense. The judgment of negating faith therefore covers all who utter it, and those who turned away are included in it by a primary inclusion.

It has been said that the reference of "those" (ulaika) is to those who turned away, but the first view is preferable.

The discourse contains two judgments: the first is a judgment upon some of them, that they turned away; the second is a judgment upon all of them, that they lack faith.

It has been said that by "those who turned away" is meant those who turned away from accepting his judgment, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace. It has also been said that what is meant is the leaders of the hypocrites. It has been said that what is meant by the turning away of this group is their return to the rest. What this verse may bear by the wording of its expression does not conflict with its having been revealed on a specific occasion, as will come its explanation.

Then He described these hypocrites by saying that a group of them turn away from answering the call to Allah and to His Messenger in their disputes. So He said: ﴿And when they are called to Allah and His Messenger, that he may judge between them﴾, meaning that the Messenger may judge between them. The pronoun therefore refers to him, because he is the one who directly issues the judgment, even though the judgment in reality belongs to Allah, glorified is He. Similar to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾. The "idha" in His saying ﴿Then when a group of them are turning away﴾ is the sudden "idha" (idha al-fuja'iyyah), meaning that a group of them suddenly turned away from being judged by Allah and His Messenger. Then He, glorified is He, mentioned that their turning away occurs only when the right is against them. As for when the right is theirs, they submit, because they know that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, judges only by the truth. So He said: ﴿But if the right is theirs, they come to him willingly submitting﴾. [p. 1022] Al-Zajjaj said: "al-idh'an" is hastening together with obedience. It is said: adh'ana li bi-haqqi, meaning he yielded to me in what I was seeking from him, and he began to hasten toward it. Mujahid said the same. Al-Akhfash and Ibn al-A'rabi said: "mudh' inin" means "acknowledging." Al-Naqqash said: "mudh'inin" means "humbled."

Then He divided the matter regarding their turning away from His judgment when the right is against them, so He said: ﴿Is there in their hearts a disease?﴾ This hamza is for rebuke and reproach toward them. "Disease" means hypocrisy, meaning: Was this turning away from them due to the hypocrisy present in their hearts? ﴿Or have they doubted?﴾, meaning they doubted the matter of his prophethood, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, and his justice in judgment. ﴿Or do they fear that Allah and His Messenger will wrong them?﴾ "Hayf" means inclination in judgment; it is said: "hafa fi qadiyyatihi," meaning he acted unjustly in what he decided. Then He turned away from these matters, which He introduced with the interrogative of denial, and said: ﴿Rather, those are the wrongdoers﴾, meaning it is not due to any of what has been mentioned, but rather due to their wrongdoing and obstinacy. For if the turning away were due to any of what has been mentioned, they would not have come to him submitting when the right was theirs.

In this verse is evidence for the obligation to respond to a judge who is knowledgeable of Allah's judgment and just in his ruling, because the scholars are the heirs of the prophets. Judgment by the judges of the Muslims who are knowledgeable of Allah's judgment, who know the Book and the Sunnah, and who are just in judging, is a judgment according to the judgment of Allah and the judgment of His Messenger. Therefore the one who calls for submitting disputes to them has called to Allah and to His Messenger, meaning to their judgment.

Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: "It is obligatory upon everyone who is summoned to the session of a ruler to respond, so long as he does not know that the ruler is an evildoer."

Al-Qurtubi said: "In this verse is evidence for the obligation to respond to one who summons to the ruler, because Allah, glorified is He, condemned with the most severe condemnation those who were called to His Messenger so that he might judge between them and their adversary, saying: ﴿Is there in their hearts a disease?﴾ to the end of the verse." End of quotation.

If the judge is deficient, not knowing the rulings of the Book and the Sunnah, and not comprehending the proofs of Allah and the meanings of His speech and the speech of His Messenger, but rather is ignorant with simple ignorance (jahl basit), meaning one who has no knowledge of any of that, or with compound ignorance (jahl murakkab), meaning one who has no knowledge of what we have mentioned, but has come to know some of the ijtihad of the mujtahids and has acquainted himself with some of the knowledge of opinion (ilm al-ra'y), then this one is in reality ignorant, and even if he believes he knows something of knowledge, his belief is false. Whoever is a judge of this sort, responding to him is not obligatory, because he is not one who knows the judgment of Allah and His Messenger so that he may judge according to it between the litigants who come to him. Rather, he is one of the judges of the false authority (taghut) and the rulers of falsehood. For what he has come to know of the knowledge of opinion was only permitted to be acted upon by the mujtahid to whom it is attributed when there is no evidence from the Book and the Sunnah, and it was not permitted for anyone else who comes after him.

When this has been established for you, and you have understood it in its proper understanding, you will know that taqlid (blind imitation), attributing oneself to one scholar of the scholars to the exclusion of others, and restricting oneself to everything that came from him of narration and opinion while neglecting whatever else there is, are among the greatest innovations (bid'ah) that have occurred in this Islamic religion, misguiding innovations and dreadful calamities. Surely we belong to Allah and to Him we return.

We have clarified this in our book that we named (al-Qawl al-Mufid fi Hukm al-Taqlid) and in our book that we named (Adab al-Talab wa Muntaha al-Arab). Whoever wishes to understand the reality of this innovation, which has spread through the Islamic lands, let him return to these two.

Then, having mentioned what the people of hypocrisy were upon, He followed it with what the believers must do when they are called to the judgment of Allah and His Messenger. So He said: ﴿The saying of the believers, when they are called to Allah and His Messenger that he may judge between them, is only that they say: "We hear and we obey."﴾ The majority read "qawla" in the accusative, taking it as the predicate of "kana" (khabar kana), with its subject being "an yaqulu" (that they say). 

Ali, al-Hasan and Ibn Abi Ishaq read "qawlu" in the nominative, taking it as the subject (ism), and "an" with what follows it as the predicate (khabar). I have preferred the first reading, on the basis of what the grammarians have established: that when two definite nouns are combined and one of them is more definite, the more definite one is made the subject (ism). As for Sibawayh, he allowed choice between any two definite nouns and did not make this distinction. We have already presented the discussion of the call to Allah and His Messenger for judgment between two litigants, and we mentioned who among the judges must be responded to and who need not be.

﴿That they say: "We hear and we obey"﴾, meaning that they should say this statement and no other statement. Although this is in the form of a report, what is meant by it is not merely that, but rather the teaching of the legal etiquette (adab shar'i) at this call from one of the two litigants to the other.

The meaning is: it is befitting for the believers to be such that when they hear the aforementioned summons, they respond with obedience and submission.

Muqatil and others said: they say, "We hear the statement of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, and we obey his command," even if that is in what they dislike and what harms them.

Then He, glorified is He, praised them by His saying: ﴿And those are the successful﴾, meaning the believers who uttered this statement are the successful, that is, the ones who attain the good of this world and the Hereafter.

Then He added to His praise of them another praise, saying: ﴿And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger, fears Allah and keeps his duty to Him, then those are the victorious﴾. This sentence confirms what came before it regarding the good state of the believers, and encourages those other than them to enter among their number, and to follow them in obeying Allah and His Messenger, in fearing Allah, glorified and exalted is He, and in being mindful of Him.

Hafs read "wa yattaqhi" with the qaf silent, on the intention of jussive (jazm). The rest read it with the qaf vowelled with a kasra, because the jussive of this verb is by deleting its last letter. Abu 'Amr and Abu Bakr silenced the ha'; Ya'qub and Qalun on the authority of Nafi' and al-Muthanna on the authority of Abu 'Amr and Hafs shortened the kasra; and the rest pronounced the kasra of the ha' fully.

Ibn al-Anbari said: The reading of Hafs follows the dialect of those who say: "lam ar Zaydan" and "lam ashtar ta'aman," dropping the yā' for the jussive and then silencing the letter that precedes it. From this is the saying of the poet:

"Sulaymā said: buy for us flour"

And the saying of another:

"I marvel at one born without a father,
and at one who has a child whom no two parents begot."

Its original form is "yalid" with a kasra on the lam and a sukun on the dal for the jussive. When he silenced the lam, two silent letters met. If he had moved the first, he would have returned to what the avoidance was meant to escape, so he moved the second, which is the dal.

It may be said that he moved the first in accordance with the original rule for meeting of two silent letters, and the sukun remained on the dal to show what this dialect's speakers do. The return to what the avoidance was meant to escape is not harmful, since this movement is different from that movement.

The reference of His saying ﴿Then those are the victorious﴾ is to those described by what was mentioned of obedience, fear, and God-consciousness, meaning they are the ones who are victorious with the worldly blessing [p. 1023] and the otherworldly blessing, not anyone else.

Then He, glorified is He, related about the hypocrites that when they disliked His judgment, they swore by Allah that if He commanded them to go out to the battle, they would go out. So He said: ﴿And they swore by Allah with their strongest oaths: "If you command them, they will surely go out."﴾, meaning, if you command them to go out for jihad, they will surely go out. And "jahda aymanihim" is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar mu'akkid) for the omitted verb that governs it, meaning: they swore by Allah, exerting their oaths with exertion.

The meaning of "jahda aymanihim" is the utmost of what they could swear, derived from their saying "jahada nafsahu," when he reaches its limit and the utmost of its capacity.

It has been said that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), the sense being: striving in their oaths, as in their saying: "do that with your utmost effort and capacity." Al-Zamakhshari combined the two possibilities and made them one.

The answer to the oath is His saying "they will surely go out." Since their statement was false and their oaths were sinful, Allah responded to them, saying: ﴿Say: "Do not swear."﴾, meaning respond to them, restraining them, and say to them, "Do not swear," that is, do not take oaths regarding what you claim of obedience and going out to jihad if you are commanded to it. Here the speech is complete.

Then He began, saying: ﴿Obedience is known﴾. The "ta'atun" is raised as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: your obedience is a known obedience, known to be an obedience of hypocrisy, not based on conviction. It may also be the subject (mubtada'), since it has been specified by the qualifying adjective, and the predicate is then omitted, meaning: a known obedience is more appropriate for you than your oaths. It may also be raised by an omitted verb, meaning: let there be obedience from you, or let it be found. In this there is weakness, because a verb is not omitted unless something indicating it has preceded.

Zayd ibn Ali and al-Tirmidhi read "ta'atan" in the accusative as a verbal noun for an omitted verb, meaning: obey with obedience.

﴿Indeed, Allah is Well-Acquainted with what you do﴾, of deeds, and with what you conceal of opposition to what your tongues utter. This sentence gives the reason for what came before it, namely that their obedience is the obedience of hypocrisy.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 24, verse 55–57 (part 2 of 3):

Then Allah, glorified is He, commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to order them to obey Allah and His Messenger, so He said: ﴿Say: Obey Allah and obey the Messenger﴾, an obedience that is outward and inward, with sincere belief and correct intention. This repetition by the Most High is to emphasise the obligation of obedience upon them, for His saying ﴿Say: Do not swear; known obedience﴾ is in the sense of a command to obey. It has also been said that the two are different: the first is a prohibition by way of rebuke and reproach, and the second is a command by way of imposing duty and obligation upon them. ﴿But if they turn away﴾ is an address to those who are commanded, and its original form is "fa-in tatawallaw", so one of the two tā's was dropped for lightness. In it there is a shift from addressing the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to addressing them directly, to emphasise the command upon them and to stress concern for guiding them to obedience and submission. The answer to the condition is His saying ﴿then upon him is what he has been charged with, and upon you is what you have been charged with﴾, meaning: know that upon the Prophet (ﷺ) is what he has been charged with of the duty of conveying, which he has done, and upon you is what you have been charged with, that is, what you have been commanded of obedience. This is a warning to them, as if He had said to them: If you turn away, then you have become bearers of a heavy burden. ﴿And if you obey him﴾ in what he commands you and forbids you, you will be guided to the truth, you will be rightly guided to good, and you will attain the reward. The clause ﴿And upon the Messenger is only the clear conveyance﴾ confirms what precedes it, and the lām is either for a specific reference, so that "the Messenger" means our Prophet (ﷺ), or for the category, so that it means every messenger. "Clear conveyance" means conveying that is plain or made clear.

It has been said that His saying ﴿But if they turn away﴾ may be in the past tense, with the wāw referring to the absent party, and this conditional clause would then be something the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was commanded to say to them, and there would be a shift in the speech from address to third person. The first view is more preferred. It is supported by the address in His saying ﴿and upon you is what you have been charged with﴾ and His saying ﴿and if you obey him, you will be guided﴾. It is also supported by al-Bazzi's reading "fa-in tawallaw" with a doubled tā', though this reading is weak because it involves joining two sukun letters.

﴿Allah has promised those of you who believe and do righteous deeds﴾. This clause confirms what precedes it, that their obedience to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is the cause of their guidance.
