This is a promise from Allah, glorified is He, to those who believe in Allah and do righteous deeds, that they will be made successors in the earth just as He made successors those who came before them from the nations. It is a promise that encompasses the whole community.

It has been said that it is specific to the Companions, but there is no basis for this, for belief and doing righteous deeds are not restricted to them; rather it is possible for this to occur from every individual of this community, and whoever acts by the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger has obeyed Allah and His Messenger. The lām in ﴿He will surely make them successors in the earth﴾ is the answer to an implied oath, or it is the answer to the promise, treating it as an oath because it is certain without doubt. The meaning of "He will surely make them successors in the earth" is: He will surely make them successors in it, who dispose of it as kings dispose of their possessions. Those who said it is restricted to the four Caliphs, or to the Emigrants, or that by "the earth" is meant the land of Makkah, have gone too far; you know that the consideration is the generality of the wording and not the specificity of the occasion. The apparent sense of His saying ﴿as He made successors those who came before them﴾ is that it applies to everyone whom Allah has made successor in His earth, so it is not restricted to the Children of Israel or to any one nation over others.

The majority read ﴿as He made successors﴾ with an open tā' (fataha) in the active voice. ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar, Abū Bakr and al-Mufaḍḍal from ʿĀṣim read it with a dammah in the passive voice. The place of the kāf is in the accusative as an adverbial of manner (maṣdar), meaning: a succession like that which He made. The clause ﴿and He will surely establish for them their religion which He has approved for them﴾ is joined to "He will surely make them successors" and falls under its ruling, being part of the answer. By "establishment" (tamkīn) here is meant firmness and confirmation, that is, Allah will make it firm and established, will widen for them in the lands, and will make their religion prevail over all religions. By "religion" here is meant Islam, as in His saying ﴿And I have approved for you Islam as a religion﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 3]. The Most High mentioned the succession for them first, which is making them kings, and mentioned the establishment second, and this conveys that this kingship is not temporary and passing, but firm and lasting, such that the kingdom belongs to them and to their descendants after them. The clause ﴿and He will surely change their state after their fear into security﴾ is joined to the one before it.

Ibn Kathīr, Ibn Muḥaysin, Yaʿqūb and Abū Bakr read ﴿yubdilannahum﴾ with lightness, from abdala. This is the reading of al-Ḥasan, and Abū Ḥātim preferred it. The others read it with doubling, from baddala, and Abū ʿUbayd preferred it. Both are dialects, and an increase in the structure indicates an increase in meaning, so the doubled reading is more preferred than the light reading.

Al-Naḥḥās said: Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā Thaʿlab claimed that there is a difference between the light and the heavy forms, that one says "baddaltuhu", meaning I changed it, and "abdaltuhu", meaning I removed it and put something else in its place. Al-Naḥḥās said: this view is correct.

The meaning is: He, glorified is He, will make for them, in place of what they were in of fear from enemies, security, and will remove from them the causes of the fear they were in, such that they fear none but Allah, glorified is He, and hope for none other than Him.

The Muslims, before the Hijrah and shortly after it, were in severe fear of the polytheists; they did not go out except armed, and they did not spend the evening or the morning except in constant watch for harm to come upon them from the disbelievers. Then they reached the utmost security and ease, Allah humbled for them the devils of the polytheists, opened the lands to them, paved the earth for them and established them in it. So to Allah belongs all praise.

The clause ﴿they worship Me﴾ is in the accusative place as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and it may be that it is a resumed clause, given in praise of them. The clause ﴿they do not associate anything with Me﴾ is in the accusative place as a circumstantial clause from the subject of "they worship Me", meaning: they worship Me, not associating anything with Me in worship. It has been said: its meaning is that they do not show off their worship of Me to anyone. It has been said: its meaning is that they do not fear other than Me. It has been said: its meaning is that they do not love other than Me.

﴿But whoever disbelieves after that, those are the defiantly disobedient﴾. That is: whoever disbelieves these blessings after that promise which is true, or whoever persists in disbelief, or whoever disbelieves after faith, then those who disbelieve are the defiantly disobedient, that is, the complete in defiance. Defiance is going out of obedience and transgression in disbelief.

The clause ﴿And establish the prayer﴾ is joined to an implied element indicated by what precedes it, as if it had been said to them: "So believe, do righteous deeds, and establish the prayer." It has also been said that it is joined to "And obey Allah". It has also been said that the estimate is: "So do not disbelieve, and establish the prayer."

The discussion of establishing the prayer and giving zakah has already been presented. He repeated the command to obey the Messenger for emphasis and singled it out for obedience, because his obedience is obedience to Allah. He did not mention what they are to obey him in, for the purpose of generality, as the omission indicates, according to what has been established in the science of rhetoric (ʿilm al-maʿānī), that such an omission indicates generality. ﴿So that you may be shown mercy﴾, that is: do what has been mentioned of establishing the prayer, giving zakah and obeying the Messenger, hoping that Allah, glorified is He, will show you mercy.

﴿Do not think that those who disbelieve can escape in the land﴾. Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamzah and Abū Ḥaywah read "lā taḥsabanna" with the yā' (third person), meaning: let not those who disbelieve think. The others read it with the tā' (second person), that is: do not think, O Muḥammad. The relative pronoun is the first object, and "muʿjizīn" is the second, since ḥasiba takes two objects, as said by al-Zajjāj, al-Farrā' and Abū ʿAlī.

As for the first reading, the first object is omitted, that is: let not those who disbelieve think that they themselves [can escape].

Al-Naḥḥās said: I do not know of any Basran or Kufan who does not criticise the reading of Ḥamzah. "Muʿjizīn" means "escaping" (fā'itīn). Its explanation and the explanation of what follows it have already been given.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted from Qatādah, concerning His saying ﴿And they say: We believe in Allah and in the Messenger﴾ to the end of the verse, that he said: "They are some hypocrites who displayed faith and obedience, while in that they were turning people away from the path of Allah, from obedience to Him and from striving alongside His Messenger (ﷺ)."

They also transmitted from al-Ḥasan, who said: "A man would have a dispute or contention with another man during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). When he was called to the Prophet (ﷺ) and he was in the right, he would submit and know that the Prophet (ﷺ) would judge in his favour with the truth. But when he wished to wrong, and was called to the Prophet (ﷺ), he would turn away and say: 'I will go to so-and-so.' So Allah, glorified is He, revealed: ﴿And when they are called to Allah and His Messenger﴾ up to His saying ﴿they are the wrongdoers﴾. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) then said: 'Whoever has a matter between himself and his brother, and he calls him to a judge from the judges of the Muslims and he does not respond, then he is a wrongdoer, with no right.'"

Ibn Kathīr, after transmitting this text, said in his words: "This is a strange ḥadīth, and it is mursal." Ibn al-ʿArabī said: "This ḥadīth is false. As for his saying 'then he is a wrongdoer', that is a correct statement; but as for his saying 'with no right', that is not sound. It may be that he means that he is in a state other than the truth." End of quotation.

I say: As for the ḥadīth being mursal, that is evident. But the claim that it is false requires proof. Three leading imams of ḥadīth, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim, transmitted it, as we mentioned. It is far-fetched in the extreme that they would all agree upon something false. Its isnād in Ibn Abī Ḥātim is thus: Ibn Abī Ḥātim said: "My father related to us, Mūsā ibn Ismāʿīl related to us, Mubārak related to us, al-Ḥasan related to us," and so he mentioned it. Among these there is no liar and no forger.

It is corroborated by what al-Ṭabarānī transmitted from al-Ḥasan, from Samurah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever is called to a ruler and does not respond, then he is a wrongdoer with no right." End of quotation.

And it is not hidden from you that the judges of justice and the rulers of the Sharīʿah, who are of the character we mentioned to you shortly before, are the rulers of religion who translate from the Book and the Sunnah, clarifying to people what has been sent down to them.

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "Some people came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, if you were to command us to leave our wealth, we would leave it.' So Allah revealed: ﴿And they swear by Allah with their most emphatic oaths﴾ to the end of the verse."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted from Muqātil concerning the verse, who said: "That concerns the matter of jihad. He commands them that they should not swear to anything; ﴿known obedience﴾ means he commanded that there should be from them known obedience to the Prophet (ﷺ) without their swearing."

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Mujāhid concerning ﴿known obedience﴾: "It means: their obedience is already known, that is, you are lying in it."

Muslim, al-Tirmidhī and others transmitted from ʿAlqamah ibn Wāʾil al-Ḥaḍramī, from his father, who said: "Zayd ibn Aslam came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'What do you think if there are rulers over us who take from us what is right and do not give us [our due]?' He said: 'Upon them is what they have been charged with, and upon you is what you have been charged with.'"

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Qāniʿ and al-Ṭabarānī transmitted from ʿAlqamah ibn Wāʾil al-Ḥaḍramī, from Salamah ibn Yazīd al-Juʿfī, who said: "I said, O Messenger of Allah," and then he mentioned something similar.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted from Ibn al-Zubayr, from Jābir, that he asked: "If there is over me a wicked imam, and I meet with him people of misguidance, should I fight them or not?" He said: "Fight the people of misguidance wherever you find them, and upon the imam is what he has been charged with, and upon you is what you have been charged with."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from al-Bara', regarding His words: ﴿Allah has promised those among you who believe﴾ the verse. He said: It was revealed concerning us while we were in great fear.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu al-ʿAliyah, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions were in Makkah for about ten years, calling to Allah alone, and to worshipping Him alone with no partner, secretly, while they were in fear and were not commanded to fight, until they were commanded to emigrate to Madinah. They came to Madinah, and Allah commanded them to fight. They were there in fear, spending their evenings and mornings in arms. They remained in that state for as long as Allah willed. Then a man among his Companions said: 'O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), will we be in this state of fear forever? Will there not come a day when we are safe and can lay down our arms?' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'You will not wait long before a man among you sits in a great assembly, wearing no iron armor.' Then Allah revealed: ﴿Allah has promised those among you who believe and do righteous deeds that He will surely make them successors in the earth﴾ to the end of the verse." Then Allah made His Prophet (ﷺ) victorious over the Arabian Peninsula, and they became secure and laid down their arms.

Then Allah took His Prophet (ﷺ) [in death], and they remained secure in the rule of Abu Bakr, ʿUmar and ʿUthman, until they fell into error and became ungrateful for the blessing. So Allah brought upon them the fear that had been lifted from them, and they adopted guards and police, and changed, so Allah changed what was with them.

Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il, and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtarah narrated from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, who said: When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) arrived in Madinah and the Ansar sheltered them, the Arabs shot at them with a single bow. They did not spend the night or morning except in arms. They said: "Do you think we will live to spend a night secure and at peace, fearing none but Allah?" Then the verse was revealed: ﴿Allah has promised those among you who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ the verse.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ﴿They worship Me, not associating anything with Me﴾, that he said: "They fear no one but Me."

al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Mujahid the like of this, and he said regarding ﴿And whoever disbelieves after that, those are the defiantly disobedient (al-fasiqun)﴾: the disobedient, the sinners.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd narrated from Abu al-ʿAliyah, who said: "It is ingratitude for this blessing, not disbelief in Allah."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd narrated from Qatadah regarding ﴿unable to escape [Allah] in the earth (mu'jizina fi al-ard)﴾, that he said: "Outrunning [Allah] in the earth."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 24, verse 58–61 (part 1 of 3):

When He, glory be to Him, had finished mentioning the proofs of monotheism that He had mentioned, He returned to what He had been discussing concerning seeking permission (istidhan), and mentioned it here in a more specific manner, saying: ﴿O you who have believed, let those whom your right hands possess ask permission of you﴾. The address is to the believers, and the believing women are included in it by way of precedence (taghlib), as in other addresses.

The scholars said: this verse is specific to certain times. They differed regarding the meaning of His saying ﴿let them ask permission of you﴾ according to several opinions. The first is that it is abrogated (mansukhah); this was said by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the command in it is for recommendation (nadb), not for obligation (wujub). It was also said: that was obligatory at the time when they had no doors for their houses, and if the situation returns, the obligation returns; this was related by al-Mahdawi from Ibn 'Abbas.

It was also said: the command here is for obligation, the verse is muhkamah (not abrogated), and its ruling is established for men and women. Al-Qurtubi said: this is the view of most of the people of knowledge.

Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami said: it is specific to women. Ibn 'Umar said: it is specific to men, not women.

By His saying ﴿those whom your right hands possess﴾ is meant the slaves, male and female. By "those who have not reached puberty (al-hulm)" is meant the children, ﴿among you﴾, i.e., among the free. The meaning of ﴿three times﴾ is three periods in the day and night, and the expression "times" (al-marrat) is used for periods because the basis of the obligation of seeking permission is the coincidence of those periods with the passing of those seeking permission in upon those addressed, not the periods themselves. The accusative of "three times" is as a temporal adverbial (zarf zamani), i.e., three periods. Then He explained those periods by His saying ﴿before the prayer of dawn﴾ etc. Or it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), i.e., three acts of seeking permission. Abu Hayyan preferred this, saying: "The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿three times﴾ is three acts of seeking permission, because when you say 'I struck you three times' nothing is understood from it except three strikes." It is rebutted that the apparent meaning here is set aside because of the stated context, which is the explanation by the three periods.

Al-Hasan and Abu 'Amr, in one narration, read (al-hulm) with a sukun on the lam, and the rest read it with a damma. Al-Akhfash said: "al-hulm" is from halama al-rajul (with a fatha on the lam), and from al-hulm comes halura (with a damma on the lam), yahlumu (with a kasra on the lam). Then He, glory be to Him, explained the three times, saying: ﴿before the prayer of dawn﴾, because it is the time of rising from the beds, removing sleeping clothes, and putting on waking clothes, and one may sleep naked, or in a state in which one does not like others to see him. Its position is in the accusative as a substitute (badal) for (three); it may also be in the nominative position, as the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "they are from before". His saying ﴿and when you put off your clothes at midday﴾ is conjoined to the position of ﴿before the prayer of dawn﴾; the (min) in ﴿from midday﴾ is for explanation (bayan), or in the sense of (fi), or in the sense of (li). The meaning: when you put off your clothes that you wear during the day because of the intense heat of midday, which is at the middle of the day, for they may strip off their clothes for the sake of the afternoon nap (qaylulah).

Then He mentioned the third period, saying ﴿and after the night prayer (al-'isha')﴾, because it is the time of stripping off clothes and of being alone with the family. Then He, glory be to Him, summarized these periods after the detail, saying: ﴿three times of privacy (awrat) for you﴾. The majority read ﴿three awrat﴾ with the nominative of "three", and Hamzah and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read it in the accusative as a substitute for (﴿three times﴾).

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the substitution is valid only by supposing "times of three awrat", so the first noun was omitted and the second put in its place. It is possible that he made the very "three times" the very "three awrat" for emphasis. It is also permissible that "three awrat" is a substitute for the periods mentioned, i.e., before the prayer of dawn etc. It may be in the accusative by an implied verb, i.e., "I mean" or the like. As for the nominative, it is as the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "they are three."

Abu Hatim said: the accusative is weak and rejected. Al-Kisa'i said: "three awrat" is in the nominative as the subject of the beginning, and the predicate is what follows it. He said: "the awrat are the hours in which nakedness occurs." Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is "let them ask permission of you at the times of three awrat", so the first noun was omitted and the second put in its place. "Awrat" is the plural of "awrah", and awrah in origin means a defect; then it became dominant for a defect in what requires protection and whose covering is obligatory, i.e., they are three times in which the covering is defective.

Al-A'mash read ('awarat) with a fatha on the waw, and this is the dialect of Hudhayl and Tamim, for they put a fatha on the 'ayn of (fa'alat), whether it is waw or ya', and from it is the poet's saying:

"Brother of the bayadat, going in the morning, yawning, gentle in wiping the two shoulders, swimming."

And his saying:

"Father of the bayadat, going in the morning or going far away, hasty, one with provision and one without provision."

And ﴿for you﴾ is connected to an omitted element which is an attribute (sifah) of "three awrat", i.e., "existing for you". The sentence is resumed (mustanafah), brought to explain the reason for the obligation of seeking permission: ﴿There is no sin on you or on them after them﴾, i.e., there is no sin on the slaves or on the children in entering without seeking permission, because there is no cause that makes it obligatory, such as disobeying the command and looking upon the awrat.

The meaning of "after them" is: after each one of these three awrat, which are the times interspersed between each two of them. This sentence is resumed, establishing the command to seek permission in those states specifically. It is also possible that it is in the nominative position as an attribute of "three awrat" according to the nominative reading.

Abu al-Baqa' said: "after them" means after their seeking permission in them, then the preposition and its object were omitted, leaving "after their seeking permission", then the verbal noun, which is "seeking permission", and the connected pronoun to it, were omitted. It was rejected: there is no need for this supposition he mentioned; rather the meaning is: there is no sin on you, nor on them, i.e., the slaves, the female slaves, and the children, in not seeking permission after these mentioned times. The nominative of ﴿circulating (tawwafun)﴾ is as the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "they are circulating among you", and the sentence is resumed, explaining the excuse permitted for leaving off seeking permission.

Al-Farra' said: this is like your saying in speech: "they are your servants and circulating among you." He also permitted the accusative of "circulating" because it is indefinite, while the pronoun in "upon you" is definite. The Basrans do not permit it to be a circumstantial state (hal) of the two pronouns, the one in "upon you" and the one in "some of you", because the governing elements differ.

The meaning of "circulating upon you" is: they circulate upon you. From it is the hadith about the cat: "It is only one of those who circulate upon you, or the female circulators." That is, they are your servants, so there is no harm in their entering upon you at other than these times without permission. The meaning of ﴿some of you upon some﴾ is: some of you circulate, or one circulates, upon others. This sentence is either a substitute for what precedes it or an emphasis of it. The meaning is that each of you circulates upon his companion: slaves upon masters and masters upon slaves. From it is the poet's saying:

"When we struck the nab' (tree) with the nab', some of it upon some, its branches refused to be broken."

Ibn Abi 'Abla read ("circulating") in the accusative as a circumstantial state, as was mentioned earlier from al-Farra'. He, glory be to Him, permitted entering at times other than these three without permission only because it was the custom that they did not uncover their awrat at other times. The reference in His saying ﴿Thus Allah makes clear to you the verses﴾ is to the verbal noun of the verb that follows it, as in the other places in the Mighty Book, i.e., like that clarification, Allah makes clear to you the signs indicating what He has legislated for you of rulings, and Allah is Knowing, Wise: abundant in knowledge of the known things, and abundant in wisdom in His acts.

﴿And when the children among you reach puberty (al-hulm)﴾: here He, glory be to Him, explained the ruling for free children when they reach puberty, after He had explained earlier the ruling for children who have not reached puberty, that there is no sin on them in leaving off seeking permission apart from the three periods. So He said: ﴿then let them ask permission﴾, meaning those who have reached puberty, when they enter upon you, ﴿as those before them asked permission﴾. The kaf is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, i.e., "permission as those before them asked permission", and the relative pronoun is an expression for those to whom it was said ﴿Do not enter houses other than your houses until you have sought intimacy and greeted their people﴾ [al-Nur: 27], and so on.

The meaning: these who have reached puberty seek permission at all times, as those before them asked permission among the adults who were commanded to seek permission without exception. Then He repeated what preceded for emphasis, saying: ﴿Thus Allah makes clear to you His verses, and Allah is Knowing, Wise.﴾ Al-Hasan read (al-hulm) and omitted the damma because it is heavy.

Ata' said: it is obligatory upon people to seek permission when they have reached puberty, whether free or slaves. Al-Zuhri said: a man seeks permission to enter upon his mother, and this verse was revealed in this meaning.

By "the women who are past child-bearing (al-qawa'id min al-nisa')" are meant the old women who have ceased from menstruation and child-bearing due to old age. Its singular is qa'id without a ha', so that its omission indicates that it is the sitting of old age, as they say: "imra'ah hamil" (a woman pregnant), so that the omission of the ha' indicates that it is the carrying of pregnancy; and it is said: "qa'idah fi baytiha" and "hamilah 'ala zahriha". Al-Zajjaj said: they are those who have ceased from marriage.

This is the meaning of His saying ﴿who do not hope for marriage﴾, i.e., they do not hope for it because of their old age. Abu 'Ubaydah said: those who have ceased from child-bearing, but this is not correct, because a woman may cease from child-bearing and still be a subject of enjoyment.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned the ruling for the women past child-bearing, saying: ﴿there is no sin upon them if they put off their clothing﴾, i.e., the garments that are over the surface of the body such as the outer cloak (jilbab) and the like, nor the garments that cover the specific nakedness. It is permitted for them because people's desires turn away from them, as men have no desire for them. So Allah, glory be to Him, permitted them what He did not permit to others. Then He excepted one state from their states, saying: ﴿without displaying adornment (ghayra mutabarrijat bi-zinah)﴾, i.e., not displaying the adornment which they were commanded to conceal in His saying: ﴿and not display their adornment﴾ [al-Nur: 31]. The meaning: without intending by putting off the outer garments to display their adornment, and not exposing themselves to adornment so that men would look at them.

Tabarruj means uncovering and appearing to the eyes, and from it comes ﴿fortified towers﴾ [al-Nisa': 78], and the towers of the sky, and from it the saying: "a ship barijah", i.e., with no covering over it. ﴿And that they refrain is better for them﴾, i.e., that they leave off putting off the garments, so that is better for them than putting them off.

'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Ibn 'Abbas read ("that they put off some of their garments") with the addition of (min). Ibn Mas'ud read ("and that they refrain") without a sin. ﴿And Allah is Hearing, Knowing﴾, abundant in hearing and knowledge, or eloquent in both.

﴿There is no blame upon the blind, nor blame upon the lame, nor blame upon the sick﴾: The people of knowledge differed regarding this verse: is it muhkamah or mansukhah? A group of scholars held the first, and a group the second.

It was said that when the Muslims went out to fight, they left behind their disabled persons, and they would hand over to them the keys of their doors and say to them: "We have permitted you to eat from what is in our houses." They were scrupulous about that and said: "We will not enter it while they are absent." So this verse was revealed as a concession to them. The meaning of the verse is the removal of blame from the disabled in eating from the houses of their relatives, or the houses of those who hand over the key to them when they go out to fight.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 24, verses 58–61 (part 2 of 3):

Al-Nahhas said: This view is among the finest of what has been transmitted concerning the verse, because of what it contains from the Companions and the Successors regarding *tawqif* (a report that the matter was determined by revelation or by the Prophet's explicit statement). It has also been said that those mentioned were refraining from eating with healthy people, out of fear of their disgust at them and fear of being harmed by their actions, so this was revealed. It has also been said that God lifted the burden from the blind regarding the obligations that require sight, and from the lame regarding the obligations that require full ability to walk in a way that cannot be performed with lameness, and from the sick regarding what sickness causes to be dropped. It has also been said that the intended "burden" lifted from these people is the burden of going out to war, meaning: there is no blame on these people for remaining behind from the expedition. It has also been said that when a man brought one of these disabled people into his house and found nothing in it to feed them, he would take them to the houses of his relatives, and the disabled would feel uneasy about this, so this was revealed.

The meaning of His words ﴿Nor on yourselves﴾ is: upon you, and upon those among the believers who are like you, that you eat yourselves and those with you. This is the beginning of a new statement, meaning: nor upon you, O people. The summary is that the lifting of the burden from the blind, the lame and the sick, if it refers to eating with the healthy or entering their houses, then ﴿Nor on yourselves﴾ is connected to what precedes it; but if the lifting of the burden from those people refers to the obligations that require sight, the absence of lameness and the absence of sickness, then His words ﴿Nor on yourselves﴾ are a new statement not connected to what precedes it. The meaning of ﴿from your houses﴾ is the houses in which their property and their families are, and so it includes the houses of children. This is what the exegetes said, because they are included in the houses of the parents, since the house of a man's son is his house. For this reason, He did not mention the houses of children, and mentioned the houses of fathers, the houses of mothers and those after them.

Al-Nahhas said: Some people objected to this and said: This is an arbitrary imposition upon the Book of God. Rather, the more apparent position is that the son should be excluded from these. The answer to this objection is that the status of children in relation to parents is not less than the status of parents in relation to children; rather, parents have greater special right over the property of their children, due to the hadith "You and your property belong to your father," and the hadith "A man's child is part of his earnings." Then God, glory be to Him, here mentioned the houses of brothers and sisters, indeed the houses of paternal uncles and aunts, indeed the houses of maternal uncles and aunts. So how does He, glory be to Him, remove the burden of eating from the houses of these people and not remove it from the houses of children? Some scholars restricted the permissibility of eating from the houses of these people to their permission. Others said: permission is not a condition. It was said: this applies when the food is available for the taking, but if it is stored away from them, it is not permitted for them to eat it.

Then He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿or what you own the keys to﴾, meaning the houses over which you have the right of disposal with the permission of their owners. This is like agents, slaves and treasurers, for they have the right of disposal over the houses of the one who has permitted them to enter his house and given them its keys. It was said: what is intended by it is the houses of slaves.

The majority read *malaktum* with a fatha on the *mim* and a light *lam*. Sa'id ibn Jubayr read it with a damma on the *mim* and a kasra on the *lam* with shadda. He also read *mafatīḥahu* with a *yā'* between the *tā'* and the *ḥā'*. Qatada read *mafātiḥahu* in the singular; *al-mafātiḥ* is the plural of *mafataḥ*, and *al-mafātīḥ* is the plural of *miftāḥ*.

Or [what you own the keys to] your friend, meaning: there is no blame upon you that you eat from the houses of your friend even if there is no kinship between you and him, for a friend in most cases permits his friend to do so, and his soul is content with it. The word *ṣadīq* (friend) is applied to the singular and the plural. Among its examples is the verse of Jarir:

*They called to passion, then shot our hearts*
*with the arrows of enemies, and they are friends.*

Similar to it are *al-'adū* (enemy), *al-khalīṭ* (close companion), *al-qaṭīn* (companion) and *al-'ashīr* (intimate companion), which are all used in the singular and plural.

Then He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿There is no blame upon you to eat﴾ from your houses ﴿together or separately﴾. The accusative of *jamī'an* (together) and *ashtātan* (separately) is by way of circumstantial state (*ḥāl*). *Al-ashtāt* is the plural of *shatt*, and *shatt* is the verbal noun meaning dispersal; one says *shatta al-qawm*, meaning they dispersed. This sentence is a new statement containing the explanation of another ruling of the same kind as what precedes it, meaning: there is no blame upon you to eat from your houses together or dispersed. Some Arabs would refrain from eating alone until they found someone to eat with, and some Arabs would not eat except with a guest. Among its examples is the verse of Hatim:

*When you prepare the provisions, seek for it a companion,*
*for I do not eat it alone.*

﴿So when you enter houses﴾: this begins the explanation of another etiquette with which God trained His servants, meaning: when you enter houses other than the houses already mentioned, ﴿greet one another﴾, meaning greet those among them who are like yourselves. It was said: what is meant is the houses mentioned earlier.

According to the first view, al-Hasan and al-Nakha'i said: these are mosques, and what is meant is: greet those in them of your kind. If there is no one in the mosques, it was said one should say: "Peace be upon the Messenger of God." It was said one should say: "Peace be upon us," intending the angels. It was said one should say: "Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of God."

A group of the Companions and the Successors held the second view, namely that they are the houses mentioned earlier. It was also said: what is meant by "houses" here is every house, inhabited and otherwise. So one greets the inhabitants of an inhabited house, and as for an uninhabited house, one greets oneself.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: The view of generality regarding the houses is the correct one. The accusative of *taḥiyyatan* (a greeting) is as a verbal noun, because His words *fa-sallimū* (so greet) mean *fa-ḥayyū* (so salute), meaning a greeting established from God, that is, God has greeted you with it.

Al-Farra' said: God has commanded you to do it, in obedience to Him. Then He described this greeting, saying *mubārakatan*, meaning abundant in blessing and goodness, lasting in both respects; *ṭayyibatan*, meaning the listener's soul is content with it. It was said: it is good and beautiful.

Al-Zajjaj said: God, glory be to Him, informed us that the greeting is blessed and good because of the reward and recompense in it. Then God, glory be to Him, repeated and said: ﴿Thus God makes clear to you the verses﴾, as an emphasis on what came before.

We have already mentioned that the demonstrative *dhālika* (thus) refers to the verbal noun of the verb. His words ﴿so that you may understand﴾ are a justification for that clarification, with the hope that you will comprehend the verses of God and understand their meanings.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Muqatil ibn Hayyan who said: "It reached us that a man from the Ansar and his wife Asma' bint Murshida prepared food for the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace. Asma' said: 'O Messenger of God, how ugly this is! Their servant enters upon the woman and her husband while they are in one garment, without permission.' So God revealed concerning that: ﴿O you who have believed, let those whom your right hands possess ask your permission, and those who have not reached puberty among you﴾." He said: meaning the slaves, male and female, and ﴿those who have not reached puberty among you﴾, he said: from your free men and women.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Suddi concerning this verse that he said: Some of the Companions of the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, liked to have intercourse with their wives at these times so they could perform the ritual bath and then go out to prayer. So God commanded them to order the slaves and the boys not to enter upon them at those times except with permission.

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Tha'laba al-Qurazi from 'Abd Allah ibn Suwayd who said: "I asked the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, about the three times of nakedness (*'awrāt*). He said: 'When I put off my clothes after noon, none of the servants who have not reached puberty may come in upon me, nor any free person who has not reached puberty, except with permission. And when I put off my clothes after the night prayer, and before the dawn prayer.'"

'Abd ibn Humayd and al-Bukhari in *al-Adab* transmitted it from 'Abd Allah ibn Suwayd as his own statement.

Ibn Sa'd transmitted something similar from Suwayd ibn al-Nu'man.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shayba, Abu Dawud, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan* transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "Most people have not believed in it, meaning the verse of permission. I used to order this maidservant of mine, a short girl standing at his head, to ask permission to enter upon me."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "People have left three verses without acting upon them: ﴿O you who have believed, let those whom your right hands possess ask your permission﴾; and the verse in Surat al-Nisa' ﴿And when the division is attended by relatives﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:8] and the verse in al-Hujurat ﴿Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of God is the most righteous of you﴾ [al-Hujurat 49:13]."

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in the *Sunan* transmitted from him also concerning the verse, that he said: "If a man is alone with his wife after the night prayer, no child or servant may enter upon him except with his permission until he prays the morning prayer. And if he is alone with his wife at noon, it is similar. They were allowed to enter at other times without permission, and this is His words: ﴿There is no blame upon you or upon them after these times.﴾ As for one who has reached puberty, he may not enter upon a man and his wife except with permission in every circumstance, and this is His words: ﴿And when the children among you reach puberty, let them ask permission as those before them asked.﴾"

Abu Dawud, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in the *Sunan* transmitted with a sound chain through the route of 'Ikrima from him as well: that a man asked him about asking permission during the three nakedness times which God commanded in the Qur'an. Ibn 'Abbas said: "God is Concealing and loves concealment. The people did not have curtains on their doors or screens in their houses, so a servant or a child or an orphan in one's care might suddenly come upon a man while he was with his family. So God commanded them to ask permission during those times of nakedness which God named. Then later God brought curtains, and He expanded provision for them, so they took curtains and took screens. The people thought that this had sufficed them from the asking of permission they had been commanded to do."

Ibn Abi Shayba, al-Bukhari in *al-Adab*, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn 'Umar concerning His words ﴿let those whom your right hands possess ask your permission﴾ that he said: "It applies to males and not to females." There is no basis for this restriction, for looking upon the nakedness at these times, which a person dislikes from males, he likewise dislikes from females.

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Abu Salama ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, from one of the wives of the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, concerning the verse, that she said: "It was revealed concerning women, that they should ask permission to enter upon us."

al-Hakim transmitted and authenticated it from 'Ali concerning the verse, that he said: "The women, for men ask permission."

al-Firyabi transmitted from Musa ibn Abi Shayba who said: "I asked al-Sha'bi about this verse: 'Is it abrogated?' He said: 'No.'"

Sa'id ibn Mansur, al-Bukhari in *al-Adab*, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from 'Ata' that he asked Ibn 'Abbas: "Should I ask permission to enter upon my sister?" He said: "Yes." I said: "She is in my care, I spend on her, and she is with me in the house. Should I ask permission to enter upon her?" He said: "Yes, for God says: ﴿let those whom your right hands possess ask your permission, and those who have not reached puberty among you﴾, the verse, so these were not commanded to ask permission except at these three times of nakedness." He said: ﴿And when the children among you reach puberty, let them ask permission as those before them asked﴾. So asking permission is obligatory upon every creature of God, all of them."

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan* transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud who said: "Upon you is asking permission to enter upon your mothers."

Sa'id ibn Mansur and al-Bukhari in *al-Adab* transmitted from him who said: "A man asks permission to enter upon his father, his mother, his brother and his sister."

Ibn Abi Shayba and al-Bukhari in *al-Adab* transmitted from Jabir something similar to it.

[p. 1028]

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 24, verses 58–61 (part 3 of 3):

Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Sunan* reported from ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yasār that **"a man said: 'O Messenger of Allah, shall I seek permission to enter upon my mother?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'I am with her in the house.' He said: 'Seek permission to enter upon her.' He said: 'I am her servant. Shall I seek permission to enter upon her every time I enter?' He said: 'Would you like to see her naked?' He said: 'No.' He said: 'Then seek permission to enter upon her.'"** And it is *mursal* (a report whose chain omits the Companion).

Ibn Abi Shaybah reported something similar from Zayd ibn Aslam, that a man asked the Prophet (ﷺ), and it is also *mursal*.

Abu Dawud and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Sunan* reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ﴿And tell the believing women to lower their gaze﴾ [al-Nur: 31], the verse, that it abrogated (*naskh*, abrogation) and made an exception from it: ﴿And women past child-bearing who have no hope of marriage﴾.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Sunan* reported from him (Ibn ʿAbbas) that he said: "It refers to the woman for whom there is no blame if she sits in her house wearing her *dir* (a shift) and *khimar* (headscarf), and she places over herself the *jilbab* (outer garment), so long as she does not display herself in what Allah dislikes." And this is His saying: ﴿So there is no blame upon them if they remove their garments without displaying adornment﴾.

Abu ʿUbayd in *Fada'il* (his *Virtues of the Qur'an*), Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn al-Anbari in *al-Masahif*, and al-Bayhaqi reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that he used to recite ﴿that they may remove their garments﴾ and say: "It is the *jilbab*."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Sunan* reported from Ibn Mas'ud regarding ﴿that they may remove their garments﴾ that he said: "The *jilbab* and the *ridaʾ* (cloak)."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Saʿid ibn Jubayr that he said: When the verse ﴿O you who believe, do not consume your wealth among yourselves in falsehood﴾ [al-Nisa: 29] was revealed, the Ansar said: "There is no wealth in Madinah more precious than food." They used to feel uneasy about eating with the blind, saying: "He cannot see where the food is." They used to feel uneasy about eating with the lame, saying: "The healthy one gets ahead of him to the place and he cannot compete with the crowd." They used to feel uneasy about eating with the sick, saying: "He cannot eat like the healthy one." And they used to feel uneasy about eating in the houses of their relatives. So the verse was revealed: ﴿There is no blame upon the blind﴾, meaning: regarding eating with the blind.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi reported from Mujahid that he said: A man would take the blind, the lame or the sick to the house of his father, or the house of his brother, or the house of his paternal uncle, or the house of his paternal aunt, or the house of his maternal uncle, or the house of his maternal aunt. The disabled people felt uneasy about this, saying: "They only take us to the houses of others." So this verse was revealed as a concession for them.

al-Bazzar, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn al-Najjar reported from ʿĀʾishah that she said: The Muslims used to eagerly go out on *nafir* (military expedition) with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and they would hand over their keys to their trustees and say to them: "We have made lawful for you to eat from what you need." But they used to say: "It is not lawful for us to eat, for they have permitted us without wholehearted consent, and we are only disabled." So Allah revealed ﴿Nor upon yourselves that you eat﴾ up to His saying: ﴿or from that whose keys you possess﴾.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: When the verse ﴿O you who believe, do not consume your wealth among yourselves in falsehood﴾ was revealed, the Muslims said: "Allah has forbidden us to consume our wealth among ourselves in falsehood, and food is the best of wealth. So it is not lawful for any of us to eat at the home of anyone else." So the people refrained from that. Then Allah revealed ﴿There is no blame upon the blind, nor upon the lame, nor upon the sick...﴾ up to His saying: ﴿or from that whose keys you possess﴾, which is the man who appoints another man to look after his property. And Allah permitted them to eat from that food, dates, and to drink milk. And they also used to feel uneasy about a man eating food alone until someone else was with him. So Allah permitted them, saying: ﴿There is no blame upon you for eating together or separately﴾.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Dahhak that he said: Before the Prophet (ﷺ) was sent, the people of Madinah would not share their food with a blind person, a sick person, or a lame person who could not compete for the food. So this was revealed as a concession for them to eat together.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Abu Dawud in his *Marasil*, Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi reported from al-Zuhri that he was asked about His saying ﴿There is no blame upon the blind﴾: "Why were the blind, the lame and the sick mentioned here?" He said: "ʿUbayd Allah ibn ʿAbd Allah informed me that the Muslims, when they went out to fight, would leave their disabled behind, and they would hand them the keys to their doors, saying: 'We have made lawful for you to eat from what is in our houses.' But they felt uneasy about this, saying: 'We will not enter them while they are absent.' So Allah revealed this verse as a concession for them."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatadah that he said: This tribe of the sons of Kinanah ibn Khuzaymah would see one of them feeling it a disgrace to eat alone in the Jahiliyyah. Even if a man was driving a herd of she-camels and was hungry, he would not eat until he found someone to eat and drink with him. So Allah revealed ﴿There is no blame upon you for eating together or separately﴾.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from ʿIkrimah and Abu Salih, who both said: When a guest came to the Ansar, they would not eat until the guest ate with them. So this was revealed as a concession for them.

al-Thaʿlabi reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding the verse: He said: "al-Harith went out to fight with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and left Khalid ibn Yazid in charge of his family. Khalid felt uneasy about eating from his food, and he was in hardship, so this was revealed."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatadah regarding His saying ﴿or your friends﴾: "If you enter the house of your friend without consulting him, and then eat from his food without his permission, there is no harm in that."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Zayd regarding His saying ﴿or your friends﴾: "This is something that has ended. It was only at the beginning, when they had no doors and the curtains were let down. A man might enter a house with no one in it, and he might find food and be hungry, so Allah permitted him to eat it." And he said: "That ended in the day when houses have their people in them. When they leave, they lock up, so that has ended."

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shuʿab* (*The Branches of Faith*) reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying ﴿So when you enter houses, greet one another as a greeting from Allah...﴾ He says: "When you enter your houses, greet one another, ﴿a greeting from near Allah﴾, which is *al-Salam* (peace), because it is one of the names of Allah, and it is the greeting of the people of Paradise."

al-Bukhari, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh reported through the route of Abu al-Zubayr from Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah that he said: "When you enter upon your family, greet them with a greeting from Allah, blessed and good."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who declared it authentic, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shuʿab* reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying ﴿So greet one another﴾ that he said: "It is the mosque: when you enter it, say: 'Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of Allah.'"

Ibn Abi Shaybah and al-Bukhari in *al-Adab al-Mufrad* reported from Ibn ʿUmar that he said: "When one enters a house that is not inhabited, or a mosque, let him say: 'Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of Allah.'"

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 24, verse 58–61 (part 1 of 3):

When He, glory be to Him, had finished mentioning the proofs of monotheism that He had mentioned, He returned to what He had been discussing concerning seeking permission (istidhan), and mentioned it here in a more specific manner, saying: ﴿O you who have believed, let those whom your right hands possess ask permission of you﴾. The address is to the believers, and the believing women are included in it by way of precedence (taghlib), as in other addresses.

The scholars said: this verse is specific to certain times. They differed regarding the meaning of His saying ﴿let them ask permission of you﴾ according to several opinions. The first is that it is abrogated (mansukhah); this was said by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the command in it is for recommendation (nadb), not for obligation (wujub). It was also said: that was obligatory at the time when they had no doors for their houses, and if the situation returns, the obligation returns; this was related by al-Mahdawi from Ibn 'Abbas.

It was also said: the command here is for obligation, the verse is muhkamah (not abrogated), and its ruling is established for men and women. Al-Qurtubi said: this is the view of most of the people of knowledge.

Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami said: it is specific to women. Ibn 'Umar said: it is specific to men, not women.

By His saying ﴿those whom your right hands possess﴾ is meant the slaves, male and female. By "those who have not reached puberty (al-hulm)" is meant the children, ﴿among you﴾, i.e., among the free. The meaning of ﴿three times﴾ is three periods in the day and night, and the expression "times" (al-marrat) is used for periods because the basis of the obligation of seeking permission is the coincidence of those periods with the passing of those seeking permission in upon those addressed, not the periods themselves. The accusative of "three times" is as a temporal adverbial (zarf zamani), i.e., three periods. Then He explained those periods by His saying ﴿before the prayer of dawn﴾ etc. Or it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), i.e., three acts of seeking permission. Abu Hayyan preferred this, saying: "The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿three times﴾ is three acts of seeking permission, because when you say 'I struck you three times' nothing is understood from it except three strikes." It is rebutted that the apparent meaning here is set aside because of the stated context, which is the explanation by the three periods.

Al-Hasan and Abu 'Amr, in one narration, read (al-hulm) with a sukun on the lam, and the rest read it with a damma. Al-Akhfash said: "al-hulm" is from halama al-rajul (with a fatha on the lam), and from al-hulm comes halura (with a damma on the lam), yahlumu (with a kasra on the lam). Then He, glory be to Him, explained the three times, saying: ﴿before the prayer of dawn﴾, because it is the time of rising from the beds, removing sleeping clothes, and putting on waking clothes, and one may sleep naked, or in a state in which one does not like others to see him. Its position is in the accusative as a substitute (badal) for (three); it may also be in the nominative position, as the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "they are from before". His saying ﴿and when you put off your clothes at midday﴾ is conjoined to the position of ﴿before the prayer of dawn﴾; the (min) in ﴿from midday﴾ is for explanation (bayan), or in the sense of (fi), or in the sense of (li). The meaning: when you put off your clothes that you wear during the day because of the intense heat of midday, which is at the middle of the day, for they may strip off their clothes for the sake of the afternoon nap (qaylulah).

Then He mentioned the third period, saying ﴿and after the night prayer (al-'isha')﴾, because it is the time of stripping off clothes and of being alone with the family. Then He, glory be to Him, summarized these periods after the detail, saying: ﴿three times of privacy (awrat) for you﴾. The majority read ﴿three awrat﴾ with the nominative of "three", and Hamzah and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read it in the accusative as a substitute for (﴿three times﴾).

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the substitution is valid only by supposing "times of three awrat", so the first noun was omitted and the second put in its place. It is possible that he made the very "three times" the very "three awrat" for emphasis. It is also permissible that "three awrat" is a substitute for the periods mentioned, i.e., before the prayer of dawn etc. It may be in the accusative by an implied verb, i.e., "I mean" or the like. As for the nominative, it is as the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "they are three."

Abu Hatim said: the accusative is weak and rejected. Al-Kisa'i said: "three awrat" is in the nominative as the subject of the beginning, and the predicate is what follows it. He said: "the awrat are the hours in which nakedness occurs." Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is "let them ask permission of you at the times of three awrat", so the first noun was omitted and the second put in its place. "Awrat" is the plural of "awrah", and awrah in origin means a defect; then it became dominant for a defect in what requires protection and whose covering is obligatory, i.e., they are three times in which the covering is defective.

Al-A'mash read ('awarat) with a fatha on the waw, and this is the dialect of Hudhayl and Tamim, for they put a fatha on the 'ayn of (fa'alat), whether it is waw or ya', and from it is the poet's saying:

"Brother of the bayadat, going in the morning, yawning, gentle in wiping the two shoulders, swimming."

And his saying:

"Father of the bayadat, going in the morning or going far away, hasty, one with provision and one without provision."

And ﴿for you﴾ is connected to an omitted element which is an attribute (sifah) of "three awrat", i.e., "existing for you". The sentence is resumed (mustanafah), brought to explain the reason for the obligation of seeking permission: ﴿There is no sin on you or on them after them﴾, i.e., there is no sin on the slaves or on the children in entering without seeking permission, because there is no cause that makes it obligatory, such as disobeying the command and looking upon the awrat.

The meaning of "after them" is: after each one of these three awrat, which are the times interspersed between each two of them. This sentence is resumed, establishing the command to seek permission in those states specifically. It is also possible that it is in the nominative position as an attribute of "three awrat" according to the nominative reading.

Abu al-Baqa' said: "after them" means after their seeking permission in them, then the preposition and its object were omitted, leaving "after their seeking permission", then the verbal noun, which is "seeking permission", and the connected pronoun to it, were omitted. It was rejected: there is no need for this supposition he mentioned; rather the meaning is: there is no sin on you, nor on them, i.e., the slaves, the female slaves, and the children, in not seeking permission after these mentioned times. The nominative of ﴿circulating (tawwafun)﴾ is as the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "they are circulating among you", and the sentence is resumed, explaining the excuse permitted for leaving off seeking permission.

Al-Farra' said: this is like your saying in speech: "they are your servants and circulating among you." He also permitted the accusative of "circulating" because it is indefinite, while the pronoun in "upon you" is definite. The Basrans do not permit it to be a circumstantial state (hal) of the two pronouns, the one in "upon you" and the one in "some of you", because the governing elements differ.

The meaning of "circulating upon you" is: they circulate upon you. From it is the hadith about the cat: "It is only one of those who circulate upon you, or the female circulators." That is, they are your servants, so there is no harm in their entering upon you at other than these times without permission. The meaning of ﴿some of you upon some﴾ is: some of you circulate, or one circulates, upon others. This sentence is either a substitute for what precedes it or an emphasis of it. The meaning is that each of you circulates upon his companion: slaves upon masters and masters upon slaves. From it is the poet's saying:

"When we struck the nab' (tree) with the nab', some of it upon some, its branches refused to be broken."

Ibn Abi 'Abla read ("circulating") in the accusative as a circumstantial state, as was mentioned earlier from al-Farra'. He, glory be to Him, permitted entering at times other than these three without permission only because it was the custom that they did not uncover their awrat at other times. The reference in His saying ﴿Thus Allah makes clear to you the verses﴾ is to the verbal noun of the verb that follows it, as in the other places in the Mighty Book, i.e., like that clarification, Allah makes clear to you the signs indicating what He has legislated for you of rulings, and Allah is Knowing, Wise: abundant in knowledge of the known things, and abundant in wisdom in His acts.

﴿And when the children among you reach puberty (al-hulm)﴾: here He, glory be to Him, explained the ruling for free children when they reach puberty, after He had explained earlier the ruling for children who have not reached puberty, that there is no sin on them in leaving off seeking permission apart from the three periods. So He said: ﴿then let them ask permission﴾, meaning those who have reached puberty, when they enter upon you, ﴿as those before them asked permission﴾. The kaf is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, i.e., "permission as those before them asked permission", and the relative pronoun is an expression for those to whom it was said ﴿Do not enter houses other than your houses until you have sought intimacy and greeted their people﴾ [al-Nur: 27], and so on.

The meaning: these who have reached puberty seek permission at all times, as those before them asked permission among the adults who were commanded to seek permission without exception. Then He repeated what preceded for emphasis, saying: ﴿Thus Allah makes clear to you His verses, and Allah is Knowing, Wise.﴾ Al-Hasan read (al-hulm) and omitted the damma because it is heavy.

Ata' said: it is obligatory upon people to seek permission when they have reached puberty, whether free or slaves. Al-Zuhri said: a man seeks permission to enter upon his mother, and this verse was revealed in this meaning.

By "the women who are past child-bearing (al-qawa'id min al-nisa')" are meant the old women who have ceased from menstruation and child-bearing due to old age. Its singular is qa'id without a ha', so that its omission indicates that it is the sitting of old age, as they say: "imra'ah hamil" (a woman pregnant), so that the omission of the ha' indicates that it is the carrying of pregnancy; and it is said: "qa'idah fi baytiha" and "hamilah 'ala zahriha". Al-Zajjaj said: they are those who have ceased from marriage.

This is the meaning of His saying ﴿who do not hope for marriage﴾, i.e., they do not hope for it because of their old age. Abu 'Ubaydah said: those who have ceased from child-bearing, but this is not correct, because a woman may cease from child-bearing and still be a subject of enjoyment.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned the ruling for the women past child-bearing, saying: ﴿there is no sin upon them if they put off their clothing﴾, i.e., the garments that are over the surface of the body such as the outer cloak (jilbab) and the like, nor the garments that cover the specific nakedness. It is permitted for them because people's desires turn away from them, as men have no desire for them. So Allah, glory be to Him, permitted them what He did not permit to others. Then He excepted one state from their states, saying: ﴿without displaying adornment (ghayra mutabarrijat bi-zinah)﴾, i.e., not displaying the adornment which they were commanded to conceal in His saying: ﴿and not display their adornment﴾ [al-Nur: 31]. The meaning: without intending by putting off the outer garments to display their adornment, and not exposing themselves to adornment so that men would look at them.

Tabarruj means uncovering and appearing to the eyes, and from it comes ﴿fortified towers﴾ [al-Nisa': 78], and the towers of the sky, and from it the saying: "a ship barijah", i.e., with no covering over it. ﴿And that they refrain is better for them﴾, i.e., that they leave off putting off the garments, so that is better for them than putting them off.

'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Ibn 'Abbas read ("that they put off some of their garments") with the addition of (min). Ibn Mas'ud read ("and that they refrain") without a sin. ﴿And Allah is Hearing, Knowing﴾, abundant in hearing and knowledge, or eloquent in both.

﴿There is no blame upon the blind, nor blame upon the lame, nor blame upon the sick﴾: The people of knowledge differed regarding this verse: is it muhkamah or mansukhah? A group of scholars held the first, and a group the second.

It was said that when the Muslims went out to fight, they left behind their disabled persons, and they would hand over to them the keys of their doors and say to them: "We have permitted you to eat from what is in our houses." They were scrupulous about that and said: "We will not enter it while they are absent." So this verse was revealed as a concession to them. The meaning of the verse is the removal of blame from the disabled in eating from the houses of their relatives, or the houses of those who hand over the key to them when they go out to fight.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 24, verses 58–61 (part 2 of 3):

Al-Nahhas said: This view is among the finest of what has been transmitted concerning the verse, because of what it contains from the Companions and the Successors regarding *tawqif* (a report that the matter was determined by revelation or by the Prophet's explicit statement). It has also been said that those mentioned were refraining from eating with healthy people, out of fear of their disgust at them and fear of being harmed by their actions, so this was revealed. It has also been said that God lifted the burden from the blind regarding the obligations that require sight, and from the lame regarding the obligations that require full ability to walk in a way that cannot be performed with lameness, and from the sick regarding what sickness causes to be dropped. It has also been said that the intended "burden" lifted from these people is the burden of going out to war, meaning: there is no blame on these people for remaining behind from the expedition. It has also been said that when a man brought one of these disabled people into his house and found nothing in it to feed them, he would take them to the houses of his relatives, and the disabled would feel uneasy about this, so this was revealed.

The meaning of His words ﴿Nor on yourselves﴾ is: upon you, and upon those among the believers who are like you, that you eat yourselves and those with you. This is the beginning of a new statement, meaning: nor upon you, O people. The summary is that the lifting of the burden from the blind, the lame and the sick, if it refers to eating with the healthy or entering their houses, then ﴿Nor on yourselves﴾ is connected to what precedes it; but if the lifting of the burden from those people refers to the obligations that require sight, the absence of lameness and the absence of sickness, then His words ﴿Nor on yourselves﴾ are a new statement not connected to what precedes it. The meaning of ﴿from your houses﴾ is the houses in which their property and their families are, and so it includes the houses of children. This is what the exegetes said, because they are included in the houses of the parents, since the house of a man's son is his house. For this reason, He did not mention the houses of children, and mentioned the houses of fathers, the houses of mothers and those after them.

Al-Nahhas said: Some people objected to this and said: This is an arbitrary imposition upon the Book of God. Rather, the more apparent position is that the son should be excluded from these. The answer to this objection is that the status of children in relation to parents is not less than the status of parents in relation to children; rather, parents have greater special right over the property of their children, due to the hadith "You and your property belong to your father," and the hadith "A man's child is part of his earnings." Then God, glory be to Him, here mentioned the houses of brothers and sisters, indeed the houses of paternal uncles and aunts, indeed the houses of maternal uncles and aunts. So how does He, glory be to Him, remove the burden of eating from the houses of these people and not remove it from the houses of children? Some scholars restricted the permissibility of eating from the houses of these people to their permission. Others said: permission is not a condition. It was said: this applies when the food is available for the taking, but if it is stored away from them, it is not permitted for them to eat it.

Then He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿or what you own the keys to﴾, meaning the houses over which you have the right of disposal with the permission of their owners. This is like agents, slaves and treasurers, for they have the right of disposal over the houses of the one who has permitted them to enter his house and given them its keys. It was said: what is intended by it is the houses of slaves.

The majority read *malaktum* with a fatha on the *mim* and a light *lam*. Sa'id ibn Jubayr read it with a damma on the *mim* and a kasra on the *lam* with shadda. He also read *mafatīḥahu* with a *yā'* between the *tā'* and the *ḥā'*. Qatada read *mafātiḥahu* in the singular; *al-mafātiḥ* is the plural of *mafataḥ*, and *al-mafātīḥ* is the plural of *miftāḥ*.

Or [what you own the keys to] your friend, meaning: there is no blame upon you that you eat from the houses of your friend even if there is no kinship between you and him, for a friend in most cases permits his friend to do so, and his soul is content with it. The word *ṣadīq* (friend) is applied to the singular and the plural. Among its examples is the verse of Jarir:

*They called to passion, then shot our hearts*
*with the arrows of enemies, and they are friends.*

Similar to it are *al-'adū* (enemy), *al-khalīṭ* (close companion), *al-qaṭīn* (companion) and *al-'ashīr* (intimate companion), which are all used in the singular and plural.

Then He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿There is no blame upon you to eat﴾ from your houses ﴿together or separately﴾. The accusative of *jamī'an* (together) and *ashtātan* (separately) is by way of circumstantial state (*ḥāl*). *Al-ashtāt* is the plural of *shatt*, and *shatt* is the verbal noun meaning dispersal; one says *shatta al-qawm*, meaning they dispersed. This sentence is a new statement containing the explanation of another ruling of the same kind as what precedes it, meaning: there is no blame upon you to eat from your houses together or dispersed. Some Arabs would refrain from eating alone until they found someone to eat with, and some Arabs would not eat except with a guest. Among its examples is the verse of Hatim:

*When you prepare the provisions, seek for it a companion,*
*for I do not eat it alone.*

﴿So when you enter houses﴾: this begins the explanation of another etiquette with which God trained His servants, meaning: when you enter houses other than the houses already mentioned, ﴿greet one another﴾, meaning greet those among them who are like yourselves. It was said: what is meant is the houses mentioned earlier.

According to the first view, al-Hasan and al-Nakha'i said: these are mosques, and what is meant is: greet those in them of your kind. If there is no one in the mosques, it was said one should say: "Peace be upon the Messenger of God." It was said one should say: "Peace be upon us," intending the angels. It was said one should say: "Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of God."

A group of the Companions and the Successors held the second view, namely that they are the houses mentioned earlier. It was also said: what is meant by "houses" here is every house, inhabited and otherwise. So one greets the inhabitants of an inhabited house, and as for an uninhabited house, one greets oneself.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: The view of generality regarding the houses is the correct one. The accusative of *taḥiyyatan* (a greeting) is as a verbal noun, because His words *fa-sallimū* (so greet) mean *fa-ḥayyū* (so salute), meaning a greeting established from God, that is, God has greeted you with it.

Al-Farra' said: God has commanded you to do it, in obedience to Him. Then He described this greeting, saying *mubārakatan*, meaning abundant in blessing and goodness, lasting in both respects; *ṭayyibatan*, meaning the listener's soul is content with it. It was said: it is good and beautiful.

Al-Zajjaj said: God, glory be to Him, informed us that the greeting is blessed and good because of the reward and recompense in it. Then God, glory be to Him, repeated and said: ﴿Thus God makes clear to you the verses﴾, as an emphasis on what came before.

We have already mentioned that the demonstrative *dhālika* (thus) refers to the verbal noun of the verb. His words ﴿so that you may understand﴾ are a justification for that clarification, with the hope that you will comprehend the verses of God and understand their meanings.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Muqatil ibn Hayyan who said: "It reached us that a man from the Ansar and his wife Asma' bint Murshida prepared food for the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace. Asma' said: 'O Messenger of God, how ugly this is! Their servant enters upon the woman and her husband while they are in one garment, without permission.' So God revealed concerning that: ﴿O you who have believed, let those whom your right hands possess ask your permission, and those who have not reached puberty among you﴾." He said: meaning the slaves, male and female, and ﴿those who have not reached puberty among you﴾, he said: from your free men and women.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Suddi concerning this verse that he said: Some of the Companions of the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, liked to have intercourse with their wives at these times so they could perform the ritual bath and then go out to prayer. So God commanded them to order the slaves and the boys not to enter upon them at those times except with permission.

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Tha'laba al-Qurazi from 'Abd Allah ibn Suwayd who said: "I asked the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, about the three times of nakedness (*'awrāt*). He said: 'When I put off my clothes after noon, none of the servants who have not reached puberty may come in upon me, nor any free person who has not reached puberty, except with permission. And when I put off my clothes after the night prayer, and before the dawn prayer.'"

'Abd ibn Humayd and al-Bukhari in *al-Adab* transmitted it from 'Abd Allah ibn Suwayd as his own statement.

Ibn Sa'd transmitted something similar from Suwayd ibn al-Nu'man.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shayba, Abu Dawud, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan* transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "Most people have not believed in it, meaning the verse of permission. I used to order this maidservant of mine, a short girl standing at his head, to ask permission to enter upon me."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "People have left three verses without acting upon them: ﴿O you who have believed, let those whom your right hands possess ask your permission﴾; and the verse in Surat al-Nisa' ﴿And when the division is attended by relatives﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:8] and the verse in al-Hujurat ﴿Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of God is the most righteous of you﴾ [al-Hujurat 49:13]."

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in the *Sunan* transmitted from him also concerning the verse, that he said: "If a man is alone with his wife after the night prayer, no child or servant may enter upon him except with his permission until he prays the morning prayer. And if he is alone with his wife at noon, it is similar. They were allowed to enter at other times without permission, and this is His words: ﴿There is no blame upon you or upon them after these times.﴾ As for one who has reached puberty, he may not enter upon a man and his wife except with permission in every circumstance, and this is His words: ﴿And when the children among you reach puberty, let them ask permission as those before them asked.﴾"

Abu Dawud, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in the *Sunan* transmitted with a sound chain through the route of 'Ikrima from him as well: that a man asked him about asking permission during the three nakedness times which God commanded in the Qur'an. Ibn 'Abbas said: "God is Concealing and loves concealment. The people did not have curtains on their doors or screens in their houses, so a servant or a child or an orphan in one's care might suddenly come upon a man while he was with his family. So God commanded them to ask permission during those times of nakedness which God named. Then later God brought curtains, and He expanded provision for them, so they took curtains and took screens. The people thought that this had sufficed them from the asking of permission they had been commanded to do."

Ibn Abi Shayba, al-Bukhari in *al-Adab*, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn 'Umar concerning His words ﴿let those whom your right hands possess ask your permission﴾ that he said: "It applies to males and not to females." There is no basis for this restriction, for looking upon the nakedness at these times, which a person dislikes from males, he likewise dislikes from females.

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Abu Salama ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, from one of the wives of the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, concerning the verse, that she said: "It was revealed concerning women, that they should ask permission to enter upon us."

al-Hakim transmitted and authenticated it from 'Ali concerning the verse, that he said: "The women, for men ask permission."

al-Firyabi transmitted from Musa ibn Abi Shayba who said: "I asked al-Sha'bi about this verse: 'Is it abrogated?' He said: 'No.'"

Sa'id ibn Mansur, al-Bukhari in *al-Adab*, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from 'Ata' that he asked Ibn 'Abbas: "Should I ask permission to enter upon my sister?" He said: "Yes." I said: "She is in my care, I spend on her, and she is with me in the house. Should I ask permission to enter upon her?" He said: "Yes, for God says: ﴿let those whom your right hands possess ask your permission, and those who have not reached puberty among you﴾, the verse, so these were not commanded to ask permission except at these three times of nakedness." He said: ﴿And when the children among you reach puberty, let them ask permission as those before them asked﴾. So asking permission is obligatory upon every creature of God, all of them."

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan* transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud who said: "Upon you is asking permission to enter upon your mothers."

Sa'id ibn Mansur and al-Bukhari in *al-Adab* transmitted from him who said: "A man asks permission to enter upon his father, his mother, his brother and his sister."

Ibn Abi Shayba and al-Bukhari in *al-Adab* transmitted from Jabir something similar to it.

[p. 1028]

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 24, verses 58–61 (part 3 of 3):

Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Sunan* reported from ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yasār that **"a man said: 'O Messenger of Allah, shall I seek permission to enter upon my mother?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'I am with her in the house.' He said: 'Seek permission to enter upon her.' He said: 'I am her servant. Shall I seek permission to enter upon her every time I enter?' He said: 'Would you like to see her naked?' He said: 'No.' He said: 'Then seek permission to enter upon her.'"** And it is *mursal* (a report whose chain omits the Companion).

Ibn Abi Shaybah reported something similar from Zayd ibn Aslam, that a man asked the Prophet (ﷺ), and it is also *mursal*.

Abu Dawud and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Sunan* reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ﴿And tell the believing women to lower their gaze﴾ [al-Nur: 31], the verse, that it abrogated (*naskh*, abrogation) and made an exception from it: ﴿And women past child-bearing who have no hope of marriage﴾.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Sunan* reported from him (Ibn ʿAbbas) that he said: "It refers to the woman for whom there is no blame if she sits in her house wearing her *dir* (a shift) and *khimar* (headscarf), and she places over herself the *jilbab* (outer garment), so long as she does not display herself in what Allah dislikes." And this is His saying: ﴿So there is no blame upon them if they remove their garments without displaying adornment﴾.
